‘Not-quite primordial’ black holes may explain baffling JWST discovery

New Scientist September 03, 2026

There may have been black holes in the early universe before the first stars, and a group of theoretical physicists has proposed a new way to explain how they could have formed using the heat of the cosmic microwave background. The idea may be a better explanation for the “little red dots” identified by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) – distant galaxies that seem to host surprisingly large numbers of astonishingly ancient black holes.

“James Webb is discovering many more black holes than most of us theorists predicted in our most optimistic models,” says Priyamvada Natarajan at Yale University. “The universe is just littered with black holes.”

An existing idea is that primordial black holes formed in violent space-time spasms in the early universe before any stars appeared. But these violent spasms are hard to reconcile with the milder ripples that astronomers see in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint light left over from the primordial universe. Theorists have had to propose complicated new physical laws to make the explanation fit.

Advertisement

We may have found a surprisingly nearby cluster of primordial stars

Wenzer Qin and Neal Weiner at New York University and Soubhik Kumar at Tufts University in Massachusetts realised there was another option. They began by assuming milder ripples of dark matter moved through the early universe, and argued that large black holes would be able to form inside clumps of this dark matter, with the hot CMB keeping gas and dust from collapsing into smaller ones instead.

They call these black holes “not-quite-primordial” and argue they provide an explanation for the black holes spotted via the JWST that doesn’t require drastic changes to cosmologists’ picture of the early universe.

The researchers reached out to Natarajan, a theoretical astrophysicist, to help confirm their logic.

“This is a case where you could actually have a black hole forming before the stars. And that I found really exciting,” says Natarajan.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“What’s nice about the model is that it invokes less speculative physics than traditional primordial black hole physics,” says John Regan at Maynooth University, Ireland, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Having says that, what we need ultimately will be concrete observations. We’ll need to see some ultra-early-Universe signatures of black holes, be that from gravitational waves or from some future CMB observations, to see if black holes truly existed at the very earliest times.”

Qin and collaborators are getting ready for those observations. Their next step will be to simulate the new process and see what it implies about the spectrum of light that should be emitted from around a not-quite-primordial black hole. They can then compare these predictions more closely to data from JWST.

They are also looking forward to future satellite telescopes like the proposed Primordial Inflation Explorer (PIXIE), which should be able to measure the CMB spectrum well enough to find evidence for their proposal.

Fermat’s last theorem formalised by AI agents in just 11 days

New Scientist September 05, 2026

AI company Anthropic has created a formalised proof of Fermat’s last theorem. It took just 11 days for a group of AI agents to complete the task, confirming that the human-found proof proposed in the 1990s is correct.

Fermat’s last theorem puzzled mathematicians for centuries until it was proved in 1995 by Andrew Wiles. It states that there are no whole numbers a, b, and c that satisfy the equation aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ, where n is a whole number greater than 2.

The theorem, though easy to state, was fiendishly difficult to prove. Mathematician Pierre de Fermat posed the puzzle in the 17th century and famously alluded to a proof that he claimed to have discovered, saying that it was too large to fit in the margins of the textbook he was writing in.

Advertisement

Mathematics is undergoing the biggest change in its history

Many mathematicians tried and failed to find a proof. Wiles worked on the problem for seven years in secret before announcing his breakthrough in 1993. Proofs often involve lengthy logical arguments that build on each other. If a single step contains an error, then the whole thing can collapse. This happened to Wiles when a flaw was found in his proof, which took him and collaborator Richard Taylor around a year to fix.

Formalising mathematical theorems is a solution to this problem. It takes them out of the realm of pen and paper, and puts them into a configuration – computer code – that allows machines to grapple with them, methodically working through the logic and exposing any flaws. There are already 2 million lines of formalised mathematics stored in a central repository called Mathlib.

Earlier this year, a conference of AI experts, computer scientists and mathematicians was held in London by Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London, who was – until Anthropic’s announcement – working on a five-year project to formalise Wiles and Taylor’s 100-page proof in a programming language called Lean, so that it can be formally checked for correctness and used as a foundation for further research.

Buzzard said at the time that when his project began he was confident of success, but that recent advances in AI had convinced him that the project would be complete much faster than he previously thought possible. Anthropic’s announcement has now overtaken that effort and wrapped up the problem.

Buzzard said in a statement published by Anthropic that the company’s proof leaves “no assumptions other than the axioms of mathematics”. In short, the problem is solved.

Mathematicians put AI to work on Fermat’s last theorem

“Along the way we see autoformalisation of algebra, harmonic analysis, geometry and number theory, and we learn that AI autoformalisation artefacts are now robust enough to be built upon; the proof is multi-layered,” said Buzzard. “If the automatic formalisation of FLT is possible now, then we have taken a big step towards automatic formalisation of the modern mathematical literature.”

In its blog post announcing the result, Anthropic wrote that its Claude model worked continuously and autonomously for 11 days to write the proof. Numerous separate AI agents were involved, with different tasks, like tackling smaller chunks of the theorem, being assigned to each.

Free newsletter

Human experts occasionally issued “high-level instructions” to keep the work on track, the company says. Several times, the agents “lost track of the project’s state and stopped collaborating effectively”. Interestingly, the company said that success came after it began using a tool designed for human mathematical collaboration called Prove2Me, which helped different agents track their work and decide on next tasks.

Anthropic’s formalisation runs to 13 million lines of Lean and covers roughly 29,500 intermediate theorems that were necessary stepping stones towards completing the overall work. That makes the proof over five times the current size of all previous work on Mathlib, which also makes it the largest Lean proof ever written.

How worried should we be about the invasive mosquitoes in the UK?

New Scientist September 04, 2026

Aedes aegypti mosquitoes and larvae – which can transmit infections like dengue, chikungunya and Zika virus – have been found breeding in the UK.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) announced on 3 September that the species had been detected at residential properties in east London. This marks the fourth time it has been discovered in the UK in recent years, and the first time it has been found breeding.

Genetic trick to make mosquitoes malaria resistant passes key test

The mosquitoes are usually found in more tropical climes. So, is this a result of climate change? How concerned should we be? Here’s what you need to know.

Advertisement

A. aegypti mosquitoes are native to North Africa, but can be found in tropical and temperate regions around the world, including parts of Europe. Although the species has been seen in the UK before, this is the first time these mosquitoes have been found breeding in the country.

The species can transmit many different pathogens, including the dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika viruses. It commonly feeds at dusk and dawn, indoors and in shady areas.

According to the UKHSA, the mosquitoes and larvae were found breeding in residential properties in east London. They were spotted and reported under the government’s Mosquito Watch scheme, which aims to detect the presence of invasive mosquitoes.

The UKHSA said the larvae have been destroyed and promised the area will be monitored closely to eradicate any further mosquitoes and larvae that might emerge.

The UKHSA insists the threat to public health remains very low. There is no evidence the A. aegypti mosquitoes found in London have transmitted any infections to people, and so far no more mosquitoes or larvae have been found in nearby public areas.

César López-Camacho at the University of Oxford said in a statement to the Science Media Centre that the discovery of their presence should be seen as an “early warning rather than an immediate public-health threat”.

It is worth noting that the UK is home to many species of native mosquitoes, but these generally don’t carry serious infections, and are largely an annoyance rather than a public-health threat.

Jolyon Medlock at the UKHSA said in a statement that the mosquitoes were likely to be “accidental importations”, having “hitchhiked” in vehicles, in suitcases or via imported plants.

The UK has just had its hottest summer on record. London has seen some of the highest temperatures in the country, as heatwaves are usually amplified in cities due to the urban heat island effect.

That may mean the mosquitoes have been able to successfully breed over the summer months this year. But Medlock said the UK’s climate is still too cold overall to enable the mosquitoes to breed over the long term – for now.

Free newsletter

Mosquitoes are expanding their range north as the climate warms. Warmer weather also increases the rate at which viruses replicate in an insect’s body.

That means mosquito-borne viruses are rapidly becoming more common in Europe as the continent warms. In late August, French authorities reported cases of locally transmitted dengue, West Nile and chikungunya viruses across the country, including Paris.

And a study published earlier this year found that the Asian tiger mosquito, another invasive mosquito species in Europe, can transmit chikungunya over several months of the year on the continent. The study authors said Europe’s rapid rate of warming was enabling virus transmission to become more widespread across the region.

Over time, the threat of mosquito-borne disease to the British public is also expected to rise. Last year, West Nile virus was detected in the UK for the first time in mosquitoes in Nottinghamshire. For now, authorities hope to keep invasive mosquitoes out of the country for as long as possible to prevent disease transmission.

When engineers struggled to make 3D printer nozzles narrow enough for their needs, they turned to nature and found the proboscis of a female mosquito had exactly the properties they needed

For most people in the UK, a mosquito bite is an annoyance but nothing to worry about. It will usually produce a red, itchy swelling that will subside within a few days. If you develop a fever or become unwell, and have recently travelled to a location where dengue, chikungunya or Zika is circulating, you should seek medical attention.

Scientist say it is important to minimise the chance of mosquitoes breeding in the UK, to try to prevent invasive species gaining a foothold on UK shores. A. aegypti mosquitoes are well adapted to human environments and can breed in small quantities of standing water, so the most important action people can take is to eliminate, as far as possible, any standing water around the home. That could include emptying water trays under houseplants, clearing rainfall from containers, keeping lids on rain barrels, washing out pet bowls and flower vases regularly and keeping shower areas as clean and dry as possible between use.

If you spot a mosquito in the UK, you can report it to the Mosquito Watch scheme.

Super El Niño could have unexpected effect on UK winter

New Scientist September 04, 2026

The unprecedented El Niño gathering strength in the Pacific Ocean could upend forecasts for UK weather this winter, bringing continuously wet, stormy conditions until spring.

El Niño is a natural climate phase that happens when easterly trade winds weaken, allowing the warm water they had piled up in the western Pacific to wash back across the central and eastern Pacific. This swathe of warm water heats the atmosphere and weakens the winds further in a feedback loop.

The phenomenon’s impact on the weather in the UK and north-western Europe is notoriously tricky to predict, because weather patterns in this region are strongly affected by weather phenomena in the North Atlantic.

Advertisement

Under an El Niño event of normal intensity, the UK is more likely to experience wetter, windier, stormier weather in the late autumn and early winter, potentially followed by a colder, drier end to winter.

5 graphs that show how the record-breaking El Niño will affect the world

However, the sheer size of the current El Niño – already one of the largest on record and still intensifying – could mean that the end of winter and start of spring continue to be wet and stormy, says Adam Scaife at the Met Office, the UK’s national weather service, who leads the agency’s long-range forecasting.

“We found that the big events show a slightly different response over the Atlantic,” he says. El Niños usually increase the likelihood of cold easterly winds prevailing over the UK during late winter. But a very strong El Niño may reverse that trend, leading to prevailing westerlies late in the season. The weather under those conditions is “still cold, but it’s not extreme”, he says.

Scaife first reported this effect of strong El Niños in a 2006 research paper he co-wrote with Thomas Toniazzo, now at NORCE Research in Norway. The study assessed the weather in the North Atlantic during El Niño years and found that very strong El Niños produced this mild and wet pattern in late winter.

Free newsletter

The El Niño in 1997-1998, for example, was one of the most powerful on record. It saw high pressure developing in the North Atlantic to the west of the UK over the late winter, leading to westerly prevailing winds that blew milder, wetter, stormier air over the UK and northern Europe. The same pattern appeared in the 2015-2016 El Niño, when the UK had one of its mildest and wettest winters on record.

“We think that’s a real effect [of strong El Niños],” says Scaife. “We’re looking for that at the end of this winter.”

A prolonged wet and stormy winter could saturate soils and make parts of the UK more susceptible to severe flooding. But it would also offer an opportunity to replenish reservoirs and groundwater after an exceptionally dry summer.

Intense fires are already burning in Indonesia, and there could be much worse to come as the Super El Niño ramps up

However, Scaife warns it is very difficult to tease apart the effect of a strong El Niño compared with that of a standard-strength one, in part because there are only a few very strong events in the historical record for which we have good data.

El Niños – and their opposite pattern, La Niñas – also vary hugely from year to year and decade to decade, so it can be fiendishly difficult to separate out a signal from the noise in the system. What’s more, it is very difficult to predict weather patterns months in advance, and there is still huge uncertainty over what late winter will hold for the UK.

This week, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) warned that the El Niño is still intensifying in the tropical Pacific and is set to be the largest on record, fuelling drought, floods and extreme temperatures around the world. In most cases, a stronger El Niño brings more pronounced impacts globally, such as severe drought in Australia, the Amazon and Indonesia, and heavy rain in parts of South America, East Africa and the southern US.

The pattern is likely to peak in November, but will persist until at least February 2027, the WMO said, bringing extreme impacts that will last well into next year.

Lucid dreams induced via multisensory stimulation

New Scientist September 04, 2026

Scientist Tobi Matzek has breathed underwater, explored outer space and even transformed into a dragon – in their dreams. “I pulled a purple-and-white pill out of my pocket and swallowed it, and immediately, I had purple dragon wings,” they say.

These adventures occurred during lucid dreams, when a person is aware they are dreaming and can often influence what happens. Matzek, at the University of Montreal in Canada, has now found that lucid dreams can be induced in some people via cognitive and multisensory stimulation.

Epic dreaming is leaving people exhausted and distressed

Fascinated by the concept of lucid dreams, Matzek and their colleagues recruited 60 adults with no known health conditions who had experienced at least one lucid dream before. The frequency of these dreams varied, with 15 of the individuals experiencing them less than once a year and others having lucid dreams several times a week.

Advertisement

The participants came into one of three labs – in Italy, Canada or the Netherlands – on two mornings to nap for up to 2.5 hours. Immediately before each nap, they were given half an hour of lucidity training.

This involved lying in bed with their eyes closed while the ZMax EEG headband, a sleep-tracking device, delivered red-light flashes, played a short melody and administered a few soft vibrations on their forehead.

At the same time, a soundtrack guided them to focus their attention on these sensations and asked them to be aware of any differences between the sensations they were feeling during this experience and what they felt during normal wakefulness.

Free newsletter

“This may train people to pay closer attention to changes in their sensory experience and make them more likely to recognise the odd or inconsistent experiences that occur in dreams and realise ‘I must be dreaming’,” says team member Claudia Picard-Deland, also at the University of Montreal.

During one of the two naps, these sensory stimulations were repeated when the participant entered the rapid eye movement (REM) stage of sleep, when we have our most powerful dreams.

Earlier, the researchers taught the participants to move their eyes from left to right to signal that a lucid dream had started and was ongoing. Overall, just over half of the participants gave this signal while the headset readings confirmed they were asleep, usually in the REM stage. After waking, these participants also reported that they’d had a lucid dream.

“The training led to a relatively high rate of lucid dreaming, even in people who rarely had lucid dreams before,” says Matzek.

Kristoffer Appel at the Institute of Sleep and Dream Technologies in Hamburg, Germany, calls the results “remarkable”. “They suggest that lucidity is far more trainable on short notice than the spontaneous and rare reputation that it usually has,” he says.

People who are terminally ill are commonly reunited with lost loved ones in their dreams and have visions of doors, stairways and light, which are said to help them accept the dying process

The lucid dreams were no more likely to occur during the nap in which the sensory stimulations were re-applied during the REM stage. However, the gap between the participants’ first and last eye signals indicated that they lasted around twice as long in this condition.

Longer lucid dreams could be useful because they are being investigated as a way to boost creativity and problem-solving, and to treat nightmares in people with post-traumatic stress disorder, says Matzek.

However, only about 55 per cent of people have experienced lucid dreams, and it is unclear if this approach can induce them in individuals who have never had one.

bioRxiv DOI: 10.1101/2024.06.21.600133

Nations and big tech to train AI using ‘gold dust’ data from Ukraine

New Scientist September 04, 2026

Global superpowers and giant technology firms are scrambling for real-world data from the war in Ukraine to build next-generation AI models that will empower militaries in future conflicts. Videos of drone strikes and other sensor data are like “gold dust” for training AI, say experts.

Last month, Ukraine signed a deal with the UK to share a vast treasure trove of data collected from drones, cameras and sensors since Russia staged its full-scale invasion. It is claimed that the deal will make the UK the first foreign state to have access to Ukraine’s so-called “Avengers AI” model, which is already being used to identify adversaries and their equipment in real time and slash the time taken to stage attacks.

The UK claims that the first fruits of this deal are about to be tested through a project that is turning buried fibre-optic cables into sensors to detect hostile intrusions at an unnamed UK defence site.

Advertisement

How Ukraine became a drone factory and invented the future of war

Peter Lee at the University of Portsmouth, UK, says the varied data will be immensely valuable in creating a wide range of defence and military tools, which will make both the UK and Ukraine more secure.

“This is the gold dust that allows the UK to enter the autonomous age of drones,” he says. “You can’t really put a price on the data they’re going to get access to. Add up everything that the UK has given to Ukraine over the last several years – this data is worth all of that and more.”

Ukraine flies thousands of drones a day, both in the war zone and penetrating deep into Russia, and has a vast array of sensors on the front line. This data has long been fed into a government department known as Brave1, which analyses it with AI to find strategic weaknesses and opportunities. It feeds that information back to troops on the front line and defence contractors.

Subscriber-only newsletter

AI models can be used to autonomously steer drones to their targets, monitor thousands of video feeds and other sensors for tell-tale signs of adversaries’ movements, or analyse footage of attacks to spot design flaws in military hardware. The models can even plan strikes and pick targets.

Numerous efforts are under way in Ukraine to use AI to eke out an advantage in all sorts of areas, including at the defence ministry’s “A1” organisation – which the Ukrainian government launched with UK government support in March, long before this latest announcement.

Lee says the possibilities are so compelling that it is almost certain that China is doing the same with Russian data, taken from the opposite side of the front line – and they probably had a head start. He thinks that, in the earliest stage of negotiations between Russia and China about military and intelligence support for the invasion, China will have raised the issue of data sharing.

“China understands that data is king when it comes to AI, and that the more data you have, the more powerful your systems are likely to be,” says Lee. “It would be a strategic oversight of grotesque proportions [if China hadn’t sought data].”

Solar-powered ambush drones can wait for targets like land mines

Joe Burton at Lancaster University in the UK says that despite the UK’s support of Ukraine with weapons, training and intelligence since the full-scale invasion, it is unlikely that raw data has been shared on a wide scale until recently. But a deterioration in relations with the US may be an incentive for Ukraine to create stronger ties with other allies.

“The Trump presidency has been very volatile in its approach to Ukraine and, if you’re in [Kyiv], it makes sense to have a broader set of partnerships around AI data, which can help support you in what will probably still be a long-term war,” says Burton. “I would not be surprised if Ukraine are hedging their bets.”

Big technology firms are also getting involved. Ukraine has long worked with AI company Palantir, and signed a data-sharing deal with the firm months before the agreement with the UK was announced. US company Clearview AI’s face-recognition technology has been used to find Russian spies operating in Ukraine, while another US firm, Scale AI, has used satellite data to identify Russian troop movements and detect building damage across Ukraine.

Injuries from the war in Ukraine have forced the country to develop highly advanced prostheses and fit them in record numbers. What can the rest of the world learn from its efforts?

“All these companies are competing for data. If you have access to actual, real, credible battlefield data from Ukraine instead of simulated data that you’re generating in a lab, that’s a big commercial advantage,” says Burton.

In short, if you are pitching your product to states looking for AI tools to protect national security or support their militaries, then having a battle-tested product is a strong selling point.

But despite the vast expansion of data collection, AI analysis and high-tech weapons systems, the day-to-day reality for troops in Ukraine remains a muddy trench, not dissimilar to those dug in the first world war.

“It’s still attritional. It’s still horribly violent. This idea that you can deploy a load of robots to the battlefield and you don’t need to send soldiers into harm’s way, it’s not [happening] in Ukraine,” says Burton.

Christopher Luxon to announce new National Party housing policy

The National Party is promising to increase first home buyers’ access to low-deposit mortgages if elected, which it says will help more buyers into their first homes.

Announcing the policy this morning, leader Christopher Luxon and housing spokesman Chris Bishop said the policy would help National achieve its goal of increasing home ownership rates back to their historical peak when about 74% of households owned their home.

That milestone was reached in the early 1990s.

The home ownership rate has fallen to about 66% today, although the recent housing crash has seen large numbers of first home buyers’ snap up their first homes.

Bishop said National will widen access to 5% deposits by extending the income cap under an existing First Home Loan Scheme to $300,000.

The Government has run the ‘In Reach’ loan scheme since 2003. Rebadged as First Home Loan scheme in 2019, it is currently administered through Kāinga Ora.

Currently, it has an income cap of $95,000 for an individual buyer with no dependents or $150,000 for a loan to multiple buyers or a single buyer with dependents.

National says that lifting the cap to $300,000 reflects the fact that incomes have grown and many young professionals with high earnings are still unable to save for a deposit.

“The scheme’s current income caps are too restrictive and haven’t been updated since 2022,” Bishop said.

“So, right now, a junior doctor on $100,000 can’t access the scheme. Nor can a young couple, like an electrician on $85,000 and a teacher on $78,000, or two friends who have just graduated from police college and are earning $77,000 each.

“The average gross income of first home buyers is around $146,000. That means around half of first home buyers earn over $146,000 now.

“So, while a combined income of $150,000 might sound like a lot of money, the reality is that plenty of young couples now earn more than that but still struggle to save for a 20 per cent deposit while juggling the cost of rent, food, and childcare.

“National’s changes will address those pressures and build on the work we have done in Government to support more people into home ownership,” Bishop said.

National promised to abolish the distinction between single and multiple buyers, creating a single income cap of $300,000 regardless of how many borrowers there are.

The scheme has so far helped over 33,000 households into home ownership and between 1 July 2025 and 30 April 2026 more than 7,700 applications were approved.

National thinks this policy will double the size of the scheme, costing the Crown $4-6 million extra a year — a cost that will be met from existing baselines.

Bishop defended the supply side reforms championed by this Government — much of which was substantially introduced under the last Labour Government.

“Our Government’s reforms have accelerated this success by enabling greater housing supply. We want to continue the momentum, with a vision of returning to peak home ownership rates of around 74 per cent, up from 66 per cent currently.

“National’s Backing First Home Buyers policy will support that vision, alongside a suite of other policies to help Kiwis get ahead. That includes introducing no new taxes, boosting KiwiSaver, extending paid parental leave, implementing a rates cap, and lowering the student loan repayment rate.

“National is sending a clear signal to ambitious young Kiwis that we back them to stay in New Zealand and get into a home of their own. It’s all part of our wider plan to fix the basics and build the future,” Bishop said.

Irish hip-hop group Kneecap have invited Foreign Minister Winston Peters to their New Zealand shows after he described them as “a bunch of low IQ weasels”.

The invitation came after the Belfast trio threw their support behind Green MP Tamatha Paul following her viral “bastard language” comments on a bill that made English an official language earlier this year.

In response, Peters took to social media platform X on Friday, calling the band “low IQ weasels who have no idea about history”.

“We are proud of our country’s history and our foundation English language — which is now an official language thanks to NZ First,” the post read.

“We are not going to sit by and be lectured by some bunch of low IQ weasels who have no idea about history, and even less of an idea about the woke cultural madness they foolishly promote — that goes for the hopeless TikTok politicians in the Green Party spouting that crap too.

“If we are the only ones to stand up for and be proud of our country, our heritage, and our language then so be it — but if this group of try-hard performers don’t like our stance on the English language they should naff off back home.

Kneecap appeared to take the comments in their stride.

In an interview with Te Ao with Moana, group members Moglai Bap and Mo Chara were asked about Peters’ remarks.

“That’s gotta go on the poster surely,” one member responded.

“He’s invited to the party,” the other said.

The trio are coming to New Zealand for two shows at Auckland’s Spark Arena and Wellington’s TSB Arena on February 9 and 10.

Email us

The invitation comes after a turbulent year for the group, with Mo Chara, also known as Liam O’Hanna, facing a terrorism-related charge in the United Kingdom.

He was charged in May last year with displaying a flag of the banned Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah at a November 2024 concert in London under the UK’s 2000 Terrorism Act.

But he walked free from a London court in September after Chief Magistrate Paul Goldspring found a technical error in the timing of the case against him.

The Crown Prosecution Service appealed in January, arguing that Goldspring erred in ruling that the written charge had been filed too late.

A two-judge panel at the High Court then dismissed the appeal, siding with the Chief Magistrate.

Meet Flicket: Bay of Plenty ticketing company powering global events

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

With Flicket, the Cosmic Takeover Tour sold 750,000 tickets across 90 sold-out events across the United States.

Eight years ago, Flicket’s founders thought they were building a simple ticketing tool for a handful of local events.

The Mount Maunganui-based company is now an award-winning exporter and a “major player” in the global events industry, powering events around the world.

Flicket, a digital ticketing, booking and visitor management software provider, was named ASB Bay of Plenty Exporter of the Year last month.

Founded in 2018, the company serves attractions, events and tourism operators around the world, helping manage ticketing, bookings and visitor experiences through a digital platform.

Flicket co-founder, director, and chief technology officer Jimmy Barwell-Smith told the Bay of Plenty Times Flicket was meant to be a “weekend project” with his fellow co-founder Ben Calvert.

“But when we rolled out the product there was so much appetite just from the domestic market, and as we kept doing it, we found that the gap in the market was huge.”

He said Flicket enabled event organisers to become their own ticketing company.

“No one likes ticketing companies. We very much understand that, and everyone’s got horror stories of platforms crashing, not being able to get tickets and information not being clear.”

Flicket was established to challenge traditional ticketing models by giving event organisers greater control over customer data, revenue streams and fan engagement.

“There was so much demand of [event] organisers wanting to know who their fans were, wanting to have better control over how their product was marketed, what data was collected and then build better engagement,” Barwell-Smith said.

“We’re effectively solving the same customer problems from eight years ago, just at a bigger scale now, which is so cool.”

Since launching, Flicket has grown from a New Zealand start-up into an international business, operating in multiple overseas markets.

The company helped power New York Fashion Week and Cosmic Baseball, one of the United States’ fastest-growing touring sports attractions.

It also supported events in Las Vegas alongside the McLaren Formula One team and continues to expand across baseball, rodeo, college sports and live entertainment markets.

“The event where we realised we could be a major player was Cosmic Baseball,” Barwell-Smith said.

“It’s glow-in-the-dark baseball and it’s the coolest thing ever. They do the first couple of innings with some trick plays and then halfway through the lights go off.”

He said Flicket would sell more than one million tickets with Cosmic Baseball in the coming year.

“The engagement is massive and the biggest pivot we’ve seen for events has been the change in sports – it’s no longer just sport, you’re putting on the most entertaining product.”

For organisers, running events was often “immensely stressful”, he said.

“You’ve got 10,000 things that can go wrong and so whatever we can do to help alleviate that stress always works really well.”

When asked about the challenges of scaling Flicket internationally, Barwell-Smith said the “biggest thing” was understanding what had made the company successful in New Zealand.

Flicket has supported ticketing for some of New Zealand’s biggest events, including Super Rugby and festivals such as Laneway, and most recently delivered ticketing for Australian DJ Dom Dolla’s New Zealand headline show.

“Each market has its own unique landscape and so it’s a blend of not wanting to completely change who you are and be inauthentic to other markets,” Barwell-Smith said.

“We want to retain what’s made us us and that’s just out-hustling our competitors.”

His advice to other companies looking to grow internationally was “to take the punt”.

“It is crazy, you’ll pull all-nighters, you pull together great people, you lean in and if you do the hard work and you’re honest and upfront, it works out.

“You’ll never think that you’re ready for it. If you’re not doing stuff that scares you and pushing you outside your limits, you’re not doing it right.”

To be eligible for Exporter of the Year, the company had to have more than five years of international operations and annual revenue above $5 million.

Flicket is on track to support more than 4000 events and process more than $350m in gross transaction value this year.

“What we’re seeing across the platform is that we double each year,” Barwell-Smith said.

He said the Exporter of the Year award was “huge” for the company.

“We do a lot of this almost in an isolated bubble. We run a pretty lean organisation so our heads are down just trying to do the good work.

“I think if you go out there trying to win awards you can lose sight of things, whereas we’ve let the hard work speak for itself.”

Barwell-Smith said in the past few years, the recognition had slowly started flowing in.

“We love the event industry and this is a long-term business for us, so we want that to be sustainable and want it to be something that we’re proud of.

“We’re looking forward to keeping the region proud and keep swinging for the fences.”

Kaitlyn Morrell is a journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post. She has lived in the region for several years and studied journalism at Massey University.

Napier school’s touching tribute to pupil who died of cancer

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

Tyler Gray with his parents Jarred Gray and Kelly Hill.

A Napier school has paid special tribute to one of its former students who died following a battle with cancer.

Tyler Gray died in 2024, aged 11, and is remembered fondly by loved ones as someone who always wore a smile on his face.

Father’s Day marked two years since his passing.

His former school, Henry Hill School, staged a Wig Wednesday event in his memory, raising hundreds of dollars for the Child Cancer Foundation.

Tyler’s younger sister Sadie Gray, 7, attends the school and dressed up for the occasion alongside her schoolmates.

The school has supported several children through childhood cancer over the years – some of whom have beaten the disease, while others have sadly lost their lives.

Tyler’s mum, Kelly Hill, recalled how quickly their lives changed when Tyler was diagnosed with osteosarcoma, a type of bone cancer, in September 2021 shortly before his ninth birthday.

Doctors also discovered tiny secondary cancer nodules in his lungs, some no bigger than grains of salt.

The family had to travel from Napier to Auckland during the Covid-19 lockdown so Tyler could receive treatment at Starship children’s hospital.

He underwent three months of chemotherapy before doctors amputated his leg, including his knee and femur. He then faced another six months of chemotherapy.

Kelly said it was a constant cycle of going back and forth to Starship.

At the end of treatment, the family had 14 months of remission.

But the cancer in Tyler’s lungs remained a concern, requiring regular trips back to Auckland and further surgeries to try to remove the nodules.

Eventually, there were simply too many and he was given about nine months to live. He survived three months.

“He was always happy. It took a lot for Tyler to tell us he was in pain,” Kelly said.

“People didn’t always know he was sick because he always had that smile on his face.”

For the family, the Child Cancer Foundation was a constant source of support throughout their darkest days.

“Having the family support co-ordinators there helped us so much,” Kelly said.

“We could talk to them, ask questions and just have someone who understood what we were going through.”

The Child Cancer Foundation also provided petrol vouchers, practical assistance and grief counselling for the family.

“And they were there for us as a family too, including helping us navigate our relationship as a couple and the grief that came afterwards.”

Kelly said the family, including her partner and Tyler’s father, Jarred Gray, also appreciated the school’s efforts to remember their son.

She said it was an amazing school.

“They have done a lot for Tyler while he was a student, and even still now.

“They planted a tree in memory of him when he passed, they put a little Lego man of him on his school house in the hall, and they still remember him, and that’s awesome for my daughter because she really misses him – they were really close.”

Tyler’s experience has also shaped the direction of Kelly’s life. She is now studying to become a hospital play specialist – a role she saw first-hand during Tyler’s treatment and care at Ronald McDonald House.

“He is my motivation,” she said.

Pōkeno Whisky chosen for world-first study into how climate shapes whisky

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

The Pōkeno Whisky Company has been selected for an international study that looks at whiskies from eight continents, including one matured in Antarctica (inset).

Waikato distillery The Pōkeno Whisky Company has been selected for an international study into how different climates shape the maturation, chemistry and taste of whisky.

The study, titled Climate-Driven Maturation Signatures in Global Whisky: A Comparative Multi-Continental Chemical and Sensory Study, examines whiskies from The 8 Continent Series, a collection curated by London-based businessman Daniel Monk of whisky business Cask World.

The series is limited to 300 sets of the eight whiskies.

In The 8 Continent Series, Pōkeno Whisky represents Zealandia, a largely submerged landmass that includes New Zealand, which was recognised as the world’s eighth continent in 2017.

Pōkeno Whisky co-founder Matt Johns said he was proud to be chosen for the project.

“We feel humbled. He could have gone to any distillery to do this.

“We always liked batting above our weight.”

Monk told the Waikato Herald in a statement he selected Pōkeno Whisky because it produces whiskies that reflect New Zealand’s culture and climate.

“From the first time I visited, I felt they were genuinely asking the same question that sits at the heart of The 8 Continent Series: how much does place shape whisky?

“Matt and the team have taken generations of whisky knowledge and applied it to New Zealand, rather than simply trying to recreate Scotland.

“Having their own cooperage on site gives them an extraordinary ability to explore cask influence and native New Zealand timbers.

“There is also a lovely thread back to whisky’s Scottish roots. Matt brought years of experience working in Scotland’s whisky industry, while Mike Tawse is a second-generation Scottish cooper now making casks in New Zealand.

“For a collection exploring how whisky has travelled across the world, I loved that connection.”

Pōkeno Whisky has been chosen alongside Penderyn Distillery of Wales, which represents Europe; Union Distillery of Brazil, representing South America; Shelter Point Distillery of Canada, representing North America; Boplaas Family Vineyards & Distilling of South Africa; Rampur Distillery of India, representing Asia; Lawrenny Estate of Australia; and La Alazana Whisky of Argentina, which represents Antarctica.

The Antarctic whisky matured at La Alazana Distillery for five years before spending a further three years maturing at Marambio Base, an Argentine research station in Antarctica, in temperatures that dropped to -35C.

Meanwhile, Monk and Johns remained tight-lipped about what whisky Pōkeno Whisky has contributed to the study and series, though the Waikato Herald understands it is a special cask from its existing range, not a new launch.

Over six months, Dr Aline Bortoletto, a Brazilian food scientist specialising in alcoholic beverages, will analyse the eight single malt whiskies from around the world.

Bortoletto and her team at beverage research and development company Inovbev will build a detailed chemical and sensory profile of each whisky.

Monk said it was the first scientific comparison of single malt whiskies matured across every continent.

He said he hoped the study’s findings would help whisky makers understand how their own climate and environment shaped the spirit they made.

“It’s already understood that climate makes a difference – this study provides an opportunity to learn more about that ... and provide data that may help whisky-making become more sustainable in the future.

“For example, if producers know how best to work with their climates, they may be able to look at every step of their production process and find ways to be more efficient and use less energy.”

Monk said the study came amid a growing interest in world whisky.

The whisky industry was initially centred on Scotland and Ireland, with established industries in the United States and Japan.

Lately, New World whisky made outside those traditional countries had grown, he said.

Johns said being part of the study was “incredibly enriching”.

“We’re very, very lucky to have been chosen for this. This, for me, is an incredible opportunity to showcase to the world what New World whisky is,” he said.

“We’re all out there battling very hard ... to explain to people that Old World whisky is really, really good, but just cause it’s got an age statement on it, it doesn’t mean it’s better than what we’re bringing out.

“The fact that we’ve got people like Daniel who are championing the cause, who are saying, ‘Well, actually New World whisky has a lot more to offer and this is why’ ... this just helps ... give the category of New World whisky more credibility.

“This is gonna ... shine a light on our creativity.”

Johns said he was excited about what the study’s results would teach distilleries.

“We all know that climate affects maturation massively.

“I mean, we look at our 9.5% Angel’s share [the natural alcohol evaporation rate that occurs as the whisky matures in a barrel] per year ... you get 2% in Scotland.

“But what elements of the climate affect it, how does it scientifically affect the whisky ... what does it do to the DNA structures of the whisky?

“[The findings are] gonna help us do our jobs better. I’m hoping it’s [also] gonna open some new innovation for us.”

It has been a busy time for Pōkeno Whisky.

In August, after working on it for almost one-and-a-half years, the company launched a special collaboration with American collectables company Syzygy Forge: Ringbearer, a whisky in honour of The Lord of the Rings’ 25th anniversary.

“We were sitting in the distillery one day [early last year] and a couple of guys rolled up,” Johns said.

“They were ... Americans and ... they were going like ‘We’ve just come from Hobbiton, we’re massive fans and we’ve got a collectibles business. Would you guys be interested in making a Lord of the Rings’ whisky?’

“It caught us off guard a bit ... but we gradually got quite excited about this.

“Pōkeno is all about making innovative and creative whiskies that are a true reflection of the culture and climate in New Zealand.

“It’s a bit kinda tongue in cheek here, but you know, New Zealand is very much Middle Earth, it’s very much Lord of the Rings and [we thought] this could be a bit of fun.”

Johns said there were a lot of hoops to jump through, as the whisky is licensed by Warner Bros, making it official Lord of the Rings merchandise.

He said while he was somewhat aware of the trilogy’s popularity and had seen the movies, he didn’t realise how big a following it had.

“There is a fan base of 17.5 million active fans and collectors around the world today ... Hobbiton still gets 650,000 visitors a year.”

When it came to composing the Ringbearer, Johns said he and Pōkeno Whisky production manager Gareth Kimpton spent about three days playing around with different cask types.

“This was all about what can we do, whisky-wise, to make this a true reflection of Middle-Earth?

“The Lord of the Rings is a powerful film, it’s an epic saga. So, we need a whisky which is robust and which is powerful, we need a whisky that is strong.”

This meant using virgin casks, Johns said.

They also wanted to add a typical New Zealand element.

In the end, Ringbearer was made of whiskies fully matured in first-fill Bourbon, virgin oak, muscat and mānuka honey casks.

Johns said the whisky tasted rich and smooth, with the honey adding texture.

“You’ve got our standard tropical fruitness ... that’s enhanced by the muscat cask ... that gives you zesty orange and pear notes. And then you’ve got this ... mānuka honey richness in the end.”

The company has released 12,000 bottles, with most distributed in Australia and the US and 2000 in New Zealand.

Johns said demand had been huge and he had received emails from people around the world asking to get their hands on a bottle – before the product was even announced or launched.

He said the team was “pretty proud” of this whisky and had entered it into the World Whisky Awards this year.

The team’s focus now shifts to other projects, including launching a whisky club and exploring other native wood casks.

They’re currently looking to trial kahikatea and tawa but are struggling to find wood, Johns said.

Danielle Zollickhofer is the Waikato news director and a multimedia journalist at the Waikato Herald. She joined NZME in 2021 and is based in Hamilton.

Rotorua-born Adele Pascoe lands lead role in New Zealand film Where Beauty Hides

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

Adele Pascoe is the leading actress in the New Zealand romantic drama, Where Beauty Hides.

After a business degree, a law career, three kids and a stint in banking, Adele Pascoe assumed her acting days were over.

That was before she walked the red carpet at The Hollywood in Avondale for the premiere of Where Beauty Hides last week.

The Rotorua-born 37-year-old plays Vivian Marsden, an investigative journalist searching for a mysterious bestselling author, in the New Zealand romantic drama written and directed by Tremaine Leaso.

Dressed in a Knuefermann gown with her hair and makeup done, she walked into the cinema and saw her face on a poster.

Pascoe said it felt “surreal”, especially as the premiere was packed.

“I’m just a mum ... how did this happen?”

Pascoe thought her acting “glory days” were over.

Her professional acting career began at 11. She travelled regularly to Auckland auditions and landed roles in commercials and feature films as a teenager.

She did speech and drama throughout her Rotorua schooling under Gabrielle Thurston, whom she described as an iconic influence on the city’s performing arts scene.

She was named Rotorua Performer of the Year in Year 13 at Rotorua Girls’ High School.

But as she got older and was moving out of children’s television, her auditions were for more mature shows such as Shortland Street or Outrageous Fortune, for which she did not feel ready.

Being “quite academic as well”, she was offered a full scholarship at 18 to study business at Auckland University of Technology and graduated with a degree in marketing and human resources.

She later studied law at the University of Waikato and secured a role at top Auckland law firm Bell Gully.

Marriage and motherhood followed.

She also did contract work for a bank.

With her youngest child starting kindergarten in the past couple of years, she found herself with more time and thought about returning to an acting class.

“It felt so uncomfortable to just show up to this class and to pick something up, like a script and just cold read it in front of [people] ...

“It was like being thrown into the deep end.”

The class led to auditions, short film roles and a table reading for Where Beauty Hides.

Two weeks before filming began, she was offered the lead role.

“It was pretty crazy,” she said.

The role required her to master an American accent and work alongside New Zealand actor Michael Hallows.

Some scenes were shot at 3am, when it was “absolutely freezing”.

It didn’t bother Pascoe, though. Those challenges “completely fade away” when snapping into character, she said.

“You’re just so present.”

Looking back, she believes taking a different path after leaving school made her a better actor.

“I can bring so many more life experiences to my work now.”

She credited the Rotorua community for giving her the confidence to return to her “glory days”.

“I was always made to feel like, ‘Yes, this is what you were made for’.”

Where Beauty Hides begins a limited cinema release at Auckland’s Bridgeway Cinema next week, with screenings planned for other boutique cinemas around the country.

Pascoe hopes Rotorua audiences will eventually get the chance to see the film.

Annabel Reid is a multimedia journalist for the Bay of Plenty Times and the Rotorua Daily Post, based in Rotorua. Originally from Hawke’s Bay, she has a Bachelor of Communications from the University of Canterbury.

Pastures Past: What an Australian farmer thought of NZ sheep in 1938

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

A visiting Australian farmer had plenty to say about New Zealand sheep farming during a 1938 tour.

Kem Ormond takes a look at the world of farming back in the day. In this week’s Pastures Past, she’s uncovered a newspaper article on transtasman sheep rivalry.

The rivalry between Australia and New Zealand has not always been confined to the sporting field.

In 1938, a visiting Australian made his views known at a special meeting of the Gisborne Young Farmers’ Club, expressing his disappointment at what he considered to be the limited range of sheep breeds being farmed in New Zealand.

He spoke about sheep management practices in Australia, including the practice of rugging Merino sheep to protect their valuable fleeces and keep the wool clean.

He explained that one Australian property had more than 2000 Merinos wearing rugs.

He also offered his opinion on New Zealand’s farming practices, suggesting that there was considerable wastage occurring in our fields.

Despite his observations, the visit concluded with the Australian taking home a little piece of New Zealand agriculture.

Before returning to Australia, he purchased a stud Ryeland ram from Massey Agricultural College, perhaps providing some evidence that, despite his criticism, he recognised there was plenty of value in New Zealand’s sheep-breeding industry.

Below is a historical story from the Poverty Bay Herald (1938).

South Australian types

Fat lamb production

“To beat New Zealand”

Poverty Bay Herald, February 15, 1938

Surprise that there were very few breeds of sheep in New Zealand, compared with many different types to suit varying types of country and conditions, was expressed by Mr Ross Theim, a member of the South Australian farmers’ party, when speaking at a special meeting of the Gisborne Young Farmers’ Club last night.

Mr Theim said that fat lambs were produced mainly by the mixed farmer close to Adelaide.

Many types of sheep were used, chiefly the British breeds, while those for fat lambs were mainly the Suffolk, Southdown, Border Leicester, Ryeland, Hampshire Down and the Dorset Horn, the last mentioned now finding its way to New Zealand.

These sheep were chiefly used as sires for fat lambs, while on the other hand, the Romney Lincoln, English Leicester, Border Leicester, and Ryeland were used for crossing with Merino ewes for lambs.

Corriedales were now becoming very popular as a dual-purpose sheep.

In his area there was early and late country, where lambs were produced from April up to October.

They tried to get the fat lambs away in time to beat New Zealand on to the market.

Few British sheep

So far in the North Island he was disappointed in not being able to find many British sheep.

He had found only two Ryeland studs and many Romneys.

He had purchased a stud Ryeland ram at Massey College to take back to Australia.

It was not unusual to see from 800 to 1000 British sheep at a South Australian show, with 75 to 90 sheep of each breed.

The British breeds would outnumber other breeds.

With his rainfall of from 30 to 40in. a year, one might think he had no water problem, but the scarcity and difficulty in procuring water were surprising.

Some sheep now rugged

A number of Merino breeders were now rugging their sheep to keep the dust out, and there had been good results, a better growth of cleaner wool being obtained.

Of course it was a problem to rug thousands of sheep, but the method was becoming popular, up to as many as 2000 sheep being rugged on the one farm.

His area, which was near Adelaide, carried from three to four, and up to five sheep to the acre.

The annual ram fair held in September.

The rams were always inspected by a committee, which had the power to reject any that did not come up to the required standard.

From 600 to 700 rams were offered at the sale annually, but more were dealt with privately or through the Royal Show.

The Dorset rams usually brought the highest prices, generally from 7 to 25gns.

The lambing averaged from 80 to 90 per cent, and sometimes up to 100 per cent.

When asked by one of the listeners, Mr Theim said that what impressed him most on his tour was the greenness of the country, the number of windbreaks and the uniformity in the type of sheep being used here.

He could understand why New Zealand secured such a big uniformity in the lamb carcasses when the country stuck so rigidly to practically one type of ram.

The same applied to the Jersey cows.

The size of the paddocks also impressed him.

“There appears to be a big wastage in your fields,” he added.

“I would feel like doing some mowing in some of the paddocks.”

- Source: Papers Past

Death, taxes and finding the devil in the detail - Letters to the Editor

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

EDs around the country are struggling to cope with staffing shortages. Photo / Jason Dorday

Devil’s in the detail over nursing staff

2100 and 54 are quite different figures, but supposedly they both represent FTE net nursing hireage. The difference is in the detail. Different terms and start and finish times (fulltime equivalent or not), but half our graduating nurses still can’t get a job.

It’s a somewhat irrelevant game politicians play, unless you’re waiting in ED for hours, but when Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s history of accidentally distorting figures is mentioned (the infamous up to $250 per family, for example) and how we’d be bowel testing more, have more cancer drugs, more EV chargers and wouldn’t be borrowing to pay for landlords and tax cuts, you lose trust because the devil is in the detail.

Do you believe it or not, or vote on gut instinct? Well, yes and no: it’s not easily verified, like a Trump promise to end a war in one day. That’s bravado and easily dismissed, so we’re being taken as naive car buyers being sold the virtues of a secondhand dunger with a tweaked odometer.

Blink, and the smoke and mirrors cloud reality. It’s pointless asking an economist – this is the game of life. You pay for what you get, more or less sooner or later.

Steve Russell, Hillcrest.

Flights of fancy

I am normally a follower and admirer of Gregor Paul and his rugby expertise, but I must take serious issue with him on the dangerously low Embraer flyover in Cape Town.

To call the New Zealand reaction “hysterical, fear-mongering and pious outrage” is in complete disagreement with virtually the entire aviation community, of which I am one. Experienced captain and formation pilot Vaughn Davis correctly summed it up this week with expert comment far from hysterical, and I need to point out to Gregor and those who agree with him (mostly South Africans) several issues which he clearly ignores.

At such a low height, there is no margin for error or unseen events, such as birdstrike, fireworks, antennae perhaps, or turbulent downdrafts caused by the airflow over the stadium.

The risk far outweighed the result.

It was a very sloppy quasi-formation, with the lead aircraft lower and slower than the No 2, which is not “highly trained and rehearsed” formation practice.

The lead aircraft started a climb over the stadium into the following overtaking aircraft, causing it to veer sharply right.

This type of formation manoeuvre cannot be practised in an airline simulator, contrary to Airlink’s protestations. Most pilots would agree that having three senior captains on the flight deck of an airliner can be very risky, not safer, because of possible authority ambiguity and abnormal crew dynamics.

We find it incredible that the South African Civil Aviation Authority would approve a 50ft flyover above a stadium, as this would not be approved in most countries even over a runway at an airshow. Maybe it didn’t approve it, which could be why they are pulling the flight data recorders.

Sorry Gregor, you are a very good rugby journalist, but you know little about flying.

Mark Easson (retired Captain), Greenhithe.

Political courage, not illusions

I heartily endorse the sentiments expressed by John Molloy (Sept 4). He hits the nail on the head: political parties are treating the electorate like short-sighted consumers rather than citizens invested in New Zealand’s future.

Prioritising brief political wins, such as “no new taxes” pledges or arbitrary spending caps, is an abdication of leadership when our core public services face systemic crises.

As Molloy rightly notes, we cannot expect a functional healthcare system, resilient climate infrastructure, or a prepared Defence Force if parties continuously starve the Crown of revenue just to buy votes. Relying on the naive assumption that no future economic or environmental shocks will hit us is dangerous.

It is time for voters to demand structural courage and realistic funding models from our leaders, rather than comfortable illusions. Thank you, John Molloy, for calling out this race to the bottom.

Jonathan Sinclair, Auckland Central.

Moving-on orders

Justice Minister Goldsmith is pressing on with his move-on order bill, disappointed with other parties who want a more reasonable approach to the homeless individuals, concentrating management on any bad behaviour. Goldsmith still has no proposal about where to move the homeless.

As he wants this bill passed before the election, I wonder whether he understands that the voters will consider giving him his move-on orders for such poor empathy?

Gary Carter, Gulf Harbour.

Of Premier concern ...

Perhaps Labour’s request that the Government “come clean” about the bill for the Premier House upgrade (Aug 30) may arise from a premonition that its leader will occupy that property after the election.

This shows commendable forward planning, a quality which seemed lacking the last time Labour was in power. One example was the KiwiBuild fiasco, incorporating a promise of 100,000 affordable homes in 10 years, which proved to be unattainable.

Another irony related to all this is that Chris Hipkins was once responsible for approving security upgrades and repairs at Premier House that were reportedly going to cost millions. Given that Hipkins already has some knowledge of how expensive the refurbishment is likely to be, and the difficulty his Government had in fulfilling KiwiBuild promises, it would seem that Labour and its leader are not very well qualified to criticise anyone in the areas of construction and refurbishment.

Bernard Walker, Mt Maunganui.

Air NZ loss

How can Qantas record a $1.5 billion profit and Air NZ lose $336 million?

Air NZ really needs investigating.

The company has the benefit of virtually no opposition on the domestic market, which Qantas doesn’t enjoy, and still Air NZ loses money.

Jock Mac Vicar, Hauraki.

New Zealand should Think Small to get big ideas moving – Glenn Dwight

New Zealand Herald September 05, 2026

Small ideas can sometimes lead to the biggest results.

Back in the late 1970s, New Zealand started Thinking Big. Really big.

Not standing in the backyard with a tape measure wondering if you could get another 2m of deck in. This was nation-building stuff.

Big energy projects, synthetic fuel plants, hydro schemes and the sort of things that required big engineering brains, billions of dollars and some very large plans spread across even bigger boardroom tables.

In fact, about the only thing that wasn’t big were the work shorts.

The idea was basically that New Zealand needed to become more self-sufficient and to do that, we needed to think bigger.

It was bold, ambitious and expensive and, like most things from the late 1970s, probably involved a lot of brown carpet and shrimp cocktails.

Anyway, I was thinking about Think Big the other day and wondering whether it might be time for New Zealand to bring it back.

Except this time, do the complete opposite.

Think Small.

I know, it’s not quite as inspiring.

You can’t really imagine a politician standing behind a podium declaring: “New Zealand, the time has come to lower our sights.”

It’s probably not even going to get an approving nod from the carefully positioned human nodding backdrop at any political press conference.

But I think being small has always been one of our greatest advantages.

Take my own career and a little radio station in Hamilton called The Generator.

That’s where I got my start and The Generator was small. Really small.

Most people in Hamilton didn’t know who we were.

I’m pretty sure some of our listeners only found us because they accidentally knocked the dial while trying to find Newstalk ZB.

But when I look back, an incredible number of people who worked at that little station went on to have pretty successful careers in radio and beyond.

I’ll only drop one name here, Mr Vaughan Smith. Yes, that Vaughan Smith. ZM radio host, small-time farmer and a Television New Zealand cardboard cut-out. That is peak Kiwi fame.

The Generator was almost like agar for talent. It gave people the right conditions to grow and all sorts of things started happening.

People who worked there went on to become radio announcers, audio engineers, marketing specialists, business owners and all sorts of other things.

And me. Radio writer and now opinion writer. Proof that not everything you grow in a petri dish is necessarily useful.

So, what was going on at this tiny little station?

Did we have enormous resources? Definitely not.

Did we have a carefully constructed staff development strategy? I’m not entirely sure we had a staff toilet.

What we did have was smallness.

Because the station was small, you had to do everything. You couldn’t have your little job description and stay safely inside it. You had to colour outside the lines.

We did radio shows, wrote radio ads, helped with promotions, talked to clients and drove the station’s FJ40 Land Cruiser like it was stolen.

We answered phones, moved things, made things, moved the things we’d just made and generally had a crack at whatever needed doing.

If something needed to happen, somebody had to make it happen and quite often that somebody was you.

Promotions were particularly interesting because we had virtually no budget, so we developed what I think was quite a clever arrangement with our audience.

We did the stupid stuff and they gave us a prize. Sort of reverse radio promo psychology.

This once resulted in a man called Dave attempting to jump the Garden Place fountain on a kid’s bike for a Creed CD.

Just take a moment to appreciate the risk versus reward equation there.

That was The Generator. We didn’t have a lot of money, so we had to have ideas and when the ideas weren’t particularly good, we just had to make s*** happen.

There were even weeks when, because one of the station owners was a farmer, we got paid in meat packs.

Now, when you’re young, being paid in meat was actually pretty good.

Sure, you can’t pay the rent with a lamb shoulder, but you can run a hell of a great barbecue.

But despite all of this, we kept turning up. More importantly, we had fun and we learned.

We were connected to everything that was happening because we had to be.

You couldn’t sit in your department and say, “That’s not really my area”, because there were no areas. It was just us and if something went wrong, everyone mucked in to fix it.

And I wonder if we’ve lost a little bit of that.

We seem to spend a lot of time being told that bigger is better.

Businesses need to scale, farms need to grow, companies merge and services centralise.

Departments get bigger, then departments get departments and eventually you need someone whose job is to explain what all the departments actually do.

Even job titles have got bigger.

You’re no longer simply in charge of something; you’re the executive general manager of strategic capability, transformation and future-focused outcomes.

Which sounds impressive, although I’m still not entirely sure what they do.

So small has some pretty good things going for it.

When you’re small, you know people. You know your customers.

You notice when something isn’t working. You can have an idea in the morning and actually try it in the afternoon without scheduling a meeting three weeks from Thursday to establish a working group to investigate the idea.

And when you don’t have a lot of money, you become incredibly good at making do with what you’ve got.

That feels very New Zealand to me.

Farmers have always done it. Small towns do it. Local businesses and sports clubs do it.

Something needs fixing, so someone knows someone who can fix it.

The rugby club needs new changing rooms, someone donates the timber, someone else turns up with a digger and somebody’s uncle apparently knows how to do plumbing.

Nobody is entirely sure how it all came together, but six months later there are new changing rooms and, thanks to that uncle, there are even hot showers.

That’s Thinking Small.

Now, I’m not suggesting for a moment that we should stop having big ideas. Quite the opposite.

I just wonder whether some of the best big ideas actually come from small places, where people are close enough to the problem to see it, connected enough to care about it and trusted enough to have a go at fixing it.

Small can be nimble. Small can be personal. Small can improvise.

Small can connect people and small can force you to find a way when there isn’t an obvious one.

So maybe, nearly 50 years after New Zealand decided to Think Big, it’s time we tried something different.

Think Small.

He may be for kids, but Shaun the Sheep is a story of grown-up obsession

Sydney Morning Herald September 06, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Half a dozen journalists are sitting around a table, heads bent, their thumbs buried in plasticine. We are getting an express class from Will Harding, a model-maker at Aardman, in making the head of Shaun the Sheep in the old-school way; I’m determined to master the ridges in his woolly topknot.

If someone had told me this is what a bunch of adults would be doing on a set visit for Aardman’s latest stop-motion feature – Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom – I would probably have said something bitter about being treated like an Insta-idiot influencer. At least, I might have said that if it had been anywhere but Aardman, where fun – and plasticine – is taken entirely seriously. This is, in fact, the most fun you will ever have visiting a film studio, but it’s also an exercise in dexterity and concentration. Everyone wants to get it right.

Getting very, very small things right is what Aardman is all about. Stop-motion is an almost inconceivably exacting way to make a film, with hand-made models moved by tiny increments on beautifully crafted table-top sets by animators. The numbers are formidable. There are 1289 shots in the film; an animator will complete 2.5 shots a week – or, put another way, two seconds a day. At its peak, this production has 47 units working at the same time: a crew on site of around 170 people.

Directors Matthew Walker and Steve Cox started thinking about this film when they were making the sixth season of Shaun the Sheep for television, which launched early in 2020. Their original idea was a Valentine’s Day special, which gradually evolved into a comedy horror.

As always, Shaun is the source of all mischief. Just wanting to help, he turns to weird science to try to boost the farm’s Halloween pumpkin crop and the farmer’s romantic prospects, cooking up potions in his makeshift laboratory like an ovine nutty professor. His solutions, however, only create more problems – not least the unhappiness of the flock, as they see their leader becoming increasingly obsessed with his test tubes.

An irony, no, to make a stop-motion film about obsession? Walker and Cox nod agreeably. “We understand Shaun’s problem,” says Walker.

Theirs is a lovely obsession, though. I have been lucky enough to visit Aardman several times; there is always the same benign buzz of people working hard to a whimsical common purpose. Our first stop is the puppet-making department, where designer Kate Anderson plunges us into her world of steel armatures, clay mixes, silicone mouldings and the problems associated with animating a furry beast.

“I don’t know if you’ve seen the film Fantastic Mr. Fox,” she says. Wes Anderson’s 2009 adaptation of Roald Dahl’s story was also stop-motion animation; obviously, it was full of fur. “They made a feature of the fact that every time you touch the fur or the air conditioning blows it, it ‘boils’, we call it. We found that our directors and animators really don’t like that. So we had to find a way to make the fur look nice, but not twitch too much.”

The Beast isn’t really scary – Shaun’s core audience is between five and eight years old, too little for scares – but it is supposed to be scruffy. “That meant we could put in a treatment that made the fur fairly rigid. But then there are lots of parts that are animatable.”

The fringe is wired; the ears rotate. “And then the fur on the body and arms is a bit flatter so they can grab it.”

The design of a new character is the work of years, although it has been speeded up by collaboration with a CGI artist who can try out different looks on screen. “I’m pleased with how successful it is,” she says. “There’s some shots that I just really want to give the Beast a hug. He just looks so sorry for himself.”

As a Halloween story, The Beast of Mossy Bottom is literally much darker than the original 2015 Shaun the Sheep film or its 2019 follow-up, Farmageddon. Director of photography Charles Copping says how enjoyable it has been to cast scenes in dim autumnal light or create Shaun’s laboratory, with luminous purple goo bubbling in a hand-blown miniature glass beaker, lit by UV lamps.

And although the mood is ’80s Ghostbusters rather than Friday the 13th, there are visual references – a version of Nosferatu’s shadow walking downstairs, for example – to provide any film-buff parents with an entertaining game of Spotto.

“I’ve been on Shaun since the start,” Copping says. “But here it’s more exciting; we’re pushing the colours, pushing the contrasts, and we’ve made it more dynamic. We’ve leaned into it being richer; there’s a Gothic feel. It’s been a joy to do.”

But then, it always is: clay animation, he says, feels honest. “Everything is in front of the camera and feels tangible.”

Effects are often created with stuff everyone has in their kitchen drawers. One character’s hair is modelled on a saucepan scourer, fetched from the Aardman canteen by an inspired puppet-maker. The sea is created with cardboard tubes with scrunched foil over them, lit to look like ripples. “Foil, cling film – we’d be lost without them. Also, KY jelly.”

Given that none of the characters speak – even the farmer merely burbles – the story has to be told through facial expressions. This is complicated by the fact the sheep faces are made of hard resin; only their eyes and the odd mouths that protrude from the sides of their heads are malleable.

“All they really have are that mouth shape and their eyelids,” says Jay Grace, the chief animator. “So you can do a little bit to angle the eyelids to create a worried or an angry expression, but there are limitations to how far you can push that.”

They also have motion, of course. Aardman’s key collective talent is an expressive physical comedy that hearkens back to Buster Keaton. Everyone unhesitatingly refers to the animators as actors, even though what they are actually doing is moulding mouths into new expressions with their thumbs and inching the characters through each scene. These are performances filtered, you might say, through puppets.

“We do think of our animators as actors,” says Grace. “We often film them acting out scenes, and they then use that information, that they have recorded themselves, to put into the characters. If there’s a moment in the film that’s a sad moment, the animator has to embody that sadness and get the emotion into the film.”

Sometimes a movement – an expression of joy or a bouncing gait – can be clearly identified with the person who animated it. “Just because they’re thinking, ‘This is the way a person walks.’ It’s their own acting going into it. It’s fascinating, really.”

Given this, a good part of Grace’s job is making sure the characters stay consistent across all the scenes being created by different animators. Where they are hand-moulding, their models have to match exactly. Occasionally, something jars.

“It can be very, very subtle things to the general audience,” he says. “They may not notice, but you can see that, say, the eyelid shape is not quite right. This nice curved shape is very Shaun, whereas this one” – he points to a reject – “is just too straight and a little bit too thick on one side. As a viewer, you wouldn’t necessarily notice what the specifics were, but you might be able to pick out that it doesn’t quite look like Shaun.”

There are short-cuts. For characters with visible mouths – most of the humans and Bitzer the dog – there are as many as 20 interchangeable mouthpieces covering basic expressions. These are squeezed into place on a resin face and can then be moulded as required. Back in the ’70s when Aardman was founded, everything would be moulded on set, but that is even more time-consuming.

“My personal preference is doing character shots where you’ve got a full clay face and you’re really pushing it around and making that piece of clay live,” says Grace. “To me, that’s what I love about stop-motion.”

As I push and pull at bits of black and white plasticine, which are turning disappointingly grey around the edges, I can imagine that. I also have to face the fact that, like most people, I’m not very good at it. I’d love to work in this house of fun but, clearly, you need to be a little bit obsessed.

Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom is released in cinemas on September 24.

Dad, I love today.”

Matt Okine had spent the day worrying he’d “not done enough” with his seven-year-old daughter, Sofia, when she gave him the sweet validation.

It had been an ordinary Saturday, with nothing booked or planned. Okine’s partner, Belinda, 44, was away for the weekend so it was a daddy/daughter day of cooking breakfast, wandering around the markets, mucking about on exercise equipment along the Brisbane River and going for ice-cream.

“I said, ‘Oh, is it because you got to have ice-cream?’” Okine recalls. “And she replied, ‘No, it’s because I got to hang out with you.’”
