Father's Day joy with Matt Okine

The comedian talks about the fun - and pressure - of modern fatherhood.

“I’d felt bad the whole day,” he explains. “I’d kept thinking, ‘Should we have gone to a theme park? Should I have taken her to some fancy museum?’ And the reality was that she’d had the best day just because we’d hung out together. Even now, I’m tearing up thinking about it because parents can be really hard on themselves without acknowledging that it’s these little moments that make the biggest impact.”

It’s a fitting anecdote for the comedian who has become a hilariously candid voice on modern Australian fatherhood. For all his achievements on stage, screen and radio, these days the 41-year-old is just as likely to be found sharing funny, unfiltered “dad content” online.

Real life has always found its way into Okine’s work. He made his name as a stand-up comic and co-host of Triple J’s breakfast show before creating and starring in the semi-autobiographical ABC-TV comedy-drama The Other Guy. His coming-of-age novel Being Black ’N Chicken, & Chips was based on his own teenage years, and he also stars in the revival of the beloved ABC sitcom Mother and Son alongside Denise Scott, in which he draws on his own experiences as a son and father.

Fatherhood is now his richest source of material and his current stand-up comedy show, No.10 Hope St, is “inherently connected to the challenges that we face as parents”. Okine also has “high hopes” of turning it into something we can watch on TV.

As an ambassador for Lego’s Little Years, Big Impact report, which highlights the importance of play in early childhood, Okine is urging parents on social media to “ditch the guilt” and lean into small, impactful moments. But despite being an advocate of not being the perfect parent, he admits he is far from immune from feeling that pressure.

“You’ve got all these incredible parents documenting all of these magical moments,” he says. “Meanwhile, you’re struggling to butter a piece of toast and get a school uniform on.

“And Bluey?,” he continues. “Bluey didn’t help [the pressure to be perfect]. Bandit has got to stop, honestly. That guy is too much. I mean, please let them have one argument about who’s going to stay home when Bluey’s sick.”

All jokes aside, Okine admits the biggest parenting pressure he faces is the understanding that time with a loved one is finite. Okine was 12 when his mother, Roslyn, died at 43. “It’s crazy to think that I’m almost the age that she was when she passed away. When I became a dad, it ignited this understanding of who my mum was, what she was going through, and just the tragedy of what it would’ve felt like to know you were going to pass away.

“The reality exists strongly within me that I will not be around forever, and that I need to make every moment count as much as possible.”

Okine’s memories of his mother are limited to his first 12 years, but the ones that have stayed with him most strongly are the smaller moments of togetherness. “I want to give Sofia as many of those memories as possible,” he says.

“I do put a bit of pressure on myself to be present as much as possible because I want her to know that I love her, and that I was there for her in the small moments as well as the big, fun moments. That’s a fundamental motivation.

“The only message I can offer as someone who lost a parent young is that you don’t have to be perfect. You just have to be present and show that you’re engaged, that you care.”

Becoming a father has also given Okine a new appreciation for his own dad, Mack, now 78. Having previously described Mack as a peripheral character in his life before his mum passed away, he says fatherhood has made him “completely understand what [my dad] sacrificed, and the position that he was thrust into”.

“It strengthened the relationship I have with him. He would have been learning so much as he went along, blindly trying to figure out how the heck you deal with a heartbroken 12-year-old kid. Suddenly, me and Dad were intertwined. Our lives connected in a way that is quite rare for a father and son, and that connection grew stronger and stronger over the years.

“Becoming a dad has certainly made me acutely aware of the complexities of fatherhood and parenting.”

That closeness makes one memory from his own childhood especially poignant. “I remember when we went down to the park and kicked the ball together,” he says. “And that memory has stuck with me my whole life because it felt like that was the only time it ever happened.”

It’s less a criticism of his father than another reminder of how much an ordinary moment can stay with a child. It’s something Okine is determined to give Sofia.

“I’d love to play with my daughter so much that she forgets 98 per cent of the times we played together,” he says. “I don’t want that time that we played together to be so unusual she remembers it for the rest of her life.”

Back living in Brisbane after 16 years in Sydney, Okine now sees his father roughly once a week, and watching Mack and Sofia together has given him a sense of an intergenerational connection.

Raising Sofia has also sharpened Okine’s thinking about identity. He has often spoken about being one of the few Ghanaian-Australian kids in his suburb (Mack is originally from Ghana). Now, he wants Sofia to grow up proud of her heritage, through “trinkets and artefacts” from his father’s house, visits with Ghanaian family and exploring the country’s food and music.

It’s Sofia’s hair, though, that makes Okine most protective. “She’s got the most beautiful curly hair,” he says. “I’m deathly afraid of the moment she comes home and says she wants straight hair because no one on TV has curly hair like hers. I want her to know she’s beautiful and that she doesn’t have to look like everyone else. She can look like herself.”

For all the big questions that come with raising a daughter, most of Okine’s day-to-day fathering is considerably more mundane. Splitting the load with Belinda comes down to practicalities. “Belinda does breakfasts and school lunches, I do dinners,” he says. “I do drop-offs and pick-ups most days when I’m not away for work.”

Bedtime, though, belongs almost exclusively to Belinda, by decree of Sofia. “My daughter acts like I’m the boogie man if I walk into her room at night – the rage that comes out because I dared come in instead of Mum!”

He’s also quick to acknowledge that Belinda still carries the heavier load overall, though “we work really hard to try and change that”.

Lego has, fittingly, become the family’s love language. What started as a Duplo set to fill the locked-down days of the COVID pandemic, when Sofia was just a toddler, has grown into an ambitious hobby. Sofia recently built herself a Lego video camera she uses to “film” pretend documentaries. “She loves giving people instructions,” says Okine, laughing.

It’s also become an antidote to a habit he’s not proud of – the phone. “We give kids such a hard time about screen time,” he says, “but parents will tell kids to stop watching TV while they’re scrolling on their own phone.”

Now, Okine and Sofia build Lego sets together: “I’m not stuck in the algorithm that’s sucking my attention out of my soul. I’m actually there in the room, and I’m present.” The only downside, he jokes, is that he’s now “the Lego guy” among friends and family to the degree that he received two sets for his last birthday.

Asked what he hopes Sofia will remember about him as a dad, Okine doesn’t hesitate. “I want her to know that I think about her all day. She is the most important person in my entire world, and she has made me an infinitely better person. She’s taught me how to play, and how to love unconditionally.”

Then he adds with a laugh: “I’d also like her to remember that I did all these things for her when she was little. So when I’m a very old man who needs looking after, she owes me one.”

But for now it’s more about being present. He says Sofia is constantly calling him over – “Look what I did”, “Come and see this” – and sometimes, Okine admits, part of him would rather stay on the couch. But that part never wins.

“She’s not going to be little forever, and soon she won’t be asking me to come and see this thing,” he says. “If I died tomorrow, would I be glad I stayed sitting down, or glad I went and looked at what she made? Every time, the answer’s the same.”

The winning formula: Do you have what it takes to be the next footy star?

Sydney Morning Herald September 06, 2026

Talent is a threshold requirement. But what else do recruiters look for in aspiring draft picks?

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

In his nearly 30 years of finding footy talent, David Walls has sat down to talk with thousands of young people who dream of becoming professional footballers. He’s watched them play from the sidelines at games and on countless hours of video; reviewed their psychological tests and physical tests; analysed their statistics; met with their coaches, employers, schoolteachers; and spent time in their orbit on training camps – to work out who they are, and who they could become.

But the picture is never complete until he visits them at their family home. “You can’t bullshit in front of Mum or Dad,” says Walls, once a fresh-faced rookie himself, now head of player personnel at Fremantle footy club. “Even siblings will start to say, ‘That’s not true’,” Walls tells us. “Dads, generally, are trying to sell them as footballers and mums just want to make sure they’re good people.”

Australian rules football has a rich history of freakishly talented players (Buddy Franklin, Nick Daicos, Erin Phillips) and legendary coaches (Leigh Matthews, the late Ron Barassi and Walls’s own father, Robert). Less lauded but no less critical to success are the recruiters and list managers. They determine who is in and out of a club, how to mix new blood – a handful of teen draft picks each year – with existing teams, a painstaking task that culminates in the nerve-wracking annual draft in November (for the men) and December (for the women).

Theirs is not a glamorous job. At games, you’ll spot them in puffer jackets, perched on camping chairs with binoculars, pen and notebook. Other times, they’ll be hunkered down scrutinising footage, crunching player data. Many fans like to think they could do a better job. “I think every sports fan in Australia is picking their footy team or cricket team,” veteran AFL talent expert Kevin Sheehan tells us. “It’s a tough business, the business of drafting, and it’s make or break for the careers of not just the boys [and girls] but the scouts who are looking at them.”

More than 624,000 children and adults play football in Australia. Whittling down the best young players takes years, money and skill. The stakes are high: the best players, like artists, can create something out of nothing while players with poor character or decision-making can drag down a whole team for years.

So how do the clubs in the national league (18 men’s, 18 women’s) find the next generation of elite players? What sets a future professional apart from a skillful amateur? And how can young people maximise their chances of playing at the ’G one day?

At 205 centimetres, Harry Van Hattum stands out in a crowd. The year 12 student is confident, warm and mature. He also has a massive running leap, 103 centimetres into the air, just a touch higher than West Coast icon Nic Naitanui’s 102 centimetres jump as a junior. High-flying ruckmen are back in vogue after the AFL changed the rules this year to stop other players wrestling them away from the centre bounce, although Van Hattum wants it known ruckmen are about more than their aerial manoeuvres: “It doesn’t matter your size when you’re using it [the ball] well … I pride myself on having elite skills,” he told ESPN in August. In short, the 18-year-old has the makings of a very modern ruckman and, consequently, he’s a top prospect in November’s draft.

Yet it was only last year that Van Hattum put aside his other sporting pursuit, basketball – which he played at state level in under 12s and 14s – to focus on footy, and recruiters became part of his life. “It was around then I started talking to recruiters a fair bit and getting calls from them and organising home visits and stuff like that over that summer,” he tells us.

On a trip to New Zealand with the AFL national academy squad, made up of 50 of Australia’s most talented draft contenders, his every interaction was noted by recruiters, on the field and off. “You sit down with them and have lunch, dinner and different meetings with them on different days,” Van Hattum says, “so you get a really good sense of what their point of view is and what they are looking for from that. I was definitely pretty nervous the first time I had a meeting with someone from a club, so I was trying to be super-professional and really well-behaved. But you have just got to be yourself, don’t lie, don’t make anything up – because obviously they will find out.”

Van Hattum has signed up with a manager, a crucial step in a junior’s progress to the AFL, and has, meanwhile, been playing footy for a dizzying array of sides: Ivanhoe Grammar, his school in Melbourne’s east; Vic Metro in the AFL national championships; the AFL academy; and the Northern Knights in the AFL Talent League, Victoria’s top under-18 competition, from which most draft picks are drawn. (Gifted players also come from state leagues, or the northern academies run by Sydney, Greater Western Sydney, Brisbane and the Gold Coast, or from next-generation academies run by all clubs for Indigenous and multicultural youth.) Van Hattum considered an invitation to play for Richmond’s VFL team, too, but enough was enough. “It’s pretty busy,” he says.

Through it all, he is trying to live a normal life: studying, playing golf, hanging out with schoolmates and getting on the tools to help his dad, Rod, build a granny flat in the backyard of his family’s Kangaroo Ground property. He admits he sometimes feels like a lab rat. “It always lingers in the back of my head that there is an expectation about me and I have to perform well, but I just try to block it out of my mind and try to play to my best level and don’t think about the expectation on me every time.”

Just days after the AFL grand final, Van Hattum and other promising teenage footballers (a total of 102 men and 89 women) will attend an event called a draft combine, either in Melbourne, Adelaide and Perth, where they will talk with clubs and compete in various trials (think sprints, agility tests, vertical jumps from a standing start).

Among attendees will be year 12 student Maddy Meagher, who plays on the wing for the Northern Knights in the Talent League, the top under-18 competition in Victoria. “I base a lot of my game just off my speed,” the 18-year-old tells us. With a background in athletics, Meagher has climbed the footy ranks since she started about six years ago, this year juggling study with two three-hour training sessions a week for the Knights, games on the weekend and private coaching to “focus on the nitty-gritty”.

Her hard work has paid off: Meagher has signed with a player agent, toured St Kilda’s facilities and met with several clubs. “Collingwood’s was just online, and Carlton’s was going to their club, and Essendon, they came to training to have a 30-minute conversation with me and a couple of other girls,” she explains, “and I’ve got Freo coming to my house.”

She is ready to take the plunge and relocate if she’s drafted interstate. “I understand it would be extremely scary,” she says, “but the support that you get given is huge and, on top of the salary that you get given as an AFLW rookie, you also get extra money if you go interstate, to pay for your rent.” Clubs sometimes house newbies with a host family, another player, or a coach for a short while. Draft picks will be paid a minimum of $125,000 in 2027 in the men’s game; women will be on a base salary of $72,363.

Recruiters watch players for up to three years before making a move, which they can’t do until the player is 18 by December 31 of their draft year, under both leagues’ rules. Even then, being picked can be down to timing and luck. “Often,” says player agent Alec Morgan, who represents both the men’s and women’s league players, “recruiters will have a whiteboard and they’ll have a whole list of names at the start of the year on that, and then as the year goes, they cross names off and they add names on. So you could be the third-best key-position defender on everyone’s list, but if the other two ahead of you don’t get taken right until the end, you might keep coming second or third. So it’s not necessarily a knock on you, the footballer.”

Scott Clayton has built playing lists for Brisbane, the Bulldogs, Gold Coast, West Coast and North Melbourne. “You’ve got to have talent,” he says. “Without that, we can’t help you.” Clayton, who these days is a future talent consultant, shows us a piece of paper on which he’s jotted the qualities he wants in a draft pick.

On the left is FOOTBALL: clean hands to control that odd-shaped ball without fumbling, aerial game (marking), ground game (running) and cue response, which, says Clayton, means, “You react in instinct and action in super-quick time [to] what is actually happening. Perhaps at times it is predicting the future and making a decision on what action you must actually take.”

Very few players possess all of these attributes at a high level – now-retired Adelaide Crows champion Erin Phillips, a former basketballer, came pretty close – but you are better off with a laser kick or elite-standard speed than being average at everything. “If you watch where even AFL and AFLW was five or six years ago to now, the game is so much quicker,” says Alec Morgan. Walls agrees: “The distance they’re covering at high speed is just getting bigger and better.” Seven-time best and fairest, Richmond’s Monique Conti, is known for her explosive speed; Joel Wilkinson, who played briefly for Gold Coast then moved to the US National Football League, still holds the 20-metre sprint record (2.75 seconds) at a draft combine in 2010.

As well as athletic flair, recruiters have to predict whether players’ bodies will cope. “We get our medical department involved heavily because players change so much physically,” says Walls. “Sometimes they can’t handle the training loads and their bodies break down and they get injured a lot.” Geelong premiership coach Mark Thompson used to have a theory that if a player was injured often in junior football, they would continue that pattern in the adult game. But with advances in medical science and more nuanced approaches to training, that theory is less fiercely held.

On the right side of Clayton’s ledger is CHARACTER. For many recruiters, it’s what sets apart the most desirable players from those who are merely technically very good. But what aspects of character, in particular, are they looking for?

Top of Clayton’s list is “competitiveness”, and he’s not the only one. “I think the biggest thing that we find with clubs is competitiveness, that’s what they love,” says agent Alec Morgan. “One of the things recruiters really look out for is, do you compete? And if you’re a competitive person on the ground, you’re going to be doing all the little things off the field to make sure you’re as good as you can be.” David Walls wants players who go all out: “You know that they’re going to give the same amount of effort, it doesn’t matter what game it is, it doesn’t matter if they start slowly and things aren’t going their way, or if the team’s getting belted.”

Next on Clayton’s list is something less obvious: self-efficacy, a term that describes possessing a belief in your ability to achieve an outcome. In footy, Clayton asks, “Do they go in knowing that they’re going to affect the outcome? Because in a competitive sport, that’s what you need: you need instinctive people who just want it, want to affect the outcome, and they’re bold.”

Take Joel Selwood, now retired but who still holds the league record for games as captain. A troublesome knee deterred some clubs (although not Geelong) from drafting him in 2006, but he devised his own leg-strengthening exercises — “the Joel Selwood program,” he’s joked — which he followed religiously for 16 years, barely missing a game. “Pick a player who you’d have in your side,” said Blues coach Mick Malthouse in 2014, after Selwood had kicked the winning goal against his team. “I’d pick Selwood every day of the week.”

Research backs up the importance of self-efficacy and its related traits in everyday life, too. The Dunedin Study, from New Zealand’s University of Otago, has followed the health and fortunes of 1000 boys and girls since 1972 and found that their capacity for self-control – self-discipline and perseverance – was the single biggest predictor of their success, more than IQ or class. “We also found that children whose self-control increased with age tended to have better adult outcomes than initially predicted, showing that self-control can change and with desirable results,” wrote research leader Terrie Moffitt in 2011.

Similarly, self-motivation appears on Clayton’s list, too, a close cousin of that propulsive inner desire we call “drive”. “The players that are really driven to be the best they can be are usually the players that succeed,” says Katrina Gill, AFLW general manager at Melbourne Football Club. “You obviously need a level of talent, but talent combined with the work ethic tends to be the winning formula.”

That applies off the field, too. Fremantle’s Walls will sometimes quiz aspirants about what they do in their spare time. “We had a kid who went to the snow [with his family], went to Canada,” he recalls, “but he wouldn’t ski because he was worried about getting injured. He just trained all day, he worked out where the gyms are, where he could find an oval, where he could get a treadmill. We’re looking for things like that – where they’re giving you examples of they’re getting up early, they’re doing extra work, they’re doing recovery, they’re doing gym. You go, OK, this kid’s really, really serious.”

A term not on Clayton’s list but that is often heard in Aussie rules circles is “footy IQ”: the ability to read, indeed predict, the play in all its fast-moving complexities, to understand the game and tactics at a deep level, to make smart decisions in a split second. If footy IQ is tricky to pin down, Walls knows it when he sees it: he drafted Murphy Reid in 2024 after 11 clubs overlooked the youngster. Reid, 20, is regarded as one of the most astute draft selections in recent history, having won the Rising Star award in his first season, and been named All-Australian in his second. Says Walls: “Footy IQ is … really, really big. Murphy Reid, for us, is one that stands out with how smart he is and how much composure [he has] and how calm he is.”

Also known for footy nous is Daisy Pearce, who balanced delivering babies (she was a midwife) with playing for the Demons in the early days of the AFLW. After having twins of her own, Pearce led Melbourne to a premiership, and now coaches the West Coast Eagles women’s team. Pearce’s footy IQ was “nothing that I’d seen before,” said football trailblazer Debbie Lee as Pearce was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame. “She was a player who had so much time, she created so much space for herself, her skills were silky.”

Why is “risk” on Clayton’s list? On a footy field, big risk-takers will be prepared to take the kick that, as Clayton says, “changes the course of events”, in front of 100,000 people and millions watching on television – even if a mistake might make them look foolish. He tests a rookie’s risk appetite with a line of questioning that he adapts to them. If they surf, he asks how big a swell they are prepared to paddle out in. If they play golf, he asks which club they would use to attack a par four. Can they back themselves to take highly consequential, calculated risks without over-thinking and second-guessing?

If many of these qualities suggest ruggedly individual star power, how players relate to others – being a “good teammate”, as Clayton puts it – is a must. Gill agrees: “You want good people who are going to come in and have a positive impact on your program and be a good teammate as well.” Walls loves going out to huddles and listening to the way players talk to each other. “Are they supportive? Are they encouraging? And it goes the other way too, where you see people speak poorly to teammates and don’t treat them well, and play in a selfish manner.”

Similarly, “ability to learn”, or coachability, is another prerequisite: recruiters will observe how a player reacts to instructions, including their body language. Off the field, they’ll check school reports and find out how the kid is with their classmates. Players do need to be able to follow rules. Their ability to do the right thing goes into the recruitment mix, as does whether the club culture and the coach are good matches for them. If the standards in the club, upheld by coaches and senior players, are positive then players, regardless of their proclivities, will generally fall into line. The best coaches can mould all types into elite players while creating an environment where positive decisions are made on and off the field, more often than not.

For kids with dreams of excelling in other sports, take note of these insights from Elissa Morley, who is performance pathways manager at the Australian Institute of Sport, which assesses more than 2900 athletes across 46 sports, each with their own “what-it-takes-to-win profile”. After a battery of physical tests, athletes are invited to trial with a sport to see if they have the right “psychological and behavioural factors”. “So, their coachability, their resilience, their grit, their fire in the belly, their self-confidence, and those things that are a bit more intangible, such as their feel for the water or their fear factor.” She adds there are some characteristics all athletes need, no matter the sport: resilience, persistence, self-belief, self-regulation and being proactive about solving problems.

It’s an impressive alchemical mix that makes up a player’s F. D. P., or future development potential. Kevin Sheehan says the sport gets drafting “right” about 80 per cent of the time. “You will make errors when you’re trying to assess talent very early. But even the NFL makes mistakes, and their entry age is post-college, 21 or 22,” he says of the US football league.

The Demons’ Katrina Gill says recruiting still requires a touch of instinct. “You’re crystal-balling, to an extent.” Fremantle’s David Walls agrees, and says it makes him “sick to his stomach” when his team recruits the wrong player. “We’ve done it before, where they’re hard work and there’s issues off the field and they cause problems,” he tells us. “I’m always, would you want to work with this guy for the rest of your career, for the next 10 years? Because we’re dropping them off with these players, and is he going to make the most of the opportunity? And is he going to be a great teammate for the players that are already there?”

Being a young footy star can be tough. Living the dream will include strangers critiquing them and their team, yelling over the fence at games, writing negative comments online, and placing bets (literally) on their performance. So there’s another factor that plays into how a player is chosen: their survivability. “It’s a pretty full-on environment that you’re going into if you’re drafted at 18 and you’re straight out of school,” says Walls. “Are they going to be able to come in and work and be resilient and deal with setbacks? And if they’re playing reserves and developing for two years, are they going to be able to grind for that amount of time?”

One recruiter from a non-Victorian club tells us survivability includes coping with travel: basic self-management, being organised, being able to manage emotions. The Dockers take notice of what sort of company a prospect is over dinner – after all, they’ll have to spend a lot of time away with teammates. Says Alec Morgan: “Sometimes you can get a vibe from players that they’re really big homebodies and the club, if they’re going to bring them interstate, they’re going to have to have a lot of support.” The Brisbane Lions changed their selection process and welfare support program after five young players requested trades back to their home states at the end of 2013. Now, all northern states ensure “resilience” is weighted heavily in assessing players.

Some factors are beyond a player’s control. In a group from the same school-year level, for instance, those born in the first six months of the year tend to have had a head start on their development, are likely to have more confidence and so be elevated – a much-noted pattern that applies in other areas of education, too.

Also known to help carve a contenders’ path to selection is attending a school with a high-performing footy program, which often offer scholarships to gifted players, too. Twenty-two per cent of last year’s draft attended an Associated Public School in Victoria, such as Geelong Grammar or Scotch College, says Luke Soulos, chief executive of APS Sport. In Melbourne, particularly, school footy is “big”, says Scott Clayton, with some clashes attracting several thousand fans. The AFLW isn’t yet dominated by APS schools, says Soulos. “We’re at, I would say, the embryonic stages in regards to girls’ football. We do get one to three players drafted in a given year.”

Some youngsters might also hail from a family of sportspeople, which can confer genetic advantages and/or the chance to model their parents’ athletic drive; or their father might have played footy, in which case they can be admitted under the AFL’s father-son or father-daughter rules. (Close to 100 players arrived at AFL clubs as father-son picks from 1998 through to 2025; over the short history of the women’s league, at least 13 players joined under the father-daughter rule, including sisters Abbie and Sophie McKay, who followed their father Andrew to Carlton.)

“Dad taught me the game, Mum took me to all my games,” the Crows’ Erin Phillips said when she was inducted into the Australian Football Hall of Fame in 2025. Phillips’ dad Greg played for Collingwood and Port Adelaide, and she was a “cross-coder”, playing footy until age 13, when pathways for girls ended, then switching to pro basketball before going back to footy for the women’s league’s first season, in her early 30s. “Having experienced being in an elite environment since I was 16 years old, I feel like I have a good grasp of what makes really successful teams.”

The Darcy family has produced three generations of footballers: the late David Darcy played 133 games, his son Luke notched up 226, and his grandsons Sam and Will are both Bulldogs. Luke, now a podcaster, has warned that hyper-competitive parents are destroying their children’s love of team sport. “They [teens] actually don’t care that much at 14 about winning or losing, but they get in the car and what happens is Mum or Dad say, ‘Why didn’t you play harder?’” he said. “You’re not their coach, you probably weren’t good enough to do it, so why are you trying to overlay your world on to your kids? If they’re there, and with their mates, end of story.”

The APS’s Soulos offers this: “The better parents are the ones that stand to the side and don’t interfere and don’t get involved, other than maybe a quiet word in the car of how well they played, or [saying], ‘It was exciting to watch you play’.” Katrina Gill concurs. “Ultimately, it’s going to be the athlete that drives their own career and determines how far they go.”

Maddy Meagher’s dad Steven, who originally coached his daughter, says he has been lucky to “watch her play a sport that many girls before her simply didn’t have the opportunity to play”. “She had a dream of playing AFLW, and once we knew how much she wanted it, our role became more about giving her opportunities to develop and see how far she could go,” he tells us. “She could potentially end up anywhere in the country, or she might not get drafted at all. Whatever happens, it certainly won’t be because she didn’t put the effort in.”

Meanwhile, Meagher and Van Hattum are chasing their dreams with level heads. “They’re not going to draft someone who isn’t committed and who isn’t going to do their part,” Meagher says. After school, she plans to combine football with a TAFE course in myotherapy (a form of physical treatment) then do university studies in it or physiotherapy. Amidst the whirlwind, Van Hattum often reminds himself why he is doing what he is doing: “Keep it enjoyable, because you have to love footy to be there [on draft night]. It’s a big commitment at this age.” His agent Max Hayes says Van Hattum is locking in on what is important now the business end of the year has arrived, and it’s not all football. “He’s hitting the books hard right now,” Hayes said.

Thousands at Jaguar Land Rover to be offered redundancies after falling profits

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 21:42:11 GMT

As many as 4,000 jobs could be cut over two years after cyberattack and US tariffs take toll

Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyberattack and Donald Trump’s tariffs.

JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported.

As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years.

Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet with JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses.

About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers.

The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain.

Under his predecessor Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack.

The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to the company posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before.

Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively.

“These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May.

The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.

Celtic come from behind to win 2-1 at St Mirren

Rangers beat Motherwell 1-0 but lose Shankland to injury

Yang Hyun-jun scored the winner as Celtic came from behind to beat an impressive St Mirren side 2-1. St Mirren were heading for the top of the Premiership when Nikolas Agrafiotis netted from the spot midway through the first half.

Liam Scales conceded the penalty with a handball but made amends when he headed home six minutes after the break. And Yang finished off a counterattack midway through the second half after good pressing from Camilo Durán.

The victory in Paisley made it five wins from five league games for the champions and inflicted St Mirren’s first Premiership defeat. Martin O’Neill’s side were made to work all the way by a Saints side who played with tempo, invention and managed 19 shots at goal.

Rangers striker Ryan Naderi accepted a gift to score the only goal against Motherwell at Ibrox, but they fear their captain Lawrence Shankland faces a lengthy spell on the sidelines after a hamstring injury suffered early on in the game.

Naderi, who came on for Shankland in the eighth minute, dispossessed Alex Paulsen as the Motherwell goalkeeper attempted to dribble the ball past him outside his box and the German had the simple task of rolling the ball into the net to score what proved to be a 12th-minute winner.

Motherwell dominated possession and created several chances but Rangers were more effective in the final third and should have added to their lead. Kim Min-su missed a first-half penalty and the debutant striker Kevin Kelsy was among those to pass up good opportunities after he came off the bench.

Rangers ultimately saw out the game without any late scares as they recorded a third consecutive Premiership victory.

Of Shankland, the Rangers manager, Derek McInnes, said he fears the injury is similarly significant to the one that kept him out for two months early in 2026. McInnes said: “He has a similar feeling to the hamstring injury he had at Hearts last January. We don’t want to speculate too much but he says it feels similar, in the same area, so we’ll get him scanned on Monday.

Dave Allen’s heavyweight clash with Thomas Carty at Croke Park ended in a bizarre no contest after the Irish favourite fell out of the ring in the first round.

The chief support for Katie Taylor’s final fight before her retirement was over after just one minute and 22 seconds with Carty – seeking the biggest win of his 12-bout career – unable to continue.

Mental health groups have ‘failed to acknowledge’ risk of violence, says Mind chief

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 20:43:02 GMT

Sector has avoided issue because of stigma fears, expert warns ahead of closure of Nottingham attacks inquiry

Mental health organisations have “failed to acknowledge” the risk of violence from a minority of people with severe mental illnesses, the chief executive of Mind has said ahead of the closure of the inquiry into the Nottingham attacks.

Dr Sarah Hughes, who has led mental health charity Mind for four years and has worked in the sector for almost four decades, said charities had shied away from addressing the risk of violence due to the fact it had increased the stigma and harassment around people with mental health conditions.

The inquiry into the Nottingham attacks is examining the events leading up to 13 June 2023, when 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, were fatally stabbed by Valdo Calocane, who was later diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia.

In 2024, Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after admitting three counts of manslaughter on the grounds of diminished responsibility and three counts of attempted murder.

The public inquiry has heard evidence from various local authorities, including health professionals and police officers, as well as Calocane’s family, in order to assess the “events, acts and omissions” that led to the killings.

The inquiry heard how Calocane had committed a string of violent incidents in the years before the attacks, repeatedly refused to take medication, and was sectioned four times in the space of two years. During her evidence, Calocane’s mother described the mental health system as “so broken”.

Speaking exclusively to the Guardian, Hughes said charities specialising in mental health had to become “more comfortable” with discussing the risk of violence that could exist from a minority of people with mental health illnesses.

Hughes’s comments come after the charity Mind held a roundtable with experts in Westminster to discuss the role mental health services needed to play to keep the public and patients safe.

“We, as a charity sector, have failed to acknowledge that violence does happen in some circumstances,” she said. “As a sector, [we] have held the narrative that the majority of people don’t commit violent crime. However, some do and the consequences are grave.”

Hughes added: “My feeling is that we haven’t always been able to articulate the topic of violence and mental health well to the public and ultimately, we have softened the truth. Stigma and discrimination are incredibly harmful, however our efforts to reduce them have, at times, meant that some of the most difficult topics have been brushed under the carpet. That’s why it’s so important to bring together a wide range of experts and experiences to have an open and honest conversation.”

Emma Webber, whose son Barnaby was killed by Calocane, said she welcomed the statement by Hughes. “I do feel like danger to others has been almost deliberately quietened down in the conversation in the past,” she said.

Webber said there had not been enough acknowledgment from mental health organisations of the risk of violence.

“It could be a really powerful voice for the charities to have that difficult conversation, and to not be fearful of saying about the risks of violence toward others, and that people that are mentally ill, like Calocane, can and do go on to kill.

“Obviously the vast majority of people with mental health issues in this country are completely safe … but if somebody’s dangerous, they’re dangerous.

“Had the risks in Calocane’s case been understood, then I genuinely believe we wouldn’t be having this conversation today.”

after newsletter promotion

Seena Fazel, a professor of forensic psychiatry at the University of Oxford who attended the event by Mind, said a minority of people with mental illnesses perpetrate violent acts and high-quality research on schizophrenia had “converged on the same picture”.

“People with schizophrenia do have an elevated risk of violence compared with the general population, even after accounting for socioeconomic factors, but the absolute risk is small. Only a minority will commit a serious violent act,” he said. “That risk increases when other factors are present, particularly drug or alcohol problems, a history of violence, or having been a victim of violence themselves. The important point is that treatments we already have, and which are widely available, can bring that risk down.”

Hughes, who said she had experienced violence when she was a mental health practitioner from people experiencing psychosis, said many in the sector feared that addressing such issues could increase stigma and discrimination, and that could lead to dangerous health outcomes.

“We are incredibly frightened of deepening that stigma and discrimination because we know how dangerous it can be,” she said. “This could risk going back to a more restrictive approach. My view is that’s not the answer, but stigma creates a pathway to that as being the only solution to this problem.”

Hughes said this meant the sector had “shied away” from difficult conversations around violence. “The public, I think, are more ready [and] we’ve got to get our act together,” she said. “Even within Mind there was a reluctance internally and we had to really talk it though.”

Hughes said the UK government’s upcoming mental health strategy must improve support and treatment for those with severe mental illnesses, as well as address matters of public safety.

This includes ensuring an adequate number of beds in hospitals, assertive outreach, and accountability and communication with services.

“I hope that by us having these conversations openly we can both make sure that the people we’re advocating for know that we’re doing this safely with their consent, but equally, the public and families and victims know that we recognise that we have to come together to solve this problem,” Hughes said.

“Crucially, there is a role for Mind – and the sector as a whole – to show that patient and public safety are not mutually exclusive. Both are possible if we want to change our mental health system so people can get the right care before or after reaching crisis point,” she added.

The Box review – no one knows what’s going on here … least of all Gary Lineker

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 20:15:45 GMT

In this bizarre new gameshow, you will encounter John Bercow doing topless karaoke while tossing glitter at pensioners and Joey Essex pounding on the walls of a shipping container. Why? Who knows!

What is The Box? It is easier, perhaps, to list the things The Box is not, if only to give ourselves something to cling to when the more recognisable trappings start to wobble, the floor gives way and we find ourselves in a tent with Joey Essex, watching in silence as a topless John Bercow hurls glitter at an audience of braying pensioners.

So. Some things The Box is not: a sitcom; a medical drama; a property show presented by sockless men with teeth that follow you around the room; a thing about badgers. Beyond this, however, we are on our own. The opening titles do little to assist. “10 BOXES” booms a caption as the camera swoops over a collection of giant yellow containers strapped to the back of a flatbed lorry. “10 CONTESTANTS” it continues, as a montage of coming attractions reveals footage of Graeme Souness squinting at an egg and a member of JLS running towards some trees. And, finally, a distinctly disobliging caption that is nevertheless pivotal to the wilfully befuddling modus operandi of this six-part series: “NO HELP”. Bloody hell. Or rather, “bløødy hell”, because The Box is a Norwegian format so something may have been lost in translation. Anyway, shh, because it’s episode one and here is Gary Lineker.

“Boxes,” he says, peering through his binoculars at 10 yellow boxes. Inside them, we learn, are a corresponding number of trembling minor celebrities. “Remember,” adds our host, chuckling mildly in a jumper the colour of patio, “the celebrities have no idea where they are or what they’re supposed to be doing!”

Tiny cameras capture the mood of the interned stars as they sweat and fidget in their metal tombs. “I don’t like surprises,” gulps broadcaster Ranvir Singh. “I’m in a state of unparalleled uncertainty,” confesses the former speaker of the House of Commons, John Bercow. “I’m Joey Essex,” bellows Joey Essex, pounding on the walls of his box like a distressed navvy trapped in an overflowing portable toilet.

Finally, the doors of the containers slide open and they – and indeed we – are off. But where? And to what end?

As the opening captions state, there is no help and few instructions for the contestants. Instead, they must “work together” to “solve challenges” such as finding hexagons to fit into hexagon-shaped holes and completing an egg and spoon race in a set amount of time. Then they are divided into teams before being sent back to a custom-made house. Then one of them is eliminated. There is no prize.

“One thing’s for sure,” gasps JLS singer JB Gill, “The Box is absolutely unknown!” Alas, this is balls. The only certainty here is that the boxes are pointless, their sole purpose being to briefly conceal contestants from their location, a task that could just as easily be achieved with a blindfold made out of old tights.

This would, however, deny us the sight of Essex bursting out of his box like a frightened horse at Epsom, or a boxed-in Danny “I’m a content creator” Aarons shouting about how he “can’t hear the skies” while frantically thrashing his horrifying Norman-era bowl cut from side to side like a one-man Battle of Hastings. So boxes it is.

Unlike, say, Taskmaster, where chaotic things happen for a reason, here, chaotic things happen for no reason and continue to happen long past the point at which either their chaotic methods or pointlessness would make some sort of sense on a conceptual level. The second episode, for instance, ends with a genuinely harrowing sing-off that climaxes with Bercow performing a rendition of Pink’s So What, while a tentful of holidaymakers aggressively demand he remove his shirt.

The Box isn’t so much a gameshow as a sustained howl of existential confusion. A gameshow that scoffs in the face of convention yet seems bewildered by the bedlam that such showmanship inevitably unleashes. A gameshow in which John Bercow bellows “Orderrrrrr!” while showing us his nipples.

I commend it to the house.

The Box aired on ITV1 and is on ITVX now.

When Dad asked me to edit his novel, I wanted to say no – but ran directly towards the lion’s den

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 20:00:46 GMT

My father doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet he asked for mine. He believed in me

My dad and I believe in many of the same things: cheesecake; the Geelong football club; my mum. And that we should immediately be experts at anything. First try. No practice. No revision.

He taught me this in kindergarten. Every day he pushed me to be brilliant. We played spelling games in the car and did maths workbooks for fun. Before I started school I had “published” a library of my own books, complete with copyright information. I had become – and I’m assuming this is true of most Guardian writers – a precocious kid who irritated everyone around her by being boisterously, aggressively right about everything all of the time. Just like my dad. (Obviously I’ve grown a lot since then.)

So when he asked, at age 77, if I would edit the novel he’d been working on, I responded with what I’ll generously call abject terror. I knew, from teaching hundreds of later-life would-be writers, that there would be feedback. Good Lord, would there. And I also knew, from a lifetime of being explicitly told, that we always got things right the first time. No exceptions.

I wanted to say no. I wanted to tell him, Dad, our relationship is too precious to me. “I’m not sure I have time,” I said, because I am the worst daughter on Earth. But, after my life had flashed before my eyes, I took a beat. The truth is: his outrageous self-belief is well founded. Most people are worse than him at most things. My dad doesn’t ask for help from just anyone. And yet, he had asked for mine.

He didn’t just believe in cake and footy and my mum. He believed in me.

So I did a 180. I ran directly towards the lion’s den. “Sure,” I said, impaling myself on the sword of my dad’s validation, “I would love to edit your novel.”

He sent me the manuscript and I sent him some ground rules: everything was open to suggestion; he wasn’t allowed to yell at me; critiquing his work wasn’t the same as critiquing who he is as a person (writers know this is a lie). He agreed. I opened his document with fear in all four chambers of my heart, and started reading.

I had a lot of feedback. He had written a gorgeous story about young men and football and friendship, but like most new writers, his dialogue clanged. His characters’ actions didn’t ring true. He told too much and showed too little. Nervously, I added comments. At first they were like, “Hi Dad, I love you so much!!!!!! I would maybe consider removing this word ONLY IF YOU WANT TO! Shall we get a coffee?” I sent him a chapter at a time, waiting for him to call and tell me I was out of the will and also a live shark was on its way to kill me.

But he didn’t. Mum sent secret photos of him bent over his laptop, writing and rewriting.

Around page 260, I noticed something. Inside this story about vulnerable young men was a vulnerable older man. As his characters trained and competed to be better than before, so did he. With his 80th birthday in the near distance, my dad was asking me to teach him something new, and I realised he wasn’t perfect at everything first go; he was perfect at persevering. When I was little and frustrated at not being the best, he didn’t show me I didn’t have to try. He wasn’t teaching me I could get things right first time but that I should never stop believing I might.

The tables turned. “This doesn’t make sense,” I wrote. “She would never do this.” I began to lean on what I knew about him. “You know how the wind comes through Norwood Oval and it brings the pie smell? Show me that.” I had a shorthand for everything. A common anecdote. A memory we shared. Family folklore, in-jokes, people we’ve known. “WHY is this character behaving like Simon from the fruit shop???” Sometimes I just called him and made him explain himself, rationalise his choices, workshop a problem until it was solved.

Dad made revisions. The harder I challenged, the better he wrote. Each chapter he returned was an improvement on the last, with people and scenes and conversations busting out of the pages. Not on his first go, or even second go, but on his ninth and tenth goes. “Thank you,” he said, over and over. “This is so helpful.”

The more honest I was, the more he appreciated it. He did not yell at me. He did not think I loved him less.

When Dad published his book this year, we did a podcast about father-daughter editing. He spoke about how much it meant to him that I said yes. I ordered my copy the minute it went live, and when it arrived, I shelved it alongside my own books. Our little library – not of getting it right first time, but of learning to believe you might.

Anna Spargo-Ryan is the author of A Kind of Magic, The Gulf and The Paper House, and a winner of the Horne prize

‘Grief becomes a routine’: Farhana lost five babies. A ‘culture of silence’ exacerbated her pain

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 20:00:45 GMT

A first-of-its-kind study shows the prevalence of miscarriage in Australia but experts fear multicultural groups remain underrepresented

On a quiet street in western Sydney, Farhana Laffernis races her curious English staffy and boisterous three-year-old daughter in the front door.

Inside, her three-year-old wears a pink tutu and excitedly babbles as she cuddles her toy doll. The family life Laffernis has built did not come easy.

The 34-year-old has experienced five miscarriages. For someone who “always wanted to be a mum”, the experience “completely shattered” her.

“Grief almost becomes practised or like a routine. You still feel the sting of it every time it happens,” she says. “It’s almost like your mind and your body know the drill.”

Laffernis isn’t alone. Three in 10 women who gave birth in 2022 had previously experienced miscarriage, meaning pregnancy loss before 20 weeks’ gestation, according to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare. One in 10 had experienced two or more.

The data comes from a first-of-its-kind study in Australia, heralded for helping create better understanding of the prevalence of early pregnancy loss. The study came about after a years-long push by Isabelle Oderberg, founder of peak advocacy group the Early Pregnancy Loss Coalition (EPLC), who was concerned about substandard care for women who had miscarriages after experiencing seven losses herself.

Currently, there is no requirement for doctors to report miscarriage, meaning the data is not collected.

But while the new study has been welcomed, experts fear the data does not capture large groups of women, particularly those from multicultural backgrounds – like Laffernis. And they say the lack of data could mean diverse families are missing out on services they desperately need.

Laffernis’s first miscarriage occurred eight weeks into her first pregnancy. It was during the height of the Covid-19 lockdowns, and she couldn’t have her partner with her at any of her appointments and scans.

“It was the first time in my life that I’d ever experienced anything like that, or felt real grief and loss before,” she says. “I was getting all of this terrible news pretty much on my own and having to kind of process that and figure it out.”

That was the first of two miscarriages Laffernis had before successfully conceiving her daughter through IVF. She remembers being “so terrified the whole way through”.

“It seems like everywhere you turn, someone is having this, like, blissful ignorant pregnancy where nothing can possibly go wrong … I could not have that, I just could not be that blissful, relaxed, unaware pregnant woman.”

Another three pregnancy losses after her daughter’s birth marked “the end of the road” in her attempts to have more children.

For Laffernis, who comes from a migrant Indian family, the pain of the miscarriages was exacerbated by a reluctance within her family to talk about what was happening.

“When I was talking to my own family about my losses, the first one was sort of ‘bad luck’, the second one was like ‘Oh, that’s a little bit of extra bad luck’… but then it happens like five times and you kind of just like stop telling people at that point.

“I think in a lot of migrant families, or at least in my experience … there is that sort of mentality in a lot of our communities where our parents have come over [to Australia] from less than ideal circumstances,” she says.

“Maybe miscarriage isn’t the worst thing that’s ever happened to anyone ever, but it was the worst thing that had ever happened to me.”

After years to trying to avoid conflict around the “deeply upsetting” interactions, she had to confront her family about the support she needed.

“I went for a long time just sort of trying not to have the argument before it all just honestly got to me. I did have to have some really hard conversations with members of my family about exactly what it was that I needed from them at this time in my life,” she says.

That reluctance to talk about miscarriage within migrant families is something Dr Fatima El-Assaad has seen many times before.

“It’s something that’s considered very icky to talk about,” says El-Assaad, who founded Sydney-based The Still Nest, a platform supporting diverse families affected by infertility, pregnancy loss, birth trauma and infant loss.

She says cultural and religious practices tied to a women’s fertility journey “may make them feel like it is not in the public arena” and “like it’s something that is meant to be kept behind closed doors”.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

after newsletter promotion

While she is encouraged to see data on miscarriage come to light, she questions how representative it is of culturally and linguistically diverse families – and worries that a culture of silence, compounded by the way the data is collected, could be contributing to “a number of holes in the picture”.

The data was collected using existing surveys and clinical registries compiled by midwives and other birth attendants. El-Assaad says flaws in the system could be leading to significant gaps and inaccuracies in the data.

“Are [surveys] primarily in English? Is there a translator that is trauma-informed? … How was the survey conducted? … Where was it captured? Was it in a clinic? Was it at home on a personal device? Was the place safe?” she says, listing factors that can affect the process.

“And we’re also asking culturally and racially marginalised people, and culturally and linguistically diverse people, to just voluntarily answer a survey on top of all the other issues that they’re currently dealing with.”

Although miscarriage is “the most common pregnancy complication”, there’s a lack of healthcare and social support – and Australia is “so far behind”, Oderberg says.

“We had no idea how many people in Australia were experiencing miscarriage, whether it was going up, down, sideways,” she says. There was also a lack of information about high priority groups, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women, newly arrived migrants people whose second language is English, people from lower socioeconomic demographics.

Oderberg says data directly helps governments understand what kind of support services the community needs and where.

Assoc Prof Jade Bilardi from Miscarriage Australia says efforts to be inclusive must “go beyond” simply translating resources into different languages.

“That’s a great first step, but it’s to work more with women, pregnant people, partners, family members, and support services that work directly with people from Cald backgrounds so that we can better understand what their needs are,” she says.

Laffernis says she hopes to see greater awareness filter through the medical system, normalising conversations about pregnancy loss.

“No one had really talked to me about the risk of miscarriage until it was already looking like that was what was happening. And then, once they had talked about the fact that it was likely to happen, it became about the fact that this happens to so many people and it’s so common,” she says.

She also holds hopes to see a dedicated focus on post-miscarriage support, including mental health services, for all women.

“I don’t think there’s really anything that can prepare you for what happens. I think it’s more what happens next that makes the difference.”

In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306, and support for people who are grieving is available from Griefline on 1300 845 745. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In the US, call the national maternal health hotline on 1-833-852-6262.

Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 19:57:21 GMT

Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions

Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover in Kent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning.

Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right.

The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways.

Videos shared online showed a large number of masked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars.

By lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings.

The number of people involved was not immediately clear. One livestreamer estimated he was marching with hundreds of people but police did not give an official estimate.

Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and chanting “stop the boats”and “England till I die.”

A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade.

The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform.

In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying: “Get there to support them.”

In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000s of men willing to fill their shoes.”

The founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream.

In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government. “Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is.

“And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.”

In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before.

“And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.”

On Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town.

Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area.”

One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said: “I was at Dover port this morning, trying to get on a ferry to France. In the end we left and returned home – it wasn’t worth our while, we were only going to Lille for the day.

“But the headlines calling it a ‘protest’ suggest something very different to what took place – which looked like a highly organised event.

“Masked teenagers in black clothes were coordinated by walkie-talkie and I directly witnessed an older man, not in black, on an electric bike – coordinating in plain sight and being applauded by the masked teenagers as he gave them the thumbs up for their ‘good work’.

“The guy on the bike then went to the nearest police stop, [he was] obviously monitoring and reporting police activity.

“There were no banners and no slogans, just pure intimidation. It was a demonstration only in the sense that they wanted to demonstrate their power and to intimidate.”

Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption.

“I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.”

Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners.

“I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused.

“We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.”

The shipping company DFDS and P&O Ferries said they would offer customers whose journeys were disrupted access to the next available departure.

“When you promise the crowd a fast race, you have a responsibility to follow through – at least in my view. This isn’t about me losing. I wasn’t good enough. It’s about taking responsibility for the commitments you’ve made to the meeting organisers, the crowd and your competitors.”

Ingebrigtsen, who returned to racing in August after 11 months out after an achilles sheath injury, ended up following the pacemakers himself after no one else went with them.

Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger review – mammoth tour movie brings the joy and poignancy of reunion

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 19:30:44 GMT

The Gallagher brothers’ comeback concerts are given the full fan-worship treatment, but it’s impossible to begrudge the euphoria they have created

“Hello … hello … It’s good to be back.” With these words – and the unfortunate possibility of a royalty payment to a certain disgraced ex-pop star – this highly enjoyable fan-worship documentary revives the memory of last year’s staggering and already mythic Oasis reunion tour. It also recollects how effortlessly funny the Gallagher brothers are, like a great comic double act. There’s a big laugh in the tense scene in the rehearsal room, when Liam finally shows up after Noel and everyone else had been there for hours – and the very first thing that comes out of his mouth is a fierce and magnificently sullen objection to the baffles on the drum kit: “They’re giving me the hump.”

Yet to the surprise of many who did not believe, and these biblical echoes are strangely appropriate, Liam and Noel did not fall out; the resulting stadium tour put a fresh coat of paint on the word “phenomenon”. Middle-aged and elderly people together with young people sporting bucket hats, some accompanied by their pets in bucket hats, sang their hearts out as if it was the 90s again and Manchester City had just won the World Cup 10-0 (although this film was evidently completed before Wonderwall’s moment at this year’s World Cup).

We see again the Oasis congregation engaging in colossal Dionysian events of mass joy – but of course, the poignancy of time passing and the irresistible narrative of the brothers’ public reconciliation give a new layer of emotion to the songs. Noel now looks like the silver-fox dad of the band; Liam, with what looks like a ridge or a scar on his nose that I don’t remember from before, looks more like a bloke whose pint you do not want to spill, a pint around which you want to put a 10-metre exclusion zone. But this was always the case. Noel’s songs always combined, in a distinctive way, euphoria and sadness, moods which seem to float free of meaning in the strictest sense. Now they and all their fans have got something to be euphoric and sad about.

As for the brothers’ togetherness, I think the film shows it is sincere and real in public, and real on stage, where it counts. Noel and Liam are rarely interviewed together; here mostly it is Noel solo. I wonder if, like Mick Jagger and Keith Richards, they now come together to make music after reaching an accommodation. Whatever wound each other up has not magically vanished, but is being managed. Part of the problem was that Noel’s songwriting credits made the big money – not Liam. Perhaps the lawyers have hammered something out here, but it is not shown in the film.

The documentary begins with an extended montage of the 90s glory days leading to the ugly falling out in the 00s, and how the non-Oasis years coincided with an era of inept politicians and terrible sadness all round. Then we see Keir Starmer chortlingly agree how great it is that Oasis reunited on his watch. But this film misses out one of the most famous moments of their career: Noel’s 1997 handshake with Tony Blair at the Downing Street victory party, which came to capture the zeitgeist of Cool Britannia. The film does not include Noel’s earlier comment at the Brits: “There are seven people in this room tonight who are giving a little bit of hope to young people in this country. That is me, our kid, Bonehead, Guigsy, Alan White and Tony Blair.” Noel is not asked about Blair here, but both him and Liam reject any notion they are “rightwing”.

From here we are immersed in the gigs themselves, on the face of it no bigger in scale than many other band’s live shows, but with the specific tearful ecstasy that U2 or Metallica or the Stones cannot manage. As Liam says, they just stand there, rooted to their mic positions; they don’t do Jagger acrobatics, it’s very relaxing and they can keep doing it for years. It was always difficult to be cynical about Oasis and now it’s impossible.

Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger screened at the Venice film festival and is out on 11 September in the UK and US

Police seize £200k Lamborghini under tightened antisocial driving laws

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 19:23:40 GMT

Officers seize supercar in Southend after reports of it being driven at up to twice speed limit

Police have seized a Lamborghini potentially worth more than £200,000 under tightened laws introduced to crack down on dangerous driving.

Essex police confiscated the Lamborghini Huracan on Saturday afternoon after receiving reports of the supercar being driven dangerously in Southend. The car was travelling at speeds suspected to be more than twice the limit, police said.

“Antisocial driving can pose a danger to other people using the road and cause misery to residents,” a force spokesperson said.

“The safety of our communities will always be our priority and we’ll take action against those who risk the safety of others.”

The online marketplace Autotrader estimates the total retail value of the Lamborghini Huracan at £238,195, depending on the model.

The vehicle was seized under section 59 of the Police Reform Act, which was strengthened earlier this year to allow police to immediately confiscate a vehicle causing – or likely to cause – alarm, distress or annoyance to the public.

Previously, drivers received a warning under which their vehicle could only be seized if they were involved in another antisocial driving incident within 12 months.

Officers can still choose to give a warning at their discretion. The law allows officers to stop and seize vehicles, or enter premises where they believe the vehicle is being held – and “use reasonable force where necessary”.

Wheelspins and burnouts, drifting in public places, racing in residential areas and repeated revving “causing nuisance” were all reasons for which vehicles could be seized, the Essex police spokesperson said.

The Metropolitan police last year seized 72 luxury cars worth more than £6m in a crackdown on antisocial driving in London.

The vehicles – which included Ferraris, Lamborghinis and Bentleys – were either unroadworthy or being driven illegally, the Met said.

Last month, a police officer drove a Ferrari Monza SP2 worth £3.7m after the open-top limited-edition supercar was seized in a separate, record-breaking crackdown.
