Putin begins talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on ending war with Ukraine

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 19:03:41 GMT

Moscow and Kyiv vow not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during negotiations

Russian president Vladimir Putin began talks with US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on ending more than four years of war in Ukraine in the Kremlin Saturday, ahead of their first visit to Kyiv expected on Sunday.

Both Russia and Ukraine vowed not to strike each other’s capitals for three days during the negotiations, as Washington tries to revive US-led talks to end Europe’s worst conflict since the second world war.

The visit came as Donald Trump suggested on Friday a new proposal to end the war, without providing any details on what his new plan might be. Trump made ending the war a priority early in his second term, but his efforts have so far yielded little results.

Trump said his son-in-law Kushner and business ally Witkoff were bringing “a proposal to end the war”.

“Dear colleagues, I warmly welcome you to Moscow. The situation is, of course, not simple,” Putin told the envoys in a grand Kremlin hall in footage aired by Russian TV. “But before we begin to address it, I would like to ask everyone to convey their best wishes and words of gratitude to US president Mr Trump,” Putin said.

The talks come as the grinding war saw increasing civilian deaths and attacks this summer. Putin has repeatedly said Moscow intends to seize the rest of east Ukraine.

The war, launched by Russia in 2022, has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced millions.

Russian strikes on Ukraine Saturday killed at least seven people, including in the Kyiv suburbs, Ukrainian officials said.

The Kremlin said it would not strike Kyiv from midnight Saturday, while the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he would halt strikes on Moscow “from now” until Monday.

“The Russian president, the commander-in-chief, has given the order from midnight tonight not to strike Kyiv for three days,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said.

Zelenskyy, who had offered a truce during the US visits, later said he had spoken to the US envoys and also promised Kyiv would not strike Moscow.

“From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow,” he said on social media.

The Ukrainian leader said he had spoken to the US officials and that he expected them in Kyiv Sunday.

Russia had earlier struck Kyiv suburbs, with Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to disrupt their visit with overnight attacks on Kyiv’s two airports – as well as on civilian targets in the Dnipro region that killed five people.

“Two people were killed in the Bucha district” outside Kyiv, the head of the Kyiv region, Tymur Tkachenko, said.

Large gaps remain between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the war. On Friday, the Kremlin said it was sticking by the position Putin set out two years earlier – that Ukraine should give up four regions claimed by Russia and not join Nato. That position is intolerable to Ukraine.

Witkoff and Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv on Sunday, which would be the first time the two envoys have visited the Ukrainian capital. Both have visited Moscow before, most recently in January when they met Putin in the Kremlin.

As peace efforts floundered in recent months, with US attention turned to its war with Iran, the conflict has intensified.

Ground troops have been locked in a grinding stalemate along the 775-mile (1,250km) frontline with little advances on either side. Both sides have intensified their aerial attacks in recent weeks, hitting increasingly distant targets.

Ukraine has carried out long-range strikes on Russian military facilities, oil refineries and e-commerce warehouses, to try to degrade Russia’s war effort and economy. Its strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to fuel shortages and rising prices at the pump.

On Friday, a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), one of the agencies responsible for carrying out deep-strike operations in Russia. Zelenskyy has vowed to retaliate. Russia has also increased its attacks on Kyiv and other cities with waves of bombardments, stretching Ukraine’s air defence systems.

Zelenskyy accused Russia of trying to disrupt the envoys’ visit to Ukraine with strikes on Kyiv’s two airports overnight. “Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said in a post on X. Officials visiting Ukraine have largely done so by train, as Ukrainian airspace has been closed since 2022 due to the war.

On Friday, Russia carried out overnight strikes, killing five people and wounding five more at a factory in the southern Dnipropetrovsk region, according to the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. He said those killed were employees working at the factory who were “doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.”

A 62-year-old man was injured and several homes and a building were damaged in another attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said.

Russia also struck a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region with drones overnight, damaging the building and injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl. Emergency services said they were repeatedly forced to withdraw because of the threat of more strikes.

Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched ballistic missiles and 167 drones overnight, including jet-powered UAVs. Ukrainian air defences disabled 128 of the drones, the air force said.

Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 53 Ukrainian drones overnight.

Glasner conceded at least one angle showed Williams appeared to handle the ball, seemingly to protect himself as Tonali went to clear the ball with his left boot, but said the footage was too unclear to disallow the goal. “I don’t think VAR can intervene when he’s guessing,” said Forest’s head coach. “It was not clear and obvious. I know refereeing a Premier League game is really difficult – refereeing a training session is sometimes really difficult – but we are told to support the referee, to keep the threshold for VAR intervention very high, to strengthen the referee’s decision and they didn’t do that today. With these kinds of situations, you weaken the referees.”

Bankes checked the goal and then the referee, Craig Pawson, took to the mic before awarding a Spurs free-kick amid a chorus of boos from the home support: “After review, the ball touches the hand of Nottingham Forest’s No 3 before the goal is scored.” Williams was adamant he did not handle the ball. “I headed it in between my arms,” said the Wales defender, who this week signed a new four-year contract. “If you’re going to pause it, it’s going to look like it hit my arm but it didn’t. The disallowed goal was undeniably the moment of an underwhelming contest. For the third successive league match, Tottenham failed to score and this time they did not even muster a shot on target. Mykhailo Mudryk was brought off the bench for his first competitive minutes for 645 days after a doping suspension but Spurs were blunt. Aside from a 5-1 win against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup, their season so far reads: five goals against and none scored.

Apart from Gibbs-White’s effort in the buildup to the disallowed goal, Forest’s only other shot on goal was a daisy-cutter from James McAtee. The Spurs league debutant Sávio, a £75m arrival from Manchester City, showed a few neat touches but he and Destiny Udogie were withdrawn after an hour on the advice of Tottenham’s medical department. “I’m not happy when we have the plan but it is for my advantage, my business, the management of the players after their injuries,” said De Zerbi, who accepted his team lacked quality in the final third. “We have to make better decisions, to keep more calm when we are very close to do something important.”

A second-half masterclass from the Boks, the relentless kind that leaves even opponents as worthy as these suffocated, gasping for air, confirms what was taken as read before this series started – South Africa remain the hot favourites for next year’s World Cup.

There is a fourth Test next week in Baltimore but the reality is it is a money-spinning appendage to the three matches in South Africa. The Springboks lost the first but have roared back on home soil. They take a 2-1 lead in the series and are unofficial winners of the best-of-three contest in South Africa. The All Blacks have failed in their quest to emulate the class of 1996.

No individual performance was more significant than their collective ability to put on the squeeze but Ox Nché’s 56 minutes at the coalface were exceptional and it is no coincidence that Siya Kolisi, who now has more Test wins than any other Springboks captain, sat out the one Test South Africa have lost this series.

The All Blacks showed their class for much of this contest, which hinged on Jesse Kriel’s decisive second-half score just after Will Jordan had struck for New Zealand. From that moment on, South Africa smelled blood and capitalised with the ruthless streak that has crowned them consecutive World Cup winners.

The All Blacks are evidently their closest challengers and matched the Boks’ four tries with four of their own. They possess a remarkable running game but eventually South African power has caught up with them. They will rue losing Savea to a shoulder injury late in the first half – “He won’t travel now,” said head coach Dave Rennie of the captain’s chances of making the Baltimore Test – and some key mistakes after the interval. Perhaps Ruben Love’s two missed kicks at goal too. Savea’s early withdrawal was certainly a setback but it is no excuse, not least because Cheslin Kolbe lasted all of 10 minutes before going off in another Test match of remarkable intensity. South Africa’s head coach Rassie Erasmus later revealed Kolbe had broken his jaw.

A breathless first half began with a statement of intent by the All Blacks. First the Springboks’ maul was stopped in its tracks, then South Africa’s bulldozing No 8 Jasper Wiese was knocked back in the tackle. A mesmerising run up the middle by Jordan demonstrated the All Blacks had come to play too and the Springboks were rattled when Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu was sent to the sin-bin for a deliberate knock-on.

From the resulting lineout move, Savea had space to pounce for the opening try and to compound matters for South Africa, Kolbe had been taken off with a head injury. South Africa’s foothold came from the set-piece superiority, however, and shortly after Feinberg-Mngomezulu’s return, Kurt-Lee Arendse was over on the right.

The All Blacks were at this point struggling at the breakdown but have showcased throughout this tour an ability to strike on the counter. Again Savea was the beneficiary for their second try which owed much to some nifty footwork from Tupou Vaa’i and plenty to their innate ability to stay patient and keep the ball alive.

For the third week in a row South Africa finished the first half the stronger and the All Blacks were dealt an almighty blow when Savea was taken off in clear discomfort. Manie Libbok proceeded to go close after an astonishing pickup by Nché but Love had infringed on his own line and became the second fly-half to be shown a yellow card. A dominant Springboks scrum yielded a penalty try and parity at 12-12 at the break.

The second half took a while to ignite but Love’s missed penalty lit the touch paper. Jordan started and finished the All Blacks’ third try with a fine chip through to Leroy Carter, who popped the ball up off the floor to his fellow winger. Almost immediately, however, the Boks responded when Kriel slipped past Carter far too easily and sped to the line. Feinberg-Mngomezulu converted whereas Love had missed his effort to nose South Africa ahead.

It was sloppy by Carter and the same can be said of Jordan, when his overhit kick led to a Springboks scrum. The inevitable penalty was kicked to the corner and a ferocious rumble by South Africa was finished off by the irrepressible Malcolm Marx. A Feinberg-Mngomezulu penalty pushed South Africa’s lead to 12 with 10 minutes to play and though the All Blacks had finished the stronger in both previous Tests, they could only muster a pushover score by Samisoni Taukei’aho with the clock well into the red.

‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 16:26:13 GMT

Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference

UK politics live

Nigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas.

The Reform UK leader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides.

Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations.

The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers.

The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time.

“I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.”

In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office.

When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.”

He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.”

Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday.

Its Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031.

But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.”

In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back.

Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on the string of allegations related to his and the party’s finances.

“And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said.

Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him.

Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes, may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing.

The final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted.

The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward.

The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police.

Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July.

“They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident.

Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives.

Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”.

Farage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”.

“Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.

Haaland edges Manchester City past Coventry as Fernández sparkles on debut

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 16:02:51 GMT

Enzo Fernández started for Manchester City after Nico O’Reilly’s back injury during the warm-up and sparkled, showing why the club paid a British-record-equalling £125m for the midfielder. The winner came courtesy of Erling Haaland’s 300th goal in club football and Fernández had a key part, feeding Antoine Semenyo, whose cross from the right was crashed home.

In the second half Coventry hammered away, but their wait for a first top-flight goal since Mustapha Hadji’s second in a 3-2 defeat at Aston Villa on 5 May 2001 goes on. The visitors did not like losing, but were heartened by holding the star-studded hosts to a slender win, though the bottom line is all three of their Premier League outings on their return have been defeats.

Frank Lampard said: “I don’t think we deserved to lose. I’m disappointed we didn’t get what we deserved – which was a point. We can walk out of here with our heads held extremely high.”

Enzo Maresca’s men have a maximum nine points so can be supremely satisfied. “Today was not a nice win, a bit ugly,” he said. “In the first half we deserved more goals – we scored one but could have scored one or two more.”

The manager said of Fernández: “The reason Enzo was on the bench [initially] was because he arrived only a few days ago. I know how frustrating it was for him in the last weeks but in the end he played some minutes and was quite good. Nico felt something in his back – not serious.”

Ayyoub Bouaddi, bought for £85m, was on the bench for the hosts, as Fernández lined up alongside Rayan Cherki in a 4-1-2–2-1 that had Semenyo and Iliman Ndiaye, another new home signing, stationed behind Haaland.

Coventry, with Ethan Pinnock and Frank Onyeka replacing Caleb Yirenkyi and Loum Tchaouna from the XI that lost at home to Hull, could have taken the lead when Abdukodir Khusanov played the ball back to Gianluigi Donnarumma and it slipped under the goalkeeper’s boot, but the Italian scrambled it clear. The visitors should then have bridged the 25 years to Hadji when a Semenyo pass meant for Rúben Dias was intercepted by Taiwo Awoniyi. But when the striker ran in his radar failed, and the shot was pulled wide.

The longer Coventry stayed level the better their prospects. Cherki fed a galloping Haaland and he twisted and let fly, but Carl Rushworth’s save was equal to the shot. Then, dazzling Cherki footwork – after a pass from Fernández – was followed by an effort that struck a post.

The frame of the goal and Rushworth could do nothing to stop Haaland’s opener. This time Fernández curved a pass in behind for Semenyo, the right-winger spun the ball over, and Haaland did the rest.

This was 26 minutes in and Coventry were under siege. Fernández collected the ball along the right, looked up and aimed a cross for Haaland but it failed to beat the first man. Then Cherki, again in Fred Astaire mode, made space and saw an effort blocked.

Maresca wants his wingers to be more direct – utilising the pace of Ndiaye and Semenyo – and the tactic spun Coventry. So, too, did an impish Cherki flick which put Haaland in again: he rode a challenge when going down might have brought a penalty, before shooting. Rushworth once more thwarted the Norwegian.

Catastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolution

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 15:00:39 GMT

Like France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risks

Devolution in England is going to be messy and slow, and brings with it huge risks that Andy Burnham ignores at his peril.

The prime minister’s devolution push will be messy because Whitehall’s ingrained anxiety about handing over money and power will lead to piecemeal deals, starting with a deal for Cornwall that will lack the much-promised driving force of a newly minted mayor.

And there is every prospect that it will be slow now that the reappointed housing secretary Angela Rayner’s reorganisation of local government, creating hundreds of unitary authorities where counties and districts once ruled, is mired in judicial reviews. Some councils have run up huge debts in the last decade and it’s not clear how these debts will be divided among the new entities.

There are claims that plans to divide some existing county councils into three, four or even five unitary authorities is politically motivated and that Labour has become seduced by the prospect of retaining a presence in local government through gerrymandering.

Last week, Hertfordshire county council and Newcastle-under-Lyme borough council became the latest local authorities to send letters to Rayner, seeking clarity on how the government reached its decision in their areas.

A week earlier, Lincolnshire county council did the same. Farther south, Essex county, which is to be divided into five unitary authorities, found that the recommendation of Whitehall officials for just three new authorities was overruled by Rayner.

Supposedly, all this infighting will be resolved by Christmas and England will be ready for an entirely new map of local authorities by next May when fresh elections will be held.

Surely these councils and combined authorities, many of which are also embryonic, will struggle to become public institutions with verve, drive, knowledge and experience, able to make good decisions in time for the next election in 2029.

When devolution is the prime minister’s big idea, one that will energise Britain’s spirit of enterprise, how it works is going to be crucial. He cannot risk Reform UK and the Tories crowing about another broken promise; or how it shows the British state is clogged with officials waiting for their generous pension, and in need of a Trumpian deep clean.

Rayner’s plan is rooted in a belief that local government has failed to work properly and that structural reform is the answer, saving much more over the longer term than the estimated £2bn initial cost.

It is a belief that has no basis in academic study. It would be a relief to all of those involved in local government and devolution to know that somewhere in the world there was data illustrating how this kind of structural change improves services, saves money and, as Burnham would have it, supercharges economic growth.

Unfortunately there isn’t any such evidence. It is, to use a well-worn cliche, just re-arranging deckchairs. And it is not just because the same people will be taking up the same roles in new offices (and yes, there will need to be five head offices instead of one in Essex).

As the Institute for Government says: “Structural reforms can be necessary, and useful. But there is nothing inherently valuable about them.”

What improves services are reforms to the way public officials work, and that means difficult discussions with trade unions. There needs to be a level of accountability that is absent in significant areas of the public sector. And it will be crucial to change how public organisations relate to each other, how they work together, breaking down old silos and protective practices. It involves giving more information to local people and including them in decision making going forward.

Sign up to Business Today

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

after newsletter promotion

Geoff Mulgan, a University College London professor and the former boss of the Nesta thinktank, says devolution must answer basic questions people should know, such as how private and public services are delivered and who determines the outcome, from broadband to banking.

“Otherwise it will remain entirely legitimate for populist politicians to say that people have lost control and to claim that they are the answer,” he says.

In most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic, not imposed. Germany grew out of mini-kingdoms. The US started as a collection of states. The Länder in Germany, and US states, agreed to a federal government while retaining a good deal of power for themselves.

The UK is more like France. It has always been centralised, and gained in many ways from that and lost out in others. So we should not underestimate how difficult it will be to impose a new political structure on England that devolves money and power to brand new councils and mayors, or in the case of Cornwall, a cabinet committee.

The public will rightly be sceptical when so many councils under the current system have fallen for the idea that they can raise themselves up if only they borrow lots of money and “invest it” in new stuff. A new high street with hotels and leisure facilities was Woking borough council’s dream until it crashed, £2bn in debt.

To say there are huge dangers in the world of finance when local council leaders are let loose, armed with a mission to generate growth, is to understate the situation. There are catastrophic dangers waiting.

‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 14:00:38 GMT

MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective

Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened.

But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality.

In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict.

This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash.

It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre.

Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer.

Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran.

It is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules.

But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme.

“[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.”

Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for.

Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said.

The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government.

No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.”

A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend.

Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”.

Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs.

Sign up to First Edition

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

after newsletter promotion

While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold.

The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt.

However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to.

The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks.

Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring.

Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down.

Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches.

Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility.

Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid.

Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.”

Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”

‘I don’t like the term neurodivergence – it sounds like political correctness’: Werner Herzog on fans, fanaticism and baby foxes

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 12:15:04 GMT

The Bavarian auteur talks directing Kate and Rooney Mara in Bucking Fastard and his popularity on Instagram

In outsider visionaries such as Aguirre, Fitzcarraldo or Timothy Treadwell, renegade German director Werner Herzog has created some of cinema’s most memorable monomaniacs – characters singularly obsessed with finding mythical cities made of gold, with building opera houses in the middle of the rainforest, or with befriending wild grizzly bears.

But suggestions that they could be role models for the modern-day neurodiversity movement send this famously fearless film-maker running for the hills. “I don’t like the term neurodivergence and ADHD, or whatever – it sounds like political correctness, which scares me under the table,” Herzog said at the Venice film festival.

The protagonist pair of Bucking Fastard, the new film that Herzog has brought to the Lido, slots right into his gallery of single-minded outsiders. Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara play siblings Jean and Joan Holbrooke, who have separate bodies but speak in unison, dress the same and share the same preoccupations.

First they fall in love with their washed-up heart-throb neighbour (played by Orlando Bloom) and exact revenge when he marries another woman, then they embark on a quixotic quest to dig a tunnel connecting a cave in County Sligo to the Orkneys. Contemporary psychiatrists might detect behaviour consistent with autism or ADHD hyper-focus. Not Herzog.

“I do not relate to all these trendy terms – I just can’t hear it, it dusts out of my ears,” said the Bavaria-born US-based director, speaking in the idiosyncratic, heavily accented English familiar to viewers of documentaries like My Favourite Fiend. “Neurodivergence sounds like there’s some sort of clinical aberration – these sisters are dead centre.”

His first non-documentary feature in 17 years, Bucking Fastard revisits old Herzogian themes but also breaks with them. The film is loosely based on the lives of Freda and Greta Chaplin, an intensely mutually attached pair of twins from York whom the German director met in the 1980s and who coined the spoonerism of the title in a court hearing.

Like the Chaplins, the Holbrookes are ostracised by their family and neighbours, but in the film they also show resilience and find allies and supporters. “What is certainly different [to my earlier films] is that the sisters are not just nice, they’re vengeful”, said Herzog. “They are arsonists, they destroy things.”

The Werner Herzog of social-media parodies is bleakly preoccupied with the cruel chaos inherent in the natural world, telling stories of suicidal penguins, man-eating bears, and birds “who don’t sing but screech in pain”. Yet in Bucking Fastard, the sisters rescue a young fox who, contrary to the warnings of a gang of overzealous hunters, doesn’t infect them with rabies.

“We had in mind to have a baby fox they would warm under their armpits, but we could not find one all over Ireland,” Herzog recalled. “There was an animal dealer who told me, ‘I can get you a little fox, but only under one condition: you must never ask how we got it.’” Herzog declined. “I’m not in this business. You want to dig up a den and bring me a little fox – I’m not into that.”

At 83, could the radical doomsayer of European art-house cinema be discovering his sentimental side? “What I do is lively and creates some inner life, some excitement and some joy in the storytelling,” Herzog said. “I’m not a control freak.”

His taste for pathos, however, remains irrepressible. Bucking Fastard features a sequence shot inside a large karst cave system near Postojna, Slovenia, which Herzog described in similarly reverential tones as the French subterranean landscape in 2010’s Cave of Forgotten Dreams: “It is a landscape of the soul, a landscape of the imagination.”

His old-fashioned way of looking at the world keeps winning him young admirers, he claimed. “A huge amount of audiences that contact me these days are 15, 16, maybe 17 years old,” he said.

Last year, he started his own Instagram account, where he has posted reels of himself barbecuing, doing DIY and unboxing packages. He said he did it at the behest of his youngest son, who told his father he shouldn’t be so isolated from his audience. Since he still doesn’t own a own mobile phone, however, he hasn’t been able to check out the content-creating competition.

“I had a big retrospective at the Centre Pompidou in Paris in 2024, and the audience was all, all, all young people. The curators told me there was a Godard retrospective right before mine, and the people who came to that? They were all Godard’s age. They were all over 80.”

The US attorney general is fretting about a ‘pandemic’ of gender transitions in schools

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 12:00:37 GMT

Todd Blanche’s remarks are part of a totally-not-invented moral panic that stretches the limits of the imagination

Being a public school teacher in the US these days is tough. You’ve got to pay for a lot of your own supplies, deal with smartphone-addicted children and perform gender-affirming surgeries on your lunch break.

Luckily our intrepid attorney general, Todd Blanche, is on the case. Blanche appeared on Fox News this week to decry a “pandemic” of gender transitions in schools across the US. “There’s not a parent in America, no matter where you live, that would want their school to change and call their child by a different name and not expect to be told about that. We partnered with the Department of Education recently to combat this very trend and, really, pandemic that’s happening in some school districts around the country,” Blanche said. He seemed more concerned with name changes than with surgery, but the president himself has suggested on several occasions that schools are furtively doing surgery on children. During a campaign speech in 2024, for example, Donald Trump said: “Can you imagine … your son leaves the house and you say: ‘Jimmy, I love you so much. Go have a good day in school,’ and your son comes back with a brutal operation? Can you even imagine this?”

No, I can’t even imagine this. The public schools near me can’t afford air conditioning, so I’m not sure where they are getting all these operating theaters and surgeons from.

Still, don’t let my lack of imagination stop you from getting outraged over this totally-not-invented moral panic, which is consuming valuable government resources. Blanche’s Fox News interview came shortly after the justice department filed what it described as a “first-of-its-kind lawsuit” against a Kansas school district, aimed at stopping it from “facilitating secret ‘gender transitions’ for children at school without their parents’ knowledge or consent”. The district, which denies wrongdoing, risks losing almost $70m in federal funds if it is found to have violated federal law.

While this all sounds terribly dramatic, the substance of the Kansas public school lawsuit is actually rather mundane. It seems what is riling the Trump administration up are some extremely reasonable internal school guidelines, never adopted as formal policy, which state, according to the justice department complaint, that if a transgender student doesn’t want their parents notified about their preferred names and pronouns “that request will be evaluated on a case-by-case basis”.

There’s certainly a sensible conversation to be had about whether teachers should inform parents if their child wishes to be known by a different name. And Blanche might actually want to ask the vice-president to weigh in on that matter, considering JD Vance has changed his own name multiple times. But let’s not pretend that Blanche and Fox News are interested in sensible conversations. One suspects they just want to whip viewers up into a frenzy about trans people, a favourite boogeyman, in order to distract from the fact that the Trump administration is pillaging the country for personal gain.

Let’s also not pretend that the attorney general, who was confirmed last month, is in his job because he is deeply invested in the wellbeing of America’s young people. Blanche was Trump’s personal criminal defense lawyer before he was brought into the White House; he eventually became attorney general following the ousting of Pam Bondi. He is a Trump loyalist who once said he’d tell the president: “Thank you very much. I love you, sir” if Trump nominated someone else for the job. He’s got his job, I’d wager, because he’s made it clear he’ll protect the president and advance Trump’s agenda. Indeed, one of the very first things that Blanche’s justice department did after he was confirmed as attorney general was to issue an opinion stating that the president’s “executive privilege” can extend to advisers who don’t work for his administration. Which makes it harder for Democrats to investigate Trump in the future.

But maybe I’m being uncharitable here. Maybe the attorney general isn’t just interested in advancing his own career by finding ways to give Trump carte blanche to do whatever he likes. Maybe he really does care about vulnerable young people. In which case, may I suggest he focus some of his attention on revisiting the Jeffrey Epstein files? I’m sure that I don’t need to remind you that the only person in jail right now because of their connection to the late sex offender is Ghislaine Maxwell. An awful lot of powerful people seem to have successfully dodged any accountability.

One would think an unpunished international pedophilia ring might worry Blanche more than schoolkids experimenting with their names in Kansas. However, Blanche seems a little resistant to taking the investigation much further – possibly because Trump is named in the Epstein files thousands of times. The attorney general also made sure to stress on Fox News earlier this year that “it isn’t a crime to party with Mr Epstein”.

Still, it doesn’t matter how much Blanche tries to distract us with culture wars – he can’t escape the ghost of Epstein. This week, the outgoing congressman Thomas Massie, a staunch Trump critic, noted that millions of Epstein files have yet to be publicly disclosed and urged the Department of Justice to launch an immediate investigation into 14 named Epstein associates, including the billionaire Leon Black. “Perhaps hearing these names will shame the Department of Justice into delivering justice,” he said. One would hope so. But it’s hard to shame the shameless.

“Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality,” Yvonne Roberts writes in the Guardian obituary. “She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion.”

That’s according to a new Gallup poll, which found perceptions of corruption are at their highest level in 20 years. Gosh, I wonder why.

Christa Pike is due to be executed at the end of the month for a murder she committed with two others when she was 18. Pike suffered child sexual abuse, neglect and violent rape growing up; according to one psychologist she “experienced more severe adverse events than 99% of the US population”. Her case raises troubling questions, Austin Sarat writes in the Guardian: “For women as well as men, capital punishment offers no solution to the problems that give rise to the most serious crimes.”

Anyone paying attention could see this was always the plan.

The US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) canceled 53 teen pregnancy prevention grants earlier this year and wants to direct millions in funding to organizations that emphasize “body literacy” and abstinence instead. This is despite (or perhaps because of) studies that have shown abstinence-only approaches increase rates of teen pregnancy. There’s now a lawsuit over this, and the HHS has defended its decision with references to dubious studies. In an opinion granting a preliminary injunction, the judge said: “On the topic of body literacy, the notices (remarkably) reference public health studies that appear either not to exist or not to support the propositions for which they are cited – a hallmark of AI-generated citations.” This is on-brand for the HHS secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, whose team released a report on children’s health last year full of fake citations. It’s almost as if the man is dangerously unqualified for his job.

“While I wouldn’t be shocked if we are living in the end times, what I’m trying to focus on is doing as much of God’s work as possible right now,” the vice-president said during a podcast interview with Bryce Crawford, a young Christian evangelist. Vance added: “And if that leads to the end times, OK.”

Jay-Z 30 tour review – the sheer profusion of nailed-on classics is dizzying

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 11:47:58 GMT

Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, LondonEven though Beyoncé rumours prove unfounded, there are plenty of guests, from Idris Elba to Lauryn Hill – but this show doesn’t need cameos to lift it

Jay-Z’s first solo tour in nine years bills itself as a celebration: it marks the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt. But it feels less concerned with nostalgic reverie than a show of strength in the present day. Hip-hop is a genre predicated on constant forward motion, in which careers tend to burn brightly, then dim as the music moves on. Jay-Z may not be the only fiftysomething rapper out on a career retrospective tour in 2026, but he is, unequivocally, the only one who’s capable of doing it at this level: packing out the biggest stadiums in the world nearly a decade after he last released an album, his standing impressively undiminished by a retreat into semi-retirement.

Moreover, he’s doing it in considerable style. The show’s musical approach can clearly trace its origins back to 2001, the year Jay-Z solved the problem of how on earth a rapper was supposed to appear on MTV Unplugged by eschewing hip-hop’s standard DJ-and-backing-tapes approach and employing a live band: the Roots were apparently astonished to be asked, but the end result was pretty jaw-dropping. Back in May, his first solo gig in five years essentially recreated it – he headlined the Roots’ annual Picnic festival with Questlove and co in tow once more – but the Jay-Z 30 tour supersizes it, featuring not just a 10-piece band, but an 18-piece string section. The resulting sound can, very occasionally, feel a little de trop – the squealing metal guitar solo appended to Can I Live definitely seems surplus to requirements – but for the most part, it works extraordinarily well, amping up the cinematic sweep of Empire State of Mind and the lush 70s-soul inflections of Izzo (H. O. V. A), adding a thunderous heft to Public Service Announcement and 99 Problems. It also serves to underline Jay-Z’s technical skill: a lesser rapper would be swallowed up by the density of the sound, but the precision of his delivery consistently cuts through.

There’s a sense in which the actual staging feels quite risky. At the rear there’s a vast LED screen that usually shows the footage you might expect – grainy video of 90s New York, black and white images of the city’s Black residents, aerial shots of the Marcy projects from whence Shawn Carter came, Jay-Z at various stages of his career – and sometimes doesn’t: at one point, presumably as explanation of where the rapper’s extravagant dreadlocks went, we’re treated to the sight of Beyoncé, clippers in hand, giving her husband a No 1 crop, a surprisingly thrifty approach to hairdressing for a couple worth an estimated $2.8bn (£2.1bn). His band and orchestra are clustered in the shadows beneath the screen, leaving a vast expanse of bare stage, which Jay-Z occupies more or less alone for most of the show. An audience of 50,000 people watching a solitary black-clad figure for two hours is theoretically a big ask, but there’s something strangely magnetic about the sight of him prowling the stage, a combination of sheer star power and genuine charisma that means you seldom tear your eyes from him.

The persistent rumour is that he’s going to be joined onstage by his wife – it’s her 45th birthday. He isn’t, although Mrs Carter gets a spotlight shone on her in the VIP box, a chorus of Happy Birthday and a firework display in her honour. Still, you don’t want for guests. The opening monologue is performed by Idris Elba and Jay-Z graciously cedes centre stage for the UK rapper Giggs to perform Talkin’ the Hardest, while Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean make an appearance towards the end of the set to perform a brace of Fugees classics to a roar of astonishment from the crowd: Fu-Gee-la and Ready or Not sound fantastic, and that Jay-Z can get Hill to actually turn up onstage when she’s supposed to feels like an achievement in itself.

But in truth, the show doesn’t really need guest appearances to lift it. The sheer profusion of nailed-on classics in Jay-Z’s back catalogue, and the intensity with which they’re performed, are more than enough: at one point, he rattles off No Church in the Wild, 99 Problems, Girls, Girls, Girls, ’03 Bonnie & Clyde, Excuse Me Miss and I Just Wanna Love U in such close proximity it feels faintly dizzying. Underneath his baseball cap, Jay-Z allows himself a rare grin. “We got a million of those,” he says: a slight exaggeration, but, under the circumstances, one you can forgive him.

Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 11:26:30 GMT

Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation

Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal.

The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel.

Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors.

Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday.

Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing.

The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge.

Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably.

At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 11:08:31 GMT

Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic

Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted WCK aid workers

Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.

A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.

The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.

However, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.

More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’s own internal data suggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.

The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).

He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”

He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”

Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in which haflala is to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.

He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas's attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”

When the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.

An IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.

The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”

The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”

Britain, Australia and Canada denounced the prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.

Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian, Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.

Mendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.

However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.

The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.

The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.

The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”

An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”

Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.

“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”

A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.

“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.

“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.

The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.

“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.”

Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.

The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.

The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”

The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.

The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.

“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”

He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”
