‘This is colonialism for clicks’: the influencers attempting to meet and film the world’s most isolated tribes

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 11:00:35 GMT

A new breed of adventurer is chasing internet fame by targeting uncontacted peoples. Critics say they are risking the wellbeing of these remote communities – and their own lives

He set out from the beach around midnight, packing his camera, a coconut and a can of Diet Coke. Mykhailo Polyakov – then 24 and a native of Scottsdale, Arizona – pointed his inflatable dinghy out towards the open water, keeping his speed slow in the hope of avoiding detection.

After hours of motoring across the Bay of Bengal, his destination came into view: a low-lying island, narrowly separating sea and sky. With the sun now high above him, Polyakov cut the engine and set his GoPro to record. “So, the goal,” he said, squinting towards the blinding-white beach. “Introduce this Palaeolithic tribe to modernity … Let’s land on this bitch.”

Polyakov was nearing North Sentinel Island, part of the Andaman archipelago governed by India. Venturing within 5km (3 miles) is strictly prohibited, let alone setting foot on shore, and authorities routinely patrol the surrounding waters. But Polyakov saw himself as on a mission: to see – and, more importantly, film – the Indigenous people who live there.

The Sentinelese are perhaps the most isolated people in the world. They are hunter-gatherers, and believed to number about 100. Beyond that, little is known about them, not even what language they speak. That is how they want it. The tribe opt to live in isolation from the outside world and have fiercely resisted attempts at contact. In 2018, an American missionary was fatally struck by arrows on his third attempt to land on the beach. Earlier, in 2006, two Indian fishers were killed after their boat accidentally washed up on shore.

Polyakov, who turns 26 this year and studied finance, believed the risks to be overstated – or at least secondary to his desire to take the first shots in crystalline 4K resolution. “I wouldn’t condone illegal activities but, in my case, the draw to go there was very powerful,” he says, a year after his illicit trip. “You see videos of the Sentinelese and it’s all grainy footage from the 90s … It was a big drive for me to get them on camera.”

He took a mirror and a whistle, “to coax them out”, and some goodwill tokens, in the event that he succeeded: the Diet Coke as a “symbol of modernity” and a coconut “because we know they like coconuts”. It wasn’t just clickbait, Polyakov adds, smirking: “It would be bad form not to bring gifts to people you’re visiting.”

The human rights organisation Survival International estimates there are 196 Indigenous communities living like the Sentinelese, in voluntary isolation. Most are in South America, in the Amazon rainforest and the Gran Chaco region of Paraguay and Bolivia, with a few more across Indonesia, West Papua and elsewhere in India’s Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Though fundamentally diverse, these communities have all chosen to reject outsiders and the industrialised world, and live self-sufficiently. They are known to policymakers and advocates as “uncontacted peoples”.

Increasingly, however, outsiders are trying to contact them – and make content from them. Survival and other organisations working to protect isolated peoples report they are increasingly being targeted by influencers chasing exclusive footage of “first contact” – and with it internet fame. For now, their numbers are believed to be few, with Polyakov a rare confirmed case, but advocates believe the threat to be real, growing and warranting action. Influencers were discussed at an international summit held in Jakarta in January, and again at a United Nations meeting in Brazil in June.

GTI PIACI, an alliance of 21 organisations working to protect uncontacted Indigenous peoples in the Amazon and Gran Chaco, has put the word out across their network, says secretary Daniel Aristizábal from Bogotá, Colombia. “It’s becoming a trend, and we have to adapt. These people have money.”

The UK-based Survival goes further, monitoring social media for influencers who might be motivated to make contact. “It’s all so unnecessary,” says Sophie Grig, head of advocacy and research, over Zoom from her home in Cambridge. She has been with Survival for 30 years, until recently focused on the Asia-Pacific, and is impatient with this “emerging threat” of influencers. The charity tracks a dozen or so accounts across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram with posts about uncontacted peoples. Many of those behind these accounts – overwhelmingly white men – are in the vicinity in South America or Asia and making content about “contacted” Indigenous communities. Their posts may also showcase weapons, snakes and “plant medicine” such as ayahuasca. “It’s very ‘look at me, I’m so macho’,” Grig says with disdain.

Though the likelihood of them ever reaching uncontacted peoples may be slim, the potential danger is great: isolated populations have historically been decimated by the introduction of unfamiliar diseases such as measles, to which they have not developed immunity. “Contact with these peoples can lead to their extinction in days,” says Beto Marubo, an Indigenous leader from the Javari valley in the Brazilian Amazon.

In 1987, Brazil’s government ended its policy of “forced contact missions” to uncontacted Amazonian tribes due to the devastating epidemics that persisted despite safeguards. For an influencer to argue against the risk and speak on behalf of uncontacted peoples is “an irresponsible, even criminal attitude”, Marubo says.

Such western “adventurer types” have long been drawn to places like the Amazon, Grig says, but influencers pose an additional risk with their global reach: those on Survival’s watchlist have a combined audience of more than 40 million followers. Even if they are not actively trying to find uncontacted peoples, by posting about them, Grig says they often affirm damaging stereotypes, spread dangerous misinformation and potentially influence others to try.

In interviews, Polyakov has dismissed Survival’s criticism that he endangered the Sentinelese, arguing that he was vaccinated and the risk of transmission low. He also claims trespassers there are more common than reported, and has even questioned whether any truly “uncontacted” people exist. This, Grig says, is self-serving semantics: while “voluntary isolation” may better reflect their position, there is no question they want to be left alone. Often, this is in response to past violence or traumatic experiences. “If you are uncontacted in 2026, that’s because you have made an active decision,” Grig says. “People like the Sentinelese have made it clear: we do not want people in our territory.”

To respect their autonomy, Survival, GTI PIACI and other advocates keep up with uncontacted groups at a careful remove, often via former members who have left the jungle or neighbouring Indigenous communities. Some uncontacted people may intermittently interact with outsiders, Grig says, often when forced to by hard times – but, crucially, it’s on their terms. “They’re not reaching out, and we must respect that.”

International human rights law supports Indigenous people’s right to choose self-isolation, and requires “free, prior and informed consent” for activity on their land, but national protections do not consistently meet that standard and enforcement is often haphazard. In Peru, for example, unauthorised entry can incur six-figure fines, but with little government presence on the ground, the chance of being caught is low.

Content creators, spurred on by platforms’ incentives for exciting and exclusive footage, may deem the risks worth it. “It feels like this is in a long line of colonialism,” Grig says exasperatedly. “People have been after land, gold, rubber, timber, souls – and now it’s clicks.”

On YouTube, Polyakov’s primary platform, he goes by @Neo-Orientalist – “because I’m bringing it back” – and a Tintin-style avatar. But he rejects being labelled a content creator, disdaining social media as a means to an end. In setting his sights on the Sentinelese, he sought to progress his goal of making “gamechanging” documentaries. “I wanted to do something that no one’s ever done before,” he says over video call, his face looming large in his phone’s camera. Behind him, the brightly painted concrete wall and harsh light suggest a youth hostel. When we speak in May, Polyakov says he is somewhere in south-east Asia, working on projects. He demurs from giving more detail, lest he embolden his online “haters”: “If you want to know where I’m going, you should subscribe.”

Polyakov claims his primary objective was to capture footage of the Sentinelese, not to interact with them, thereby reducing the risks to both sides. “You can always film them from outside of arrow range,” he shrugs. But when he finally made it to North Sentinel, on his third attempt, in March 2025, “ultimately I failed to coax anyone out”, he says. After beaching his dinghy, he walked around for five to 10 minutes, blowing his whistle to no apparent response. He then pushed back out to sea and filmed himself tossing the Coke can towards the shore. “It was anticlimactic … I was a little let down.”

He says he was more worried about encountering authorities than the Sentinelese. But in the footage he eventually posted on YouTube, Polyakov seems scared, then a little defensive. “Look, I can’t force the natives to come out,” he tells his audience, once safely back on the water. He made it back to his hotel without being caught, but was later arrested. Authorities had been alerted to a dinghy in the open water, and Polaykov had forgotten to remove his camera’s memory card. “They had me saying, ‘What’s up, guys? I’m at North Sentinel,’” he says ruefully. “From there it’s kind of tough.”

Polyakov was charged under two laws, but says he felt confident that, as a foreigner, “I wouldn’t be stuck in India for years.” He pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 25 days’ imprisonment and a fine of about £120.

His first “dispatch” from North Sentinel was posted on YouTube this April. The commentary has been mostly negative, as Polyakov concedes. (“Bro’s got main character syndrome,” reads a top-ranked comment.) He blames the “slanted” reporting, and takes every opportunity to speak to the media, partly for publicity, but also to defend himself against criticism from groups such as Survival, who called him “idiotic and reckless”.

Polyakov in turn calls Survival an activist organisation pursuing a “misguided” agenda “to keep certain groups stuck in the past”, and says he is acting in the public interest, “bringing information into the world”. He denies he was endangering the Sentinelese, pointing to the plastic refuse he found washed up on their beach. “They are very much aware of the outside world … It’s not like I’ve accelerated globalisation by going there. If it wasn’t me, it would be someone else.”

In explicitly targeting the world’s most isolated people, breaking multiple laws and getting caught, Polyakov is a clearcut case. More typically, content creators posting about uncontacted peoples are harder to pin down, not least because of the potential gulf between what they say online and what they may actually be doing. One individual monitored by Survival (who they requested not be named, believing him to be a serious risk) publicised detailed plans to visit North Sentinel to his six-figure following, but no evidence of an earnest attempt in the two years since. Other influencers boast of travelling through “uncontacted territory”, when they are in fact on widely used routes or even touristic tribal experiences. Some, Survival fear, might be doing the opposite, posing as legitimate while making covert efforts to find and film uncontacted people. With the geographical, legal and ethical lines ill-defined, content creators often operate in a grey area.

To his 276,000 followers on Instagram, where he goes by @yankiguayo, 30-year-old Nathan Seastrand bills himself as a film-maker, producing documentaries about Paraguay’s Gran Chaco region and its Indigenous Ayoréo people. From Utah, but based in Paraguay since 2016, Seastrand publicly presents as a champion of the Chaco and its people, telling local media he is motivated by “curiosity and wonder”. But this reputation has recently been publicly challenged, with Seastrand accused of exploitation, a claim he denies.

In early August, an influencer who has asked not to be named posted on YouTube about his experiences collaborating with Seastrand on a documentary last year. He said Seastrand seemed “obsessed” with finding and filming uncontacted Ayoréo, making multiple visits to their territory, setting trail cameras and trying to acquire a thermal-imaging drone to search from the air.

There are estimated to be 150 uncontacted Ayoréo, living in small nomadic groups in the dwindling areas of the Chaco not yet cleared by deforestation. Local advocates monitor them through traces such as the prints from their tapir-leather sandals, but they have not been photographed in decades. The Paraguayan government signed a protocol in 2018, requiring it to prevent unwanted contact, but it does not specifically outlaw it, while access to Indigenous lands is granted at the discretion of individual community leaders.

Having accompanied Seastrand on two journeys into the Chaco, the influencer said he grew increasingly concerned by his “morally questionable” approach. He claimed Seastrand gave money and alcohol to Ayoréo leaders to secure access to their reserve and permission to film, later leading to conflict with neighbours who wanted in on the deal. The influencer said he cut ties with Seastrand not long after, accusing him of “exploiting the poorest and most marginalised segment of Paraguayan society in order to become rich and famous”.

In an email to the Guardian, Seastrand rejects the influencer’s account, saying all his activities on Ayoréo land were legal and authorised by community leaders. He calls the claim he had gained access with alcohol “absurd”, saying that he developed friendships over multiple visits. “They were not tricked or coerced … It is normal to invite your friends to a cold pack of beer.”

Seastrand confirms he paid money, not unusual for film-making, but dismisses the conflict described by the influencer as “no more than a jealous neighbouring tribe”.

As for the camera traps, Seastrand says they were set in a developed area and his goal was to film jaguars. “The likelihood of an isolated tribe living in this zone is extremely small and … there is no hard evidence of their existence. I would have better luck trying to get footage of the Loch Ness monster or Bigfoot.” He says his on-camera references to “wild Ayoréo territory” were an effort to engage viewers. “There is no such thing … No one really knows where they are.”

Others have spoken out against Seastrand’s activities in the Chaco. An Ayoréo lawyer accused him of sharing a photograph of his late grandfather without consent, and refusing to remove it when asked (Seastrand says he had consent from the grandfather and has since taken the photo down). According to Paraguayan media, Seastrand has also been accused of offering to pay people to find uncontacted Ayoréo. In mid-August, following the intervention of the Paraguyan National Indigenous Institute (INDI), a court granted emergency measures be taken against Seastrand, including removal of his camera traps. Seastrand continues to deny wrongdoing, and is still posting from the Chaco on Instagram.

Before he became “one of the most-known influencers in Paraguay”, as he puts it, Seastrand had a different motive: he was a Mormon missionary. According to a 2023 New York Times profile, Seastrand baptised more than 30 people before leaving the church and pursuing content creation.

The pathway is less incongruous than it might seem, GTI PIACI’s Aristizábal points out: both influencers and missionaries pursue Indigenous people, rather than their lands or resources. John Allen Chau, the 26-year-old Christian missionary killed by the Sentinelese in 2018, chronicled his travels on Instagram and even had endorsement deals – one with a jerky brand. When word of his presumed death reached Survival, Grig says, “Our first assumption was that he was an influencer.”

Chau was allegedly motivated to reach the Sentinelese because their extreme isolation made them more highly prized souls to save. Now, missionary influencers blur roles by openly documenting their efforts to reach Indigenous people in the Amazon and beyond.

Earlier this year, footage of uncontacted Mashco Piro (or Nomole) people on riverbanks in the Peruvian Amazon created a sensation online, drawing headlines everywhere from the New York Post and the Sun to social-first outlets such as LADbible and Worldstar Hip Hop. It had been shared by Paul Rosolie, the American founder of Junglekeepers, a nonprofit working in the Peruvian Amazon.

Not straightforwardly a content creator, Rosolie isn’t a typical conservationist, either. He calls himself an “explorer”, has 2 million Instagram followers and shares stories about his encounters with uncontacted tribes on high-profile platforms not necessarily concerned with sensitivity, such as The Joe Rogan Experience. His footage of the Mashco Piro was shared exclusively with the podcaster Lex Fridman, trailed as a “world first” and timed days before publication of Rosolie’s new book. The footage had been taken more than a year earlier.

Rosolie declined an interview, but a representative of Junglekeepers says in an emailed statement that the encounter was overseen by a Peruvian government official and met no-contact protocols. The spokesperson says Rosolie released the film to call attention to Junglekeepers’ work to save Mashco Piro territory from illegal logging. “We are not in the business of publicity … The world needs to understand what is at stake.”

With his Indiana Jones style and showmanship, Rosolie’s intrepid tales capture imaginations, and open wallets: Junglekeepers raised $3.3m in 2024, enabling it to buy and protect more than 135,000 acres of forest. But Survival and other groups working to protect uncontacted peoples say he perpetuates dated and damaging tropes. On Steven Bartlett’s Diary of a CEO podcast in February, Rosolie described his encounter with the Mashco Piro: “It’s like a time capsule, a thousand years between us … this aperture into the history of what humankind used to look like.” His stories emphasised the danger from naked “warriors” with “seven foot-long” arrows and spears, and the simplicity of their existence, “so deep in the jungle that they’ve never heard of a spoon or the wheel”. Later, Rosolie presented Bartlett with a selection of snakes to handle.

His other interviews hit the same beats. Grig points out Rosolie first came to prominence with a controversial Discovery Channel stunt in which he set out to be “eaten alive” by a 20ft-long anaconda: “If he’s not an influencer, he has massive influencer tendencies.” She is critical of his characterisation of the Mashco Piro as “not even stone age”: “They’re living in the 21st century, just as much as we are.” Using such “sensationalist, derogatory, dehumanising language” poses a threat to uncontacted peoples, Grig says, amplifying arguments long used to justify stealing their lands, removing them from their communities and imposing so-called “development”.

Rosolie has accused Survival of running a smear campaign by grouping him with the likes of Polyakov; there is no evidence of him ever breaking the law, and he discourages attempted contact. A Junglekeepers representative said they view the trend of influencer stunts “with serious concern” and Rosolie’s own position “has always been one of respect”. His comments about the Nomole were “never meant as any sort of judgment”, but to highlight their real and “practical distance … [from] modern global civilization”. The footage was shared as “a reminder of how close the outside world already is, and why protection from it matters”.

Junglekeepers’ strategy – protecting rainforest by buying it up – differs from that of Survival and other organisations fighting for Indigenous control of their land, highlighting the different worldviews. The representative said its work was Indigenous-led, and Rosolie was only “the main communicator”.

In interviews he has expressed ambivalence about the future of uncontacted peoples, suggesting they might benefit from “basic life hacks” and “a future … where their kids don’t have to worry about eating monkeys” and can work as park rangers instead. To Grig, that is irrelevant. “We’re not saying this is an idyllic life. We’re saying this is the life they have chosen.”

Many advocates for uncontacted peoples feel they walk a fine line in calling attention to their struggles without turning them into a spectacle. For contacted tribal Indigenous communities, online visibility can drive valuable tourism, increasingly important to their survival – but it’s not without costs.

As Fearless & Far, Mike Corey sells online courses and leads retreats claiming to help men conquer their fears and wake the warrior within – all marketed with videos of his own “tribal adventures” with contacted groups. On YouTube, where he has 3.1 million subscribers, he highlights his “wild moments with lost tribes”, such as the “SNAKE TRIBE of Tanzania” and the “DEATH TRIBE of Indonesia”. Many videos hit 10m views.

Canadian-born Corey has visited about 40 tribes globally, spending up to three days living with them and filming for social media. He claims to have pioneered that “immersive” format five years ago with the Hadza hunter-gatherers of Tanzania, who now routinely receive tourists and content creators – attention that has been a “double-edged sword”, Corey says. “When I met them, they would never even touch Coca-Cola … They’re slowly becoming less hunter-gatherer.” At the same time, he argues, tribal tourism is supporting their survival, reviving young Hadza people’s interest in their ancient culture and customs, and providing an economic framework through which to preserve them.

Though there was “very little” tribal content when he started out, Corey does not believe his videos contributed to its growth. “It would have happened regardless – but I wish people were more respectful, and doing it for the same reasons we are.” “New-gen YouTubers” can be especially unscrupulous, Corey says, scripting encounters for entertainment. Some even pay or coerce Indigenous people to dress up or perform aggression. “That’s where I get butthurt. You are not helping anything, you’re creating a false reality that’s very clickable: ‘I got captured by cannibals.’”

Corey says he is motivated by curiosity and a desire to “meet people in all these four corners, and find a human connection”. A former television presenter, he follows a similar process for content production. Stays are arranged in advance by a local fixer, while hosts are well compensated, with supplies if not money (in the communities that use it, alcohol can be a “big problem”). He says he always asks permission to film, in advance and on location, and has only been refused once. More often, tribes want him to stay longer or return, he says, crediting his “documentarian” mindset and sense of responsibility. “We’re trying to tell a story about people that are going to be gone in 10 years.” But it is still packaged up for platforms often resistant to nuance, and some question whether they are his stories to tell.

In April, Corey posted a video to Instagram about his stay with the Himba people of north-western Namibia, known for their practice of Okujepisa, or “wife-lending” with guests. A traditional display of hospitality, it has been increasingly controversial within Namibia and misrepresented, sometimes gleefully, by outsiders on social media. Corey’s video emphasises his awkwardness with the Himba women’s “too friendly” approach, but concludes by calling for viewers to comment “MAP” to receive their location: a common digital marketing ploy for engagement. Roughly half the 100 commenters condemned the video as exploitative or sleazy; the other half commented “MAP”.

“I was the one uncomfortable,” Corey says, adding his conscience is clear. “I know we’re doing good work.”

Content creators argue they seek to spread awareness, build connections or preserve culture, but it is difficult to separate their message from the medium. Some have argued that social media, primarily US-owned, yet shaping global culture, necessarily imposes a white, western gaze and affirms colonial power structures – termed “platform imperialism”. Viewed this way, even the most conscientious content creators’ encounters with tribal people are undone once posted online.

Whenever such videos pop up on María José Andrade Cerda’s social feeds, she blocks and reports them. “I don’t want to see those kinds of videos,” she says from Tena, Ecuador. Cerda, 31, is herself Indigenous, belonging to the Kichwa community of Serena. She is also a member of Yuturi Warmi, an Indigenous all-female patrol of the Ecuadorian Amazon, and has addressed world leaders at Cop. But Cerda denies that she’s an activist: “For us, it’s about surviving.”

Cerda has been trying to use social media to benefit her community and advance Indigenous rights. Last year she hosted MrBeast collaborator Nolan Hansen in Ecuador for a video partnership with the charity WaterAid. Cerda briefly features, discussing a local water filtration project; the video now has 127m views.

Cerda says even well-intentioned content creators tend to conflate distinct communities and cultures, and spread simplistic narratives: “I feel they are not treating the issues how they should be, with respect and the full context.” Yet at times when an international platform would be welcome, “when it’s about our rights, they don’t care”. Cerda compares the widespread silence from influencers on Indigenous-led protests against the Ecuadorian government’s proposed expansion of oil exploration in the Amazon, with the wealth of content on Indigenous culture, traditions and women – at least those deemed to meet western beauty standards, she adds. “They only want the Pocahontas.”

With the recent explosion in the creator economy, it is difficult to imagine how influencers might be reined in. Cerda wonders whether they could be interrogated about their plans at airport customs, or if platforms could require them to provide proof of the “free, prior and informed consent” of the Indigenous people they filmed. But even if such measures were practicable, she adds, they would not address the gaping, fundamental inequality. “Influencers have double lives: they can be in the jungle for one month with these tribes, then go back to the US, where they live in big houses and drink potable water.” Sometimes, Cerda says, communities will accept gifts from content creators, then later realise “they were being used: ‘He is making money because of that video. What about us?’”

Others, unable to beat the creator economy, have joined it, starting social media accounts to appeal to tourists directly. Members of Ecuador’s Waorani tribe have even struck deals with content creators, offering cheaper stays in exchange for coverage. The Waorani Experience markets itself on Instagram as offering “100% Authentic Tours … As seen on YouTube”. Operator Boya Tegairis, Waorani himself, says over WhatsApp that he was motivated by the memory of his grandfather, who “defended this jungle”. “With the tourist income, we can buy medicines for our families … and take care of the jungle for future generations.”

The price, however, is bringing influencers deeper in. On the long journey to the Waorani compound, boats pass briefly through the territory of uncontacted Waorani, known to respond with violence to outsiders – including their contacted relatives. Guests are accompanied by their hosts, briefed and required to sign a waiver; the boats do not stop. Content creators hosted by Tegairis emphasise the danger regardless.

For all the lengths Polyakov went to in securing his footage from North Sentinel, at time of writing he has still only just cracked 10k subscribers on YouTube; news of his arrest travelled far further than his videos. But he is not dissuaded, with a forthcoming series filmed in Haiti and a trip to the Middle East. He blames the muted response on his refusal to play to YouTube’s algorithm with a sensationalised or falsified account. “I could’ve gone to some other tribal group and said ‘This is North Sentinel’, but I didn’t. I went for the real thing, despite the risks,” he says hotly. “Maybe in 10 years I’ll sell out – but I actually care about being accurate.”

‘I don’t have any friends’: why do young people today have fewer mates?

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 10:00:34 GMT

Social media, mental health problems, the pandemic and financial instability all contribute to the phenomenon

On Tess Lavanda’s YouTube channel there is one video with substantially more views than the rest: it is titled “I don’t have any friends” and has been watched more than half a million times since she posted it a month ago.

Over on Instagram she has posted dozens of reels with titles like “I turned 22 alone”, “Living alone in London” and “Feeling alone this summer is OK”, each garnering thousands of views and hundreds of comments, many from people feeling the same way.

A quick search for terms like “solomaxxing”, “loneliness influencer” and “no friends aesthetic” brings up hundreds of videos and posts from people – many of them teenagers and young adults – talking about what life is like without friends.

“I think people feel relieved it’s finally being spoken about,” says Lavanda, 22. “No one felt brave enough to speak about it because there is this culture where people think being alone is embarrassing and wrong.”

New research from the Institute for Public Policy Research published this week found the number of young people in England with no close friends has risen fivefold since 2014, now standing at one in 20, and a growing number saying they are not happy with the friends they do have.

Lavanda says: “I think there’s a lack of drive for people to go out and meet people, and when you do go out, people are on their phones so it’s harder to approach them.”

She has always struggled with making friends but it was only during the pandemic when “that lack of a genuine friendship really hit” and she started to feel isolated. “I had no one to talk to and I went into quite a dark place,” she says.

Then one night when she was about to head out alone feeling “so scared and awful”, she put on her camera and started talking.

Lavanda says: “I had no intention of posting it. This was just purely a video for myself, about how I was feeling to try and hype myself up, really. But then I thought maybe this will help someone, so I posted it.

“I was fully expecting to be judged and bullied but the response was overwhelmingly positive. People were sharing their own stories, and I realised that so many people feel the exact same way.”

She says there is a growing trend for solo life to be “aesthetic or romanticised” but her videos are more about showing people without friends they’re not alone. “I think people take comfort in the fact there’s now a voice about this topic,” she says. “It’s more important to just be honest and speak up.”

There has been growing discussion around why young people today report having fewer friends than previous generations – a combination of social media, mental health problems, the Covid pandemic and financial instability are all often thrown into the mix.

Pamela Qualter, the UK’s leading scientific expert on child and adolescent loneliness, says there are no straightforward answers. But it is clear that, as a society, we’ve stripped back places where young people can practise basic social skills like saying “hello”.

“We’re really lacking those very simple conversations you have each day with somebody you just bump into,” she says. “More people are working from home, and people have less disposable income at a time when there are very few free or cheap places for people to come together.”

Qualter says it is these “weak ties” – small interactions with acquaintances – that form the building blocks and social skills that can build into solid friendships.

But she emphasises there is not much evidence to suggest young people are actually getting lonelier: those aged 14 to 24 report the highest levels of loneliness in the UK but this has always been the case.

“Maybe our expectations of friendships are changing. Maybe those people with fewer close friends are happy with that,” she says.

However, there is also evidence to suggest young people are increasingly dissatisfied with the friendships they do have.

Jodie-Leigh Foster, a training and development officer at UK Youth, teaches youth workers about youth loneliness and isolation, as well as empowering teenagers to launch their own projects tackling the problem.

She says it is the quality of friendships that many young people struggled with. “These are friendships that often play out on social media and group chats, which can quickly turn to bullying and harassment,” she says. “That leads to them becoming isolated and withdrawn.”

Money is also often an issue: some young people reported not being able to afford to get transport to see people outside school. Others struggle with large crowded spaces, especially since the pandemic, which increased levels of anxiety.

Foster says: “People make assumptions about being a young person, that it’s a carefree time in their lives, and the whole world’s at their fingertips. But for some young people, that’s actually really overwhelming and daunting. It’s a tough time to be a young person.”

The pressure on Burnham to appease the right is huge. But now is the time to step out of Reform’s shadow

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 09:00:32 GMT

A scandal-besieged Reform still has a loyal base that won’t budge. That should free up the PM to deliver some home truths

Despite the bright start to Andy Burnham’s premiership, and Reform UK’s sudden disarray, a shadow still hangs over British centre-left politics. Labour has a small poll lead, a cautious air of confidence and a leader who seems energised rather than overwhelmed by trying to solve the country’s problems. Meanwhile, Reform is having a terrible 2026: mired in deepening funding scandals, losing winnable byelections and, thanks to the drama and novelty of Burnham’s leadership coup and new government, no longer the freshest story around.

Yet Reform UK’s support has either held up or fallen only slightly in most polls since Burnham entered Downing Street. Even in the Makerfield byelection, where he beat it more decisively than expected, Reform’s vote share and total support actually rose. Nigel Farage may have spent the year uncharacteristically avoiding journalists, or in his prickly rather than jolly public mode, but the overwhelming majority of Reform supporters, almost a quarter of the electorate, remain faithful. “Power is within our grasp!” insisted Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesman, at its party conference in Birmingham on Friday, and they applauded with determined gusto.

Meanwhile, their preoccupations continue to shape politics and how the media processes it. Immigration, crime, the benefits system, “wokeness”, net zero policies: all are constantly presented as out of control and contributing to national decline. From our overcrowded prisons to our almost exhausted North Sea oil- and gasfields, what are widely considered to be the most politically realistic options for the government are generally what most Reform voters would like to happen. The likelihood that permanent crime crackdowns and further large-scale fossil-fuel drilling – which the government looks increasingly likely to approve – will be disastrous for a country with an ever more obvious climate crisis and unprecedentedly large prison population, by historical and European standards, does not disturb this deep-rooted rightwing consensus. The pressure on Burnham to go along with it as prime minister will be never-ending.

Yet the risks of governing under Reform’s shadow, while less discussed, are much larger. So far, Labour’s fragile poll recovery has mainly been built by taking support back from the Greens and Lib Dems, as the dip in their poll ratings since a Burnham premiership became likely has demonstrated. This change would almost certainly be undone if Burnham decided to follow a Reform-defined agenda. Keir Starmer’s abrupt announcement that he will leave parliament is the ultimate result of him making exactly that mistake in Downing Street – and has given the Greens’ leader, Zack Polanski, a chance to reverse the momentum shift from his party to Labour by standing as a byelection candidate.

Meanwhile, with Reform, Restore and the Tories all competing to be the most rightwing, and this country’s many reactionary media outlets doing the same, many right-leaning voters are even more convinced than usual that no Labour government is acceptable. So the appeasement of conservative Britain, designed by Morgan McSweeney and carried out by Starmer, not always with conviction, was never likely to win many converts for long. In a deeply divided country, the days of Labour premiers attracting and holding on to large numbers of rightwing voters, as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and Clement Attlee once did, are gone, at least for now.

As a politician unusually keen by modern standards on cross-party collaboration and broad coalitions, Burnham could waste much of what may not be a long premiership trying to build bridges with the right. But there are some early signs he may pursue a more streetwise strategy. His debut contributions as prime minister in parliament this week mixed consensual catchphrases such as “problem-solving over point-scoring”, which made the Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, sound rigidly confrontational in response, with sweeping attacks on areas where the right is vulnerable. Austerity, Brexit, privatisation and the centralisation of power in London have dwindling electoral support and even less credibility, however loudly the Tories and Reform defend some or all of them, because for decades these old-fashioned rightwing remedies have clearly failed to revive the country.

“Far from ‘taking back control’, the combination of those policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain,” said Burnham, deftly turning a key promise of populism back against the rightwing populists. He knows that while Margaret Thatcher is still revered by Farage and Badenoch, the sometimes brutal economic changes that she and her Conservative successors drove through are not popular with all Tory and Reform voters. They may never switch to supporting Labour, but could support parts of Burnham’s programme, such as stronger public control over “the essentials of life” currently provided at excessive cost by toxic Thatcherite creations such as Thames Water.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The approval, tacit or otherwise, of usually hostile voters on a specific issue can provide useful political cover for a government – especially an unpopular one, which Burnham’s is likely to be, however he performs, given the number of parties arrayed against him in our fragmented political landscape. He may well need that cover if his government is going to restructure the economy even half as ambitiously as he promises. The shareholders, financiers, lawyers and corporate executives who have done extremely well out of privatisation are not going to give up their gains and privileges without a fight.

A temporary coalition of leftwing and rightwing voters may be the only way to overcome them. The economy is not democratic – much to the disappointment of generations of radical leftists – but in a democracy, powerful interests can be curbed or even defeated if they are challenged by a premier acting with broad public consent, as Attlee and Franklin D Roosevelt once did against some of the 20th century’s most entrenched economic elites.

Yet if Burnham is to govern with anything like those legendary reformers’ effectiveness, then in other policy areas his government is going to have to stand up to Reform supporters. New research about them by King’s College London and UK in a Changing Europe shows that, despite this summer being the UK’s hottest ever, almost two-thirds “want to scrap the 2050 net zero target”. Meanwhile, a new Ipsos poll shows that immigration remains the number one public issue, particularly for Reform and Tory voters, despite the fact that immigration is rapidly falling.

Sooner or later, Burnham is going to have to use his celebrated communications skills to tell Britons some home truths, whether rightwing voters want to hear them or not. Otherwise, Reform’s shadow will chill his government for good.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

Booyakasha! Ali G is back – but even he can’t match the absurdity of modern Britain

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 07:00:30 GMT

Sacha Baron Cohen’s character once exposed the contradictions of an emerging multicultural nation. But nearly 30 years on Britain has changed – and so has the joke

And so the nostalgia machine grinds on, dragging another pop culture corpse back into the light: yes, it’s the return of Ali G. Respeck.

Sacha Baron Cohen’s skull-cap-wearing, “rudebwoy” wankster is staging a comeback with Ali G: Who Iz I?. The new film, premiering next month, is a mockumentary that sees the character starting a family with long-term companion Julie (thinking his approach to fatherhood will be “absent”) and embracing TikTok, all while donning new fake dreads and a rastacap.

It’s taken little time for this revival to enter Britain’s terminal “ARE U OFFENDED, SNOWFLAKE?” culture-war cycle. The Telegraph’s chief film critic, Robbie Collin, wrote that Ali G would save us from comedy’s offence police: “We need a good dose of this sort of puerile needling more than ever.” And now there is a pressure campaign asking cinemas not to screen Baron Cohen’s “racist caricature”, which has accrued more than 46,000 signatures.

The old hits never die. Yet I think this reboot, however tedious, prompts some worthwhile reflection about the changing state of Britain. Since Ali G’s debut in 1998, there has been disagreement over who the joke is on. Erstwhile defenders viewed the character’s absurdity as a reflection of society’s soft bigotry, a satire of white liberal elites’ prejudices.

Ali G’s initial premise was interviews with unsuspecting public figures while posturing as a low-educated wannabe, and lobbing inane questions that reliably wrongfooted the interviewee. With a few exceptions, these interviewees were white, from Noam Chomsky to Newt Gingrich to Donald Trump (who walked out). The socialist MP Tony Benn, victim of such a set-up on the 11 O’Clock Show, admitted in 2000 that “at no stage during our talk did I suspect for a second that it was other than a genuine programme”. The idea then was that you were laughing at the gullibility of the liberal middle classes.

But some viewed this interpretation as apologia for something sinister. Black British comedians in particular viewed Ali G as a straight-up racist caricature. Comedian Felix Dexter was candid: “I feel that a lot of the humour is laughing at black street culture and it is being celebrated because it allows the liberal middle classes to laugh at that culture in a safe context where they can retain their sense of political correctness.”

I think the most interesting intervention worth revisiting is that of the sociologist Paul Gilroy, who saw the comedy as a reflection of multicultural Britain’s coming-of-age. Writing in 2002, after the premiere of the film Ali G Indahouse, Gilroy posited that the character provided “a satirical Rorschach blot in which even the most neurotic scrutineers of the national psyche can discover their fears and hopes”.

That interpretation fit with Gilroy’s theory of cultural hybridity: Ali G’s incoherence as a “shapeshifting” white English man performing a pastiche of Black urban street culture embodied the cultural mongrelisation that had been shaping Britain under New Labour. Ali G represented a cartoonish version of the very real destabilising of racial categories that was happening at the time. Some were optimistic about cultural diversity, while others were anxious. In particular the influence of nascent “yardie” culture, American hip-hop and conspicuous consumption was sometimes viewed as a social contagion impeding British youth.

The salient question for me, then, is less whether it’s OK to find Ali G funny, or if it’s offensive, but rather what the character’s function and purpose is in 2026. His particular cultural bricolage is now being thrown into a far more charged political environment.

Cultural boundaries remain porous, but the political boundaries around national belonging have hardened. Ali G emerged from a politics fascinated by cultural change and mixing, and returns to a politics dominated by a more severe policing of who gets to be British. The anxiety Ali G once represented is now a far more antagonistic struggle; just take a look at the ubiquitous “yookay” meme, the idea that multiculturalism has socially corrupted the UK.

The mediums through which we absorb culture have also changed. Ali G’s racial politics were originally mediated through television: editing, scheduling and official channels for regulation meant that, however controversial, Baron Cohen and his collaborators could control its message. Online, that control disappears. You can easily imagine an Ali G scene now being clipped and shared as an anecdote of Britain’s decline.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

And so Ali G arrives from the analogue world into one that is far more racialised, online and politically volatile. But the character has become obsolete because it is no longer transgressive: the cultural mix that once made Ali G ludicrous is now mundane. The seemingly exotic language Ali G parodies has for a long time now been understood as Multicultural London English.

There is also the problem of Baron Cohen himself. His original approach had an incredibly effective comedy mechanism, using interviews to make powerful establishment figures reveal themselves. But Baron Cohen is no longer the outsider performing the outsider role, he is now a very famous 54-year-old multimillionaire attempting a last-gasp revival. Will anyone be duped, and what exactly could he reveal now anyway?

It’s easy to dismiss the furore around Ali G’s return as political correctness. But it’s not that Britain has become too sensitive for the joke, it may be that the joke simply doesn’t work any more. And so what returns with Ali G is little more than the same old stereotype in a new costume, detached from the time in which it meant something more.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

Uefa legal case may be beginning of the end for Infantino as Trump’s support evaporates

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 07:00:29 GMT

The order of discovery related to Fifa’s failed plan to sell the World Cup will worry the American president, a situation that tends to end badly for the culprit

“Tell Mike it was just business. I always liked him.”

“He understands.”

“Tom, can you get me off the hook? For old times’ sake?”

“Sorry can’t do it.”

I never believed it would actually happen. Not really. Not until this week, when, for the first time, there was a sense, as The Godfather makes so abundantly clear, that you really can get to anyone.

Gianni Infantino is beleaguered. Gianni Infantino is re-beleaguered. Gianni Infantino has been beleaguered for almost six weeks, since news emerged of his grotesque undercover plan to sell off, for related personal gain, the shared global property he’s employed to preserve, protect and safely pass on.

There has been hopeful talk in that time of toxic status attained, a base being hollowed out, a rival presidential candidate next March. But power runs deep. Entrenched dictatorial power runs even deeper. Time passes. The doorway narrows. Infantino is already the man who sold the world, not once, but twice, most recently to Donald Trump in return for a peace prize, a scrunchie and a fawning presence around the sub-table of power.

Give it a month. Chuck in a Football Jesus turn at the lighted lectern a few weeks from now, arms whirling like a street magician, reeling off the usual stuff about caring and sharing, égalité, fraternité, fiscal stimuli. Look deep into those weirdly flat painted-on eyes, cold and hard behind the papier-mache mask of power. You don’t buy me out. I buy you out.

But something has shifted this week. It was never going to be the gnats around his ankles that did for Infantino: another thundering newspaper column, the latest stern denouncement from – whoah, hang on – former Manchester United utility defender Mikaël Silvestre.

Hard power is something else, however. And two things have now happened, both responses to the threat of a Uefa lawsuit, which I believe has no really serious notions of ultimate victory, but which may turn out to be an expert chess move, a zugzwang that leaves the king having to go somewhere, but with no safe spaces left to hide.

The first response was Josh Kushner’s statement this week after being named as a party to discovery in Florida. Kushner was the money guy behind the Fifa Forward fiasco. Nuts isn’t it? The person you come to for finance and macro-favour just happens to be, by an accident of talent and destiny, the brother of the president’s son-in-law.

Kushner said he “would not have gotten involved” in Fifa’s plans had he known the full picture. He said this was all regrettable. Ostensibly mild and reasonable words, but with a sense of distance being carved out, of a cutting loose from the protective apron.

Kushner has also hired a nuclear option lawyer, Alex Spiro, who defended Elon Musk when he called a caver “a pedo” and Alec Baldwin when he accidentally shot someone. It’s a serious defensive move. As is, to a more rattled degree, Fifa’s counter-filing this week, which dismisses the whole episode as a “smear campaign”, then says the quiet thing out loud. Specifically, Fifa mentions discovery and a very urgent intention to resist it.

This is the real point. No one on the Infantino side wants discovery. Which is, to be clear, the sharing of related documents, from internal memos down to relevant emails sent from your smartphone on the golf course after lunch.

This, as Gianni knows, is always a worry to those in power. And you really don’t want to be a worry to anyone in any way connected to Trump. This is why, behind the sabre rattling, there is for the first time a sense of a thinning out, of nobody there on the ward, no cops on the doors, of the old man up there unprotected.

Even Trump’s early support for Infantino was a little over-juiced in the media. The president Truth Socialed his assurances in early August. It still felt a little qualified. “If for any reason” Fifa got rid of Infantino, well, this would be really bad. And nothing since.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

There is a vague sense of a shrug here, of an amble away from the stage. We remember the good times for the Gianni-Trump bro-tocracy, laughing together like men in a Brooks Brothers senior knitwear advert, the gleaming bald impresario to power and his tolerant daddy-patron looking as ever like a giant man-size unit of American food, as though something deep-fried, honey-glazed and dished up at an out-of-town hotel conference buffet has somehow learned to walk around in a baggy suit and say things like “a very tall, very handsome man”.

This is always brittle. Trump will walk you in, remember your name, glad-hand you by the stairwell. But once you’re gone you really are gone. There is no loyalty, and logically so, because Trumpian politics has no core belief, no substance, just a cold, hard matrix of winners and losers.

And if you lose, or look like you might, then by coincidence bad things tend to happen. The Guardian published a list a while back of Trump enemies who now find themselves subject to charges, exile, security clearances revoked, mortgage fraud investigated. And that list does include some pretty high-profile one-time golden boys.

Michael Cohen, the fiercest of Trump loyalists, who famously stated he would “take a bullet” for the big man? Legal difficulties and fallings-out intervened. Cohen has since been imprisoned, disbarred and sent into exile. The former US attorney general Jeff Sessions was among the first to call Trumpism “a movement”. He’s now not only out of the game, but has apparently been described by Trump, variously, as weak, confused, dumb, an idiot, a disgrace, and “mentally retarded”. There is a pattern here. If you’re in then you’re in. But don’t fly too close to those flames.

The decision of the court on allowing discovery could well be key. Make no mistake, Uefa is accusing Fifa and Infantino of “criminal mismanagement”. The key issue is an alleged undervaluing in the sale of the World Cup. Unrelated, and arguably standard industry practice, Infantino also stood to take a huge personal salary from all this.

It is a clear attempt to peer inside and see what, if anything, is in that box. Uefa wants discovery from Fifa, Thrive Capital and the Trump donor and deal adviser Greg Maffei, all of whom will have paper trails from that period when Infantino was granted intoxicating access to the halls of power. It puts you in mind of the Club World Cup trophy, a weird, frightening-looking thing, all razor-sharp odd nooks and crannies, the secret little drawer full of human toenails. Do you really want to know what’s in there? Is it safe to look?

“Please Mike, don’t do this, don’t do this to me”

“Today I settle all the family business. So don’t tell me you’re innocent.”

How is this going to play out? Infantino is doing what he can, touring his outer provinces and pressing the flesh. Saudi Arabia has offered qualified backing (“at this time …”). There’s a Fifa congress in November. Really, though, you wonder about votes, and to what extent votes are the thing here. It is hard not to muse on how it ended in football for Sepp Blatter and Michel Platini. That one-shot illegal payment allegation really did come out of the blue.

For now the process will simmer on. Legal challenges often fail or melt away. Uefa just needs to keep pressing, to make it clear that coals will be raked. Keep the pressure up and you never know what may fall out, or from where. Mr president, you can have my answer now. Our offer is this. Nothing.

Losing a parent is a bewildering, lonely experience. Here are the things I wish I had known before

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 05:00:30 GMT

There’ll be exhaustion, love tinged with occasional rage, even moments of black humour. But my mum would want me to tell you: don’t be afraid

My mother’s house looks exactly as she left it.

Two novels sit by the armchair, their pages neatly marked for book group. Pinned to the noticeboard is a shopping list in only slightly shaky writing, with “FRUIT!” in urgent capitals, and “make soup” underlined. The sole outward signs of something missing are her cats twining needily around me – loneliness having finally overcome their innate horror of visitors – and the one thing I can’t bear to look at, which is the empty hospital bed marooned bleakly in the sitting room. Delivered by social services when it was deemed she could no longer manage stairs, it is now stripped bare, awaiting collection. Another family will be needing it.

This is not my childhood home – my parents moved here only a few years ago – but it’s the one, I suppose, where childhood formally ended. Washing up at her kitchen sink a fortnight ago, looking out at the same scarlet fuchsia I remember blazing in the garden when my father died, it struck me for the first time that soon I would no longer be anyone’s daughter. What I didn’t know then was that the loss of both parents would feel less like the end of a relationship and more like its transition to a new stage, of finally being able to see them clearly as people in their own right.

I thought I’d nailed that years ago, but of course I was wrong. When news spread of her diagnosis – an aggressively fast-moving cancer, erupting from nowhere to overwhelm her in six weeks – my mother’s friends descended in hordes, bringing soup and cake and clove-scented sweet peas from their gardens. But they also brought stories I hadn’t heard before. Though my father was the outwardly gregarious one and my mother more self-effacing, evidently she was the one who watched and listened and caught what others missed. I already knew that for a while she’d channelled that into volunteering as a Samaritan – her way of dealing with the suicide of a close family friend – and training as a Relate counsellor. I was vaguely aware, too, that in retirement she’d founded local hillwalking groups, a social club for widows – and who knows what else. But stupidly, I hadn’t realised what the things we took for granted – “there goes Mum, on one of her missions again” – meant to others. She had been the author of small kindnesses remembered for decades.

double quotation markHave a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affair

Why wait for a funeral, one of her friends argued, to say nice things? There was talk of a pre-party, a wake Mum could actually join in, abandoned when it became clear she was already too tired. But the urge to invent new rituals makes sense. With modern medicine rendering heart attacks and strokes more survivable, death increasingly announces itself to elderly people not suddenly overnight but slowly, and with plentiful warning. The creeping degenerative diseases of old age allow more time to say goodbye, or make amends if necessary. But they also force us all to look death squarely in the face, and that takes no little courage.

Fiercely independent at 84, my mother dreaded going into a home. So when she was given less than three months to live, my sister and I promised to nurse her at home, despite having no real plan for managing that alongside jobs and teenage children, beyond somehow basically winging it. Have a baby and the world falls over itself to offer advice. But losing a parent remains a private, bewildering, lonely affair. Here, then, are a few things I wish I’d known at the beginning of summer, in case – like that empty bed – another family can use them.

That care for the dying will trigger the instant muscle memory of caring for small children, if you had them: the same broken nights, same constant vigilance, same exhaustion after a day in which you can’t name a single thing you actually did, and the same unmistakable feeling of love tinged with occasional rage. Then as now we wouldn’t have coped without understanding employers, good friends and neighbours, an army of often overworked NHS and care staff, and things my sister learned from training as a midwife. (For the love of your lower back, get a professional to show you how to move a bedbound patient safely.)

That there are moments of unspeakably black humour to be found even in dying, if you’re that kind of family.

That there are times when your role is to argue with their doctors, and times for shutting up and listening, and you may never be wholly certain which is which.

That if an old person in beady possession of all their marbles goes seemingly mad overnight, test for an underlying infection causing delirium. Antibiotics work miracles.

That you should keep the bad photographs, because afterwards they’re the ones you invariably want to look at: anything where the kids were scowling, the haircuts sorely regrettable, the beach day rained off. It’s the life actually lived, not the one curated for Instagram, that you miss.

That death can trigger an overwhelming urge to put one’s house in order in ways that make sense to the dying, but absolutely nobody else. (My mother had to be dissuaded from getting the sitting room repainted; a friend’s father insisted on alphabetising his CDs.) Within reason, don’t fight it. Like the manic nesting phase of late pregnancy, it’s all part of the process.

That if you find old letters, you should read them only when feeling resilient. Your parents had lives before you existed and secrets they may not have shared.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

That death itself is different for everyone, but that even the most peaceful kind looked to me like a form of work. The best way I can describe it is like a reverse childbirth: you can comfort the person going through it, but you cannot be in it with them.

That it wasn’t nearly as frightening as that may sound.

That grief doesn’t always wait for death. Dementia meant I lost my father in some ways years before he died, and a wise friend said that nursing my mother might feel, in retrospect, like starting to work through bereavement in advance. She wasn’t wrong.

That adrenaline may power you through initially, and kindness may undo you.

And lastly, what I think my mother would have wanted me to say: that if this is something you have yet to face, don’t be afraid. But if you’re already there and struggling, then you are nowhere near as alone as you think.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

From Nish Kumar to the Bayeux tapestry: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

Our premier political comedian heads out on tour, while the 70-metre-long woven story of 1066 arrows its way to Britain for the first time

Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex PassOut now Widely popularised by an episode of Friends in which Ross makes an ass of himself with Isabella Rossellini, the notion of the “celebrity sex pass” completes some sort of cultural loop here as another Friends star, Jennifer Aniston, comes full circle to play a version of herself, the subject of Tom’s (Michael Cassidy) get-out-of-jail lust freebie. A romcom from David Wain (Wet Hot American Summer).

The IncomerOut now This British comedy follows a pair of isolated siblings, Isla (Gayle Rankin) and Sandy (Grant O’Rourke), whose parents disappeared 30 years ago. Having fended for themselves ever since, they aren’t eager to welcome Daniel (Domhnall Gleeson), who has been given the task of relocating them from their remote Scottish island home.

Super NatureOut now Filmed on Super 8mm film via cameras sent to 40 collaborators across 25 countries and five continents, this nature documentary is the brainchild of director Ed Sayers, and edits together footage of all creatures great (including rhinos) and small (snails).

Late FameOut now Willem Dafoe and Greta Lee star in Kent Jones’s adaptation of a posthumously published novella by Austrian modernist author Arthur Schnitzler. Dafoe plays a post office worker and former poet living in downtown Manhattan who is flattered by the attention of a group of wealthy young writers who apparently want to revive his career. Catherine Bray

Hilary Duff6 to 15 September; tour starts Dublin After breaking a decade-long musical hiatus with February’s Top 5 album, Luck … Or Something, the artist formerly known as Lizzie McGuire keeps up the momentum with this arena tour. Probably best to save your voice for 2003 teen-angst classic So Yesterday. Michael Cragg

Melanie MartinezThe O2, London, 11 September; touring to 12 September With the follow-up to March’s alt-pop opus Hades apparently due by the end of the year, the gloriously OTT New York curio brings her head-spinning show to the UK. Expect elaborate set pieces, skin-singeing flames and theatrical, dark-hued anthems. MC

Tête-à-Tête: The Opera festivalThe Cockpit, London, 8 to 20 September It may be annual, but this showcase by the Cornwall-based new opera powerhouse is always one of a kind. This year’s crop of novelties features Orpheus and Mary, Queen of Scots, folk horror, morris dancing and Old Norse: a typically colourful retort to anyone who thinks that opera is dead. Flora Willson

Emma RawiczLondon, 5 September; Manchester, 9 September; Gateshead, 10 September The whirlwind evolution of UK sax original Emma Rawicz since her 2022 debut album at 19 now finds her leading her own exciting orchestra, working with A-list players, and gigging all over Europe. She brings the big band to Ronnie Scott’s (5 September), then follows that up with shows with her fusion-angled Inkyra quintet. John Fordham

Monika SosnowskaSouth London Gallery, London, 10 September to 22 November Ultra-minimal installation and half-tonne hanging sculptures all about architecture and its impact on everyday life by this Polish artist, who uses a whole raft of industrial materials to look at the legacies of modernism and communism.

The Bayeux TapestryThe British Museum, London, 10 September to 11 JulyThe world-famous Bayeux tapestry is finally making its long-awaited journey back to England for the most hyped, hotly anticipated and sure-to-sell-out blockbuster exhibition in a decade.

A Mughal SongbookThe Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge, 8 September to 7 MarchA fascinating, colourful, melodious look at the ornate pages of the Plowden songbook, a rare manuscript of songs from the Mughal empire, which ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857.

Tschabalala SelfTrafalgar Square’s fourth plinth, London, from 10 September We’ve had a big thumb, a giant ship in a bottle and a huge dollop of cream; now the fourth plinth is going to be home to something more traditional for public sculpture: an enormous human figure, striding positively forwards in a blue dress, by American artist Tschabalala Self. Eddy Frankel

Scottish Ballet: EmergenceTheatre Royal, Glasgow, 10 to 12 September; touring to 3 October A visually arresting ballet by Crystal Pite is the main draw here. Pite’s Emergence, from 2009, uses the impact of the corps de ballet en masse to great effect. There’s also a premiere from Julia Cheng, award-winning choreographer of Cabaret and Fiddler on the Roof. Lyndsey Winship

Nish Kumar9 September to 27 November; tour starts Belfast Impassioned but never pious, righteous but never smug, Kumar’s ability to temper strident takes with goofy likability means he’s fast becoming our premier progressive political comedian. New show Angry Humour from a Really Nice Guy sees the 41-year-old mine laughs from the threat of autocracy and the ageing process. Rachel Aroesti

Bloodsport: After Helen of TroyTheatre Royal Stratford East, London, to 10 October Brilliant new(ish) playwright Ava Pickett (1536) imagines what might have happened when Helen returned home from Troy, after a war fought in her name. Starring Michelle Dockery and Laura Aikman. Miriam Gillinson

Tartuffe (Remixed)Marylebone theatre, London, to 24 October Mark Rylance stars alongside an ensemble of Intermission Youth graduates in Darren Raymond’s modern take on Molière’s classic comedy – which sees, in this case, a Nigerian-Jamaican family’s wedding plans blown apart by the arrival of a mysterious guest. MG

after newsletter promotion

Last SeenApple TV, 9 September In what is quite the career gear change, Colin from Accounts star Patrick Brammall sloughs off his warm and fuzzy romcom associations to lead this chilling drama with Maxine Peake about a police dispatcher convinced he’s answered a call from his daughter, abducted a decade earlier.

The PaperSky One & Now, 10 September, 9pm Season one of this feelgood and impeccably performed US Office-universe comedy saw ambitious editor Ned (Domhnall Gleeson again) take the Toledo Truth Teller from depressing clickbait factory to award-winning bastion of actual journalism. Now he’s searching for a showstopping scoop to cement his reputation.

Britain’s Forgotten GirlsBBC Two & iPlayer, 9 September, 9pm Alessia Camoirano Bruges’s 2022 film about the Italian mafia’s recruitment of young teenagers via social media was nominated for an Emmy; now the documentarian turns her attention to the vulnerable children abused and trafficked by drug-dealing gangs in the UK, and asks why the authorities have done so little to help.

The Drop: A Snowfall SagaDisney+, 9 SeptemberThis spin-off from the critically acclaimed Damson Idris series Snowfall shifts focus from LA’s 1980s crack epidemic to the following decade’s west coast hip-hop scene. Gail Bean’s Wanda is now clean and ready to capitalise on rap’s thrilling rise – something that requires a savvy navigation of street politics and nerves of steel. RA

Halloween: The GamePC, PS5, Xbox; out 8 September Play as a hapless teenager or take on the role of masked psychopath Michael Myers in this multiplayer gorefest set during the original film’s timeline. It looks like an absolute scream.

ValheimPC, PS5, Switch 2, Xbox; out 9 September The acclaimed Viking-inspired survival adventure is finally getting a full release after several years in “early access”. Survive in a hostile purgatory with up to nine pals as you conquer beasts, gather resources and, of course, build pretty houses. Keith Stuart

Kasabian – Act IIIOut now Flamboyant rock wizard Serge Pizzorno and his band of merry men are back with their ninth album. Co-produced by Mark Ralph (Years & Years, Clean Bandit), Act III mixes bright pop moments (Superpowers) with more noodly new wave songs such as the festival-ready Great Pretender.

Natalie Imbruglia – Algorithm Out now Pop’s other Ramsay Street resident turned singer returns with this seventh album. Mykki Blanco – Cafe ParadisoOut now Inspired by a life lived in transit, and influenced by New York, Paris and Tangier (where the American rapper and performance artist is now based), Cafe Paradiso is billed as a record for “artsy kids”. They should find a lot to love in the scuzzy art-rock of Butt Sex.

Adéla – PrimaOut now With the Bangerz-esque current single Ain’t in LA all over TikTok, the Slovak alt-pop experimentalist releases her long-awaited debut album. As you’d imagine for someone who auditioned to be in girl band Katseye, pop runs through Adéla’s veins, as shown on the bratty KGB and Red Bottoms’ sultry midtempo catharsis. MC

What Music Looks Like Podcast Writer Paul Weedon explores how artful design can enhance music, speaking to artists such as Adam Smith on his immersive stage visuals for the Chemical Brothers and Laura LiPuma on her 1980s work with Prince.

InCinematicYouTube Video essayist InCinematic presents fascinating and often niche takes on the efficacy of different creative techniques in cinema. A recent highlight explores Leslie Nielsen’s deadpan delivery in Airplane! and the experimentalism of The Lion King.

Hamza: African Birds of PreyBBC iPlayer Wildlife cameraman Hamza Yassin takes his infectious enthusiasm for nature to Kenya in this beautiful film where he goes in search of some of Africa’s most threatened birds of prey, such as the crowned eagle. Ammar Kalia
