How posh are you? Do you have a therapist? What would you say to Trump at a party? Marina Hyde answers readers’ questions

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

We asked you what you most wanted to put to our Guardian columnist. You responded in droves, querying her ‘beef’ with Burnham, who she thinks is this generation’s Hugh Grant, and what she really thinks about Richard Osman ...

‘There is light at the end of this tunnel. But the tunnel is filled with sewage’: an exclusive extract from Marina Hyde’s new book

What are your bunker plans?James, Portugal Masses of things to read, incredible food and an unethical doctor with an insane war chest of interesting pills. The second that bunker door closes, the doors of perception are opening.

Will Restore gain more traction by the next election and genuinely split the rightwing vote?Natasha, London They won’t split it in some 50‑50 way, but they could peel off a bit more from Reform’s right flank. Nigel Farage is looking vulnerable. In the Woody Allen film Deconstructing Harry, Robin Williams plays an actor who literally goes out of focus. Having once been sharp and clear, his nervous system is so shot that he becomes a physically blurred and imprecise distortion of himself. Metaphorically, something similar has happened to Farage in recent months.

Who do you think is this generation’s young Hugh Grant (ie witty, funny, sexy, intelligent and gorgeous)?Anna, New Zealand It’s being done as a job share between Jude Bellingham and Cole Palmer.

Are the men of the manosphere right about anything?Kate, London I saw Clavicular say, “My life is a horror story”, which feels about right.

I have noticed a more serious tone in your columns this year. In light of recent events, here and abroad, are you finding it increasingly difficult to maintain your humorous disposition?Tim, London No. I’m sorry, I must have been tired when I wrote those ones. It’s always more effort to be funny than serious.

If you met Andrew Tate, Elon Musk and Donald Trump at a hideous dinner party, how would you greet and say goodbye to each of them?Becky, Bristol “You must try the beef bourguignon. I hear our hostess foraged the mushrooms herself.”

What would you have said to Margaret Thatcher’s face if you’d had a whole two minutes alone with her?Eamon, Ireland So much is known and has been written about her that new lines of inquiry can feel hard to come by. But I would have liked to find a way of getting her to reveal how she felt about being the object of so many men’s crushes. Both those who worked around her and what Norma Desmond called “all those wonderful people out there in the dark”. She knew, of course, and would most certainly have had Inner Thoughts about the phenomenon. However, I have to say, it would be quite difficult to build the rapport required to get them out of her in two minutes

Why are journalists failing to make the case to the public that rightwingers such as Nigel Farage, Richard Tice and Stephen Yaxley‑Lennon are dishonest, self‑serving and not terribly bright?Alexis, Kent I really don’t think the vast majority of people pay the slightest direct attention to journalists at all. There are still some heavily invested continuity Corbynites out there who will imply that two or three critical columns I wrote about their absolute boy had something to do with him losing his second general election on the bounce in 2019. To which my reply would be: “Yes, dear, I’m sure they talked of little else but my columns on the doorsteps of the ‘red wall’. Yet, if we were to humour your notion that the whimsical musings of some silly cow in London make one nanoparticle of difference, how come I wrote 937 critical articles about Boris Johnson and he still won a landslide?” On the rightwingers front, however, I would point out that it is journalists and not anyone else who have been exposing, for example, Farage, Tice and Yaxley‑Lennon’s financial arrangements, and I’m very grateful to them for their work.

The citations in your columns have taken me down some scurrilous rabbit holes I would not otherwise have encountered. How much of your research is spent in corners of the web you would rather not be? And do you have a therapist?!Ian, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire Hahahahaha. Someone once told me they found out about edging videos from something I wrote about Theresa May’s endlessly inconclusive Brexit votes in the Commons. I can only apologise. Personally, I love the fact that I can spend my days wading through the more recherche bits of contemporary culture, and if anyone sees me, just say, “It’s for my WORK????” As far as the last part of the question goes, I don’t have a therapist. It’s so unfashionable, of course, but I have to say I’m a big, big believer in pushing it all down. I know, I know – I consistently note people’s looks of distaste when I tell them that. But I’m just putting the counterpoint out there.

Your articles usually speak to power. Have you ever felt fear of the potential consequences?Chris, near Brighton, East Sussex The most credible politically motivated threats I have faced have been from the far right and the far left – and always from supporters rather than any publicly known figures. But – so far! – I’ve always found the bigger danger to be lone men who develop obsessions of one kind or another.

Do you work on resilience?Mary, Dublin Not particularly consciously. But I valorise it. The older I get, the more I see that it is an endlessly useful kind of freedom. But that’s easy for me to say, because I’m so lucky. The resilience it takes to be, say, a woman in Afghanistan or a little girl in Congo is quite simply utterly inconceivable to me. I basically think that everything I have, and everything that I have achieved, is overwhelmingly the result of luck and good fortune, and not remotely to do with any kind of exceptionalist skill.

If you had to spend a month on a desert island with a group of footballers, politicians or celebs, which would you choose and why?Charlie, Switzerland Hot footballers, let’s face it.

Will Andy Burnham’s plan for a No 10 North in Manchester be a stroke of genius or his undoing?Patrick, LaSalle, Canada Neither (the most versatile answer in politics).

Clearly, politicians are worse than useless. Who would you pick as prime minister?Eric, Newton Abbot, Devon JK Rowling.

What’s always off-limits to critique? And what would feel important enough to make you reconsider your own boundaries?Josh, Palm Springs, US In general, I think everything can and should be written about, as long as you get the right tone. Anything involving children is always what I’d be most cautious about.

Do you have a writing routine?Michael, Gijón, Spain I try to be at my desk at 5am, because I’m definitely a lark. Something that takes me five minutes at 5am will take me an hour at 5pm. So the morning is definitely my best writing time. As far as column-writing goes, I tend never to start with the first sentence. I just put a few things down in a Word document and move them all round till some kind of column starts to stagger out of the primordial soup. I mostly don’t know what I think until I’ve gone through the act of writing about it, so the conclusion can often be as much of a surprise to me as to anyone kind enough to read it.

Which ludicrous situation involving a UK PM has made you laugh the most during your career?Richard, NSW, Australia Tony Blair having someone at the Foreign Office during the Iraq war whose official, ask-at-reception job title was “head of story development”. That was quite a mirthless laugh, obviously. David Cameron? Either leaving his daughter in the pub during a “troubled families” initiative week, or the shagging-the-pig’s-head thing. Theresa May calling a general election and the exit poll coming out at 10pm showing she’d lost her majority. Boris Johnson hiding from the media in a big fridge. Liz Truss spending her entire career wanging on about the infallibility of free markets, then getting her arse handed to her by them in about 10 minutes. Rishi Sunak calling the election in the driving rain, and then not realising that binning off Normandy D-day celebrations for a media interview would play badly. Keir Starmer calling for the return of the Gaza sausages. Andy Burnham: TBC, but it’s coming, I assure you.

The 1970s was a time of revolution, with so many groups up in arms. I sensed the same energy at June’s Dublin Dyke March: outrage, we’ve had enough … Do you think young people today have revolutionary energy?Ger, Dublin Not at all, I have to say. I think as long as people have smartphones in their hands, they will be too narcotised to rebel. There’s a kind of dropout energy in a lot of young people, which is as completely understandable as it is completely sad. I really feel for them.

What is your favourite meal?Douglas, Germany Honestly, my next one. At home, I make a huge amount of schnitzel in all kinds of ways. And multiple types of apple pie. Very pleased (and culinarily jealous) to be giving this answer to someone based in Germany.

Celebrity culture and AI promise a world where some people are valued and others deemed worthless. What human qualities do you most value?Sean, Swinford, County Mayo Compassion, tolerance, wisdom, kindness, bravery, strength of character. And GSOH.

Across your articles and podcasts, I note you consume a huge amount of news and media. How on earth do you find the time? And do you have to take comprehensive notes in case you need to make connections between people or events at a later date?Simon, Windsor, Berkshire I love the idea of notes, but, no – I have never taken any! Maybe I need to get Stacey Solomon to do an episode of Sort Your Life Out in my memory palace. The truth is my brain just works quite associatively, so something in politics will always remind me of something in sport or music, and it often ends up feeling more illuminating to me that way.

I’m intrigued by your somewhat startling animus towards Andy Burnham. What is driving this?Ricardo, Carshalton, south LondonListen, I’ve been hurt before. Meet you back here in two years?

How posh are you?Rob, New Zealand I guess I can hold my own.

What’s the worst thing about working with Richard Osman on The Rest Is Entertainment?Katie, Dublin He’s funnier than me. Also, he only pretends to support Fulham. That second one might not be true – I just wanted to say something in a public forum that would incense him but where he wouldn’t be present to reply. (Try writing to the letters page, Richard – see how you get on.)

Are you still on X? If so, why?Caroline, Switzerland Yes, I am. I don’t use it much at all as I find social media a massive time‑suck. I hear Bluesky is truly ghastly, but have never visited.

What’s your favourite Brooklyn Beckham career?Martin, Weston-super-Mare, Somerset 2042 chairman of the Federal Reserve.

You often draw equivalence between Labour and the Tories: “They’re all as bad as each other.” Do you ever worry that you’re contributing to an anti‑political climate that is one of the factors rendering Britain ungovernable?Shaun, Punta del Este, Uruguay I hope I’ve never used that phrase, Shaun. However, when any side falls short of the standards we should expect in public life, it massively undermines trust in all politicians. That’s happened a lot since the turn of the millennium. But I don’t think Britain is ungovernable, and I fundamentally believe that politics is still the best way we have of making people’s lives better.

Will art save us?Steven, London Unclear. Still, what a way to go.

What usually drags you out of bed in the morning?Peter, Perth Insomnia’s pretty helpful. But I’ve usually got lots to do and I love a new day.

Does anyone care if Prince Harry is in or out? Are the people ahead of the papers on this one?Paul, London I definitely think stories about him and Meghan do a lot of traffic, which is why he gets written about so much. I think a lot of people claim they’re not at all interested and yet still read huge amounts about him. I’m like this about The Rock’s multiple business ventures. Could not care less about them; have read 23 articles this week about them.

What makes you feel hopeful and optimistic?Pauline, Bristol Love, human ingenuity and listening to pop music.

What’s your favourite word in the English language?Rick, Manchester Cocktailhour.

What a Time to Be Alive! Scenes from a Strange Age by Marina Hyde will be published by Guardian Faber at £20 on 24 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy for £15 at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Why the Bayeux tapestry and Franco-British relations are natural bedfellows

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 05:00:27 GMT

Tapestry’s loan to UK is just another chapter in the love-hate relationship that has spanned the centuries since it was created

Five British prime ministers ago – and six French ones – when Emmanuel Macron first confirmed that France would return the Bayeux tapestry to Britain after 1,000 years, he told an audience at Sandhurst and Theresa May – the No 10 seat-warmer of the day – that when it came to France and Britain there were “two things that nothing can change, be it a vote or a political decision: our history and our geography”.

It was January 2018, 18 months after the UK had voted to leave the EU, and relations between the near neighbours were not good. The French political establishment had been shocked and angered by Brexit; personal relations were frazzled, and cross-Channel government contacts measurably dwindling. This was not a rupture that a piece of embroidered medieval linen, however perfectly it represented that tangled history, was going to solve on its own.

It took only eight and a half years and many, many changes in personnel, but this week Macron finally made good on that pledge with the unveiling of the tapestry at the British Museum in London, in scenes of such amitié that one could almost forget the bilateral chill that had gone before.

No one pretends that the Bayeux tapestry alone has been responsible for stitching together two nations whose connections had visibly frayed. (When it comes to the tapestry, as every commentator this week has shown, the needlework metaphors are hard to resist.) But the French president’s single-minded commitment to drive through a loan that he has previously called “seemingly impossible” illustrates that, in diplomatic terms, the London exhibition is not just a decorative sideshow.

“It is much more than just a linen canvas embroidered with wool,” Macron told an audience at the museum on Wednesday. “It represents a whole chapter of French, British and European history.”

In that context, it was notable that he speculated that people “decades or even centuries from now” would look back not only on the tapestry itself but on “what we did here today” – the very fact of its loan to the British Museum – as being a significant marker in the long span of Franco-British relations. “Two countries which, after centuries of shared history, [chose] to forge a bond as close as the threads of this thousand-year-old embroidery,” he said.

The latest UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, agreed in language tailored to suit his own political project. As a “tremendous demonstration of goodwill”, he said, the loan “says so much about the friendship of our two nations … It shows the power of collaboration to lift people’s lives.”

The Bayeux tapestry, of course, was always a highly political artefact, even before it acquired its status as a foundational text for the English nation (1066, the date of the Battle of Hastings, is “the nation’s pincode”, the British Museum chair, George Osborne, noted drily on Wednesday).

Much remains unknown about the circumstances of its commission and creation, but a vast artwork showing a clash of kings and wholesale invasion of a nation is not a neutral object. “It was definitely designed with a political purpose in mind when it was first made,” says the historian Dr David Musgrove, who has written a book, The Story of the Bayeux Tapestry, with Prof Michael Lewis, the curator of the exhibition.

“That political purpose was essentially to legitimise the invasion of William the Conqueror, to explain why he did it, why he chose to send his fleet across the Channel,” argues Musgrove, who is the content director of HistoryExtra magazine and podcast. The “crux scene”, he argues, is not the famous bit where Harold takes an arrow to the eye, but an earlier portion that shows the then English earl Harold making an oath to support William’s future claim to the English throne.

Harold reneges on this later when he has himself crowned king of England. “So he perjures himself and that gives William the reason to invade,” Musgrove says. “My take is that the tapestry is entirely predicated on making that justification. So it’s very modern in that sense; people trying to justify military action today is kind of the same thing. It’s a retrospective justification for what happened.”

Most historians believe it was made in Canterbury, but “just about everything around [the tapestry’s creation] is a little bit uncertain”, according to Leonie Hicks, a professor of medieval studies at Canterbury Christ Church University. She says historians’ “best assumption” – based on the internal evidence of the embroidery itself and other contemporary documents – “is that it was likely commissioned by Bishop Odo, who was William the Conqueror’s half-brother, bishop of Bayeux and also earl of Kent after the conquest. Or somebody very close to Odo.”

Odo and Willliam had fallen out, so an elaborate narrative wall covering at Odo’s Norman cathedral celebrating the new English king could be seen as an attempt to regain favour. But if the tapestry undoubtedly flatters William, it is not a piece of crude propaganda, argues Hicks, and the politics of its depiction are nuanced. “It’s not a straightforward piece of ‘Yay, aren’t the Normans great, they dumped the English and took the throne.’”

Among the most intriguing details, she notes, are the depictions in the margins of the human cost of war – all stitched, most likely, by English women who may have lost husbands and sons in the battle. “We have the scene where a house is being burnt and a woman is holding a child’s hand and leaving the house. [There are] very graphic depictions in the margins of decapitated soldiers, and bodies being looted. It does give that sense that war is horrific and terrible.”

It is context which, we can assume, was lost during the tapestry’s long afterlife. History records nothing about it until it turns up in an inventory of the Bayeux Cathedral treasury in 1476. The tapestry, it noted, was hung around the cathedral for a few days each year. During the French Revolution it was narrowly rescued from being used as a wagon cover.

It would not be long, however, before the tapestry’s political usefulness would again be recognised. Napoleon, planning an English invasion of his own in 1803, displayed it in Paris where “it was quite a sensation”, says Musgrove. “I think Napoleon probably thought it was useful to have an artefact which showed a previous cross-Channel invasion by forces from France into Britain.” When the invasion plans foundered, the tapestry was quietly returned to Bayeux.

The Nazis were “obsessed” with the tapestry – “they basically saw it as part of their worldview of Aryan Teutonic supremacy”, says Musgrove – and in the days before the liberation of Paris planned to whisk it away to Germany. They were, however, frustrated by the French resistance, who had been alerted by codebreakers at Bletchley Park.

Eight quiet decades followed before the renovation of the museum where it is housed in Bayeux prompted its removal from display. But if that immediate circumstance opened the possibility of the artwork being loaned to Britain, there was certainly no inevitability that this would happen.

Britain first made a request almost a century ago, in 1931. A request to borrow the artwork in 1953 to mark Elizabeth II’s coronation was initially agreed by France, before it reversed the decision over conservation concerns. Another attempt in 1966, to commemorate 900 years since the battle, foundered in the face of local and national French opposition. Another bid in the 1980s came to nothing.

Macron could easily have come to the same judgment, not least because there was plenty of opposition in France to the loan, including from artists and conservation experts. Why, then, such commitment to making happen a loan which, he only half joked last year, had been more complicated to negotiate than the Brexit withdrawal agreements?

To Helen Drake, a professor of French and European studies at Loughborough University London, making the loan happen fits with Macron’s view of himself as a cultured international statesman – but also with the value he attaches to repairing the Franco-British relationship in the face of mutually threatening global forces.

“Macron is a French president who has pulled the maximum levers that the constitution give him to operate on the international stage, and that will probably be his legacy. So from that perspective it would make sense to him to be seen to be behind the transfer of the tapestry.

“But he has also very much made it part of his mandate to be at the forefront of ameliorating France’s relations with the UK.” On Ukraine, defence and security, migration and Trump, British and French shared interests have become ever more pressing, she says. “The external environment, to put it bluntly, has pushed the two together.”

But for all the genuine bonhomie over a dazzling piece of history, Drake says, neither side has any illusions about the dynamic tension that has always characterised their love-hate relationship. “The fact is that France habitually plays hardball with the UK in its negotiations with the EU post-Brexit,” she says. “You can have all the warmth you like in the British Museum, [but] the Quai d’Orsay will still drive a hard bargain. The two co-exist and they’re not even contradictory – they’re just part of how we see the Franco-British relationship.”

‘Then who or what did we cremate?’ Daughter’s horror at finding bones in British wildfire victims’ car

The Guardian Sat, 05 Sep 2026 04:00:26 GMT

Danielle Gillam-Kirton claims police botched investigation into her parents’ deaths in Spain and is demanding answers

When Danielle Gillam-Kirton’s parents, Pete and Fran Gillam, were killed in July’s Spanish wildfires, she felt her nightmare could get no worse. The much-loved couple had built their home in Bédar in Almería after retirement, becoming part of a tight-knit community. Fran, a former headteacher, loved to organise quiz nights to raise money for the local school and the couple enjoyed playing padel at a nearby sports club.

Spanish police told Gillam-Kirton that the vehicle in which her parents died had been “inspected meticulously” and no possessions had been found. But Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, was sure her parents must have been wearing their wedding rings when they died.

She was invited to search the vehicle herself, which was parked in a police compound in Mojácar. “You won’t find anything,” she was told.

She describes crying out in shock when she looked through the door of the burnt-out car. On the front seats was what appeared to be a human hip bone. “I honestly can’t describe what that felt like. I remember staring at what was in my hand, and the slow realisation of what I thought I was looking at hit me. I shouted out in shock,” she says.

She and her partner searched the car and found more bones, which appeared to be the remains of the couple. They also found her parents’ mobile phones, sets of keys, jewellery, money and other personal effects.

The Gillams were among 14 people killed in the fires, including Belgian, French, American and Spanish nationals. Some of the bereaved families are now searching for answers and claim the Bédar authorities have botched the investigation into their deaths.

There has already been a funeral for the Gillams. “It makes you wonder: who or what did we cremate?” Gillam-Kirton says. She is demanding answers from the Spanish government and asking the UK Foreign Office to hold the authorities to account.

The bones she found have been sent for DNA testing after weeks of delay from the Bédar local authority. Forensic scientists who have looked at pictures of the bones have told Gillam-Kirton they appear to be human.

“The whole sequence is incredibly difficult to understand. We were told there was nothing left, and yet when we were finally able to look ourselves, we found significant personal belongings and what appeared to be human remains,” she says.

“We were initially told it was probably animal remains.” She says she had to push the Spanish authorities to send them off for DNA testing. “The bones were big. I can’t see how a large animal like a cow would have climbed into the passenger seat of the vehicle during a fire.”

Gillam-Kirton says she helped another family who were told their loved ones died while attempting to escape the fires on foot and that their remains had been cleared by a forensic team. She arranged for a search party – including a police officer and one of the victim’s relatives – to travel to the hillside on which they died. There they found what appeared to be human bones lying in plain view along with various personal belongings.

“These were people who were caught in the same horrific fire as my mum and dad,” she says. “They lost their lives in terrifying circumstances and they deserved dignity and respect, in the way they were treated at the time and afterwards. And for us and the other families, those personal belongings aren’t just objects. They’re the last physical things connecting us to the people we have lost.”

Gillam-Kirton has previously criticised the Spanish authorities for failing to alert her parents to the danger of the fire in good time. Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come for another three hours and was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house”. Thirteen residents from the Gillams’ village died.

Gillam-Kirton says she wants the UK government to “keep pressing the Spanish authorities for proper answers”. She adds: “Eight British people died in this fire, including my mum and dad, so I think it is really important that the UK government continues to take an interest in what happened. After all, we are talking about the treatment of British nationals – the deceased and the living.”

She and the other families are asking the Spanish authorities for “a proper, thorough and transparent investigation … and I mean the whole thing, not just what caused the fire, but what happened during the emergency response, what warnings were given, when they were given, who received them, what evacuation arrangements were in place and what happened to the victims afterwards”.

Initially, the Spanish authorities blamed the victims for not understanding or following the evacuation instructions. However, it later emerged that no such instructions were given.

“I think that’s one of the things we’ve found hardest,” Gillam-Kirton says of the police response. “At the beginning, there seemed to be a lot of emphasis on the idea that the victims had ignored instructions or hadn’t evacuated when they were told to. And that was incredibly painful for us. And now, months later, we’re still asking basic questions.”

She adds: “That, along with what appears to us to have been a lack of proper search-and-preserve procedures at the scene, has left us feeling that there has been a real lack of empathy towards the victims and their families.”

The families hope that if there is a proper investigation into the deaths of their relatives and the behaviour of the authorities afterwards, others will not have to go through the unbearable situation they have had to face.

“Wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe, and communities are going to face these situations again,” Gillam-Kirton says. “There will be another fire somewhere, and there will be other people who need to be evacuated.

“If you don’t properly investigate something, you can’t learn from it. We don’t want Mum and Dad to simply become two names in a list of people who died in a wildfire. We want to understand what happened to them, and if something went wrong, we want the lessons to be learned.”

The Foreign Office said that any investigations were the responsibility of the Spanish authorities. A spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British couple who died in Spain, and our thoughts are with those affected by the devastating wildfires.”

The Bédar local government has been contacted for comment.

Five Great Reads: After the flood, leaving Maga, and sex doll ethics

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 22:17:54 GMT

Guardian Australia’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This week, we have selected stories that will move you. A dispatch from a disaster zone, where rescue teams are sifting through scattered, buried remnants, a feature about walking away from a community that once welcomed you, and a piece on running just to see how far you can go.

Enjoy.

In the aftermath of the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster, thousands remain missing and access to aid remains hindered by treacherous conditions. On the ground in some of the worst-hit areas, our south Asia correspondent, Hannah Ellis-Petersen, and journalist Gaurav Pokharel write that while the scale of the damage caused by the flood is unfathomable, so too is the human suffering as communities almost wiped out of existence reckon with what comes next. Notable quote: “Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”

Scattered fragments: The ruins of the lives of thousands are now buried in and among the debris. “Kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses” remind rescue teams of the hundreds still missing.

How long will it take to read: Three-and-a-half minutes.

Further reading: Trapped workers could still be alive, families hope DNA can be used to find their loved ones, and desperate relatives of the missing fear attention is already drifting away from the ongoing crisis.

Donald Trump and his “Make America Great Again” (Maga) base of supporters have come to dominate American politics. For many Trump followers, the movement built on lies and conspiracy theories offered a shared identity. For others, it became something closer to religion. But after more than 10 years, some devotees are finally walking away, making amends, and offering support to others who are reckoning with their role in Trump’s America.

What drew people into the Maga “cult” and why did they leave? Rich Logis found a second family in the Maga community. He found belonging, camaraderie and a common enemy. But after the politicians he lionised platformed Covid anti-vaxxers he started to diversify his news sources. Logis slowly began to realise that what he believed was false and he had been “complicit in dividing this country”.

Notable quote: “My loyalty wasn’t to Trump. My loyalty was to God and the church.”

How long will it take to read: Four-and-a-half minutes to read, and less than one minute to share with a friend who has fallen down a rabbit hole.

Further reading: You can learn more about Life after Maga, and how the non-profit Leaving Maga is fighting Trumpism like a disease.

Mary Austin was the quiet girlfriend of rock band Queen’s flamboyant figurehead. They dreamed of marriage until they both finally spoke the unspoken. Thirty-five years after his death, Austin’s new book lays out Mercury’s life in lyrics.

‘No, Freddie, I think you’re gay’: Austin and Mercury had been living together for four years when they both realised Mercury was only attracted to men. But rather than destroying their relationship, Austin says the revelation felt like a relief. They continued living together for the next 18 months and, as Queen and Mercury became a global phenomenon, Mary and Freddie became better friends.

Mercurial money: Austin has inherited half of Mercury’s estate (now estimated at about £150m). Asked where the money will go when she dies and if much of it will go to charity, she said, “It’s going to go to my children.”

How long will it take to read: Just over 13 minutes. Enough time to listen to Bohemian Rhapsody two times through.

Further reading: Check out Freddie Mercury’s “splendid things”, or pick up a copy of Mary Austin’s book from the Guardian Bookshop.

On a quiet country road south of Sydney, two distressed citizens stumbled across what they assumed was the mangled corpse of a woman stuffed into a suitcase. But the woman was not a woman at all and, after forensic analysis revealed it was a sex doll, questions about the booming sex doll industry have garnered global attention.

A flourishing trade: Estimates show that the global sex doll market is valued at more than US$6bn. But as the industry grows, Madison Griffiths asks, does it matter how these dolls get treated?How much? Lifelike sex dolls are now increasingly customisable and you can walk away with one for about US$1,790. But Caitlin Roper, the Australian author of Sex Dolls, Robots and Woman Hating: The Case for Resistance, calls these kinds of dolls “replica female sex slaves”. How long will it take to read: Just under four minutes. Further reading: The rise of “sex robots”, how police mistook a sex doll for a “body”, and what can we learn about male desire in a sex doll factory?

In a remarkable feat of physical and mental endurance, the Australian endurance athlete Phil Gore ran 6.71km every hour for an entire week just to see how far he could push himself.

Finding your limit: Having already set the world record in 2025, Gore knew he had “a lot more left to give”. But the rules of backyard ultra running require the final runner to stop one lap after the second-place runner drops out – limiting the potential boundaries of the winner. Gore wanted a challenge that would push him further. This time around, competing only against his own body and mind, Gore says, “that’s what I’ve done. Maybe [there is] a little bit of disappointment that I wanted my limit to be a bit further away.”

Fuel fit for a champion: Running for a week straight requires calories. A steady stream of “speckled snakes and Nerd clusters, jelly cups, custard pouches, simple sugars like that” kept Gore going for days.

How long will it take to read: Just over two minutes.

Further reading: What happens when you don’t finish a race, and why would anyone run an ultramarathon anyway?

Could this radical idea transform social care in the UK?

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:59:12 GMT

Readers respond to Paul Sagar’s article suggesting a ‘Care First’ year for students in exchange for 50% off university fees

I am sorry that Dr Paul Sagar experienced his injury, but grateful for his moment of enlightenment (The big idea: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?, 30 August). It is the sort of suggestion that family carers such as myself have been making for years, having been failed by the statutory services for decades.

It needs backing up with some infrastructure: more special schools, more special colleges, better provision in mainstream schools for children with special needs via smaller class sizes, and through more care villages/intentional communities with accommodation, not only for those needing care and support but also for the staff and volunteers on the same site, and housing for family carers.

For our family, enlightenment came more than 60 years ago when my younger brother was born deafblind with additional complex multiple disabilities. When my parents asked the authorities which special school he could attend, the reply was devastating: there was nowhere in the north of England that could cope with the severity and complexity of his disabilities. My parents were left in despair.

Thankfully, we embarked on a tour of the UK as a family with our car and caravan in search of a special school that could help. By some form of divine intervention, we came across the Camphill Rudolf Steiner school in Aberdeen.

My brother started there at the age of five and a half, and within a few weeks was toilet-trained and feeding himself – something that the officials at South Shields town hall had said was impossible.

The houseparents at the school were supported by a team of unwaged voluntary workers, many of whom were from other European countries and doing their “civil service” – an alternative to military service in their own country.

Our family was saved by the conscription policies of other countries and the civilian alternative provided by Camphill. The young voluntary co-workers gained a lifetime of experience and expertise, a confidence in working with and supporting vulnerable children and adults, and training in social care, communication and life skills, as well as learning English with an Aberdonian twang. Simon BurdisMorpeth, Northumberland

Paul Sagar is right to think that radical solutions are needed to transform social care in the UK, but social care deserves more consideration than an amped-up Duke of Edinburgh award. Care work is too often unfairly maligned as unskilled work and kept on low wages by an economy that favours profit over worker wellbeing.

These proposals to incentivise participation in social care work through student debt forgiveness and voluntary service won’t change that without engaging with the poor working conditions and pay in the sector. Rather, we need to consider what an economy that centres care in all its decisions looks like.

Moving away from extractive capitalist models of care provision is an essential part of this, and one that Andy Burnham has acknowledged. So too is a new narrative about care as being valuable, alongside meaningful support for the 6 million unpaid carers and an investment in care work and conditions. Our welfare state, public services and communities all have a role to play in a more caring economy, and we shouldn’t have to twist anyone’s arm to know that. Hannah WebsterCo-founder, Care Full, and former unpaid carer

Paul Sagar’s “Care First” proposal assumes that almost any school leaver can become a suitable carer after training. But caring is not easy or interchangeable work. It requires patience, judgment, emotional maturity, safeguarding awareness and the ability to preserve someone’s dignity during intimate or distressing situations.

What evidence suggests that school leavers motivated principally by reduced university fees would remain in demanding social care roles for a full year?

Social care already has a retention crisis. More than one in five domiciliary care staff leave their roles annually. Turnover rises to 38% among workers under 25 and 43.5% among those with less than a year’s experience. Recruiting a rotating supply of school leavers would do nothing to address the low pay, insecure hours, exhausting travel and working conditions driving experienced carers away.

Most importantly, people needing care have a right to choose who supports them and to expect competence, continuity and genuine commitment.

The proposed reward is also remarkably unequal. At current fee levels, one year in social care could earn a student up to £14,685 in tuition-fee reductions. A family carer providing at least 35 hours of care a week receives only £4,495.40 a year through carer’s allowance – and many receive nothing.

After more than 30 years as an NHS midwife, I left my career to care full-time for my mother, who has dementia. I lost earnings, pension growth and the freedom to work normally. If care is worth thousands when performed temporarily by a prospective student, why is sustained care provided by relatives valued so little?Jacqueline HyltonLeeds

In the picture and missing out

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:58:12 GMT

A camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment, writes Greg Lewis, while Alan Payling recalls the privacy of the photo booth

Phoebe Greenwood is right (Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?, 29 August). Having been a photojournalist, I find that the camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment.

Many years ago, my wife discovered previously unknown relatives in Denmark. When we visited, they took us to a cemetery where one of her ancestors was buried.

She stood there quietly for a few minutes and began to cry. I started photographing and suddenly realised that I had shifted into work mode, both physically and mentally. I put the camera down and gave her a hug.

After deciding that I wasn’t going to take photos when not working, we were on a whale-watching trip. I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones. Greg LewisClovis, California, US

In the absence of a personal camera, in the late 1960s, the commonly used alternative for young lovers to record their undying devotion to each other was the photo booth.

Apparently they were used by some to provide passport photos, but I recall that on Friday and Saturday evenings in Birmingham city centre, they were an essential part of a good night out. Not only would you get four photos to share; the curtain also provided a few moments of privacy, although only from the waist upwards! Alan PaylingTorquay, Devon

Good riddance to those dull Sundays that Tony Hancock and I loathed

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:55:12 GMT

Sundays in the 1950s are remembered by Bob Waring and Martin Cooper

In 1958 Tony Hancock had a very different take on the British Sunday from Sian Dudley’s bucolic vision (Letters, 30 August), as outlined in the Hancock’s Half Hour episode Sunday Afternoon at Home: “I might just as well be in bed: there’s nothing else to do. [Sigh] I wish I hadn’t got up now … I hate Sundays. It’s not like this on the continent: it’s their big day over there. All the cafes open and football matches and race meetings – everybody’s gay. Aahh! Not over ’ere though! Everything’s shut up.”

My memory accords with the bard of East Cheam. What we have now, and didn’t then, is choice. Bob WaringSouthport, Merseyside

Sian Dudley was lucky having such a relaxed Sunday as a child. My 1950s Sundays were rather different. My brothers and I had to go to church in the morning and Sunday school in the afternoon, we didn’t have a telly and I hated board games. I like my 2026 Sundays. Martin CooperBromley, London

Have a little fun scamming the scammers

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:54:12 GMT

Gary Calder responds to an article by a Guardian Money reader who got even by stringing the fraudsters along

Anyone wishing to get their own back on bank-card scammers using the method described in your article (‘I’ve £80k in the account, here’s my pin’: turning the tables on the scammers, 29 August) might like to add a touch of realism to a made-up bank-card number by picking a known issuer identification number (the first six to eight digits) and ensure that the last digit conforms to the Luhn algorithm (it’s a check digit used to pick up errors in entering all the other digits). Further fun could be had by choosing an interesting postcode, such as SW1A 2AA (or 2AB – 10 and 11 Downing Street), SW1A 2JL (New Scotland Yard) or SL4 1NJ (Windsor Castle). Gary CalderChandler’s Ford, Hampshire

The Guardian view on Reform’s funding scandal: Nigel Farage has questions to answer

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:52:08 GMT

An undercover investigation raises issues around foreign money, political transparency and the rightwing populist party’s fitness for power

Reform UK’s conference was to open showcasing a party ready for government. It did so with two top aides removed after an investigation aired on Channel 4, its finances under police scrutiny and seven in 10 voters, polls suggest, regarding its leader, Nigel Farage, as sleazy – double the number who thought the same of Andy Burnham. Reform, a rightwing populist party, says it will take power back from a corrupt establishment. The latest scandal raises a question: does Reform oppose the influence of big money – or just who benefits from it?

Undercover reporters from Verbatim Investigations, founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting, pretended to be a wealthy American father and his UK-based son who wanted to donate to Reform. In the UK, foreign donations are banned from politics. But that allegedly was ignored. Verbatim’s team filmed their meetings with James Orr, a Cambridge academic specialising in ethics, and Reform’s head of policy, as well as with Dan Jukes, Mr Farage’s close aide. Both have been “removed” from their posts.

Reform officials allegedly commissioned £32,500 of polling, arranged for what they believed was a US company to pay the bill, hid the party’s role and used the results to generate favourable newspaper headlines. Verbatim wired the money from a US firm to pollsters JL Partners, whose boss was filmed saying that he should have disclosed that his client was Reform. JL Partners admits procedural “weaknesses”. When the supposed American benefactor later explained the arrangement to Mr Farage over lunch, the Reform leader’s filmed response was not alarm but celebration: “It worked. Boom.”

The second main allegation is that the American father was willing to provide Reform with £500,000 through a “permissible” British intermediary – his son. This, if true, would be unlawful. At the lunch Mr Farage does not say that the father cannot be the cash’s source or that the son can legally only donate his own money. Rather, he is filmed saying “thank you both” when it was explained.

Gavin Millar KC, a noted media lawyer, told reporters that “there is enough being said, in the presence of Mr Farage and to Mr Farage, for it to be a red flag – for it to be understood as the reality that this money is coming from an American in a disguised form. And he should be questioning that … On the contrary, he seems to be quite happy to receive the money.”

In response, Reform says that it has “broken no laws”. Mr Farage told LBC that while his party had done “nothing wrong”, the footage looked bad and hence party aides were suspended. Reform has not offered much of an explanation, preferring to claim that it has “been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists”. Political opponents have reported Reform to the police and the Electoral Commission.

Reform’s problem is not that two aides forgot about the rules. It is that senior figures appear to have understood them, discussed how to circumvent them and assumed that nobody able to stop them would find out. A party accused of plotting how to get around the law is now promising to impose a “national emergency” so that judges and officials will not get in its way. That is a telling and ominous reveal about how Reform understands power.

The Guardian view on music and drama education: reversing elitism starts at school

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:49:26 GMT

The number of students taking creative subjects at A-level and GCSE is at a record low. The arts must not become the preserve of the most privileged

How many of the young people who attended Reading and Leeds festival or a Prom this summer will be picking up a guitar or clarinet when they return to school? New figures suggest not many. The number of students taking A-level music is at a record low: under 5,000, a drop of nearly half from 15 years ago. “We are facing the worst-case scenario prospect of A-level music disappearing from English state schools entirely,” warned Deborah Annetts, the chief executive of the Independent Society of Musicians. Music GCSE entries have also fallen. It has the widest attainment gap for disadvantaged students of any subject. Private violin lessons are beyond the purse strings of most parents.

The statistics for drama are similarly bleak. A-level drama entries have almost halved in 10 years, with by far the biggest drop in state schools. Forty per cent of state schools no longer even offer music or drama GCSEs. Leading universities have been forced to close music departments and arts courses. The number of teachers training in creative subjects has also declined sharply over the past 15 years. It is no coincidence that the Ebacc, which prioritised core academic subjects at the expense of the arts, was introduced by the Conservatives in 2010. No wonder the worlds of music, theatre and television have become so privileged.

“How did British singers get so posh?” asked a recent piece in the New Statesman. Exceptions such as Adele, Raye and Olivia Dean are all alumni of the Brit school, the only state-funded vocational school for the performing arts in the UK. “Learning an instrument and getting up on stage … is now a luxury not every child can afford,” Ed Sheeran wrote in an open letter last year, asking the government to commit £250m of funding for music education. Its 600 signatories included Elton John, Harry Styles and Stormzy. Alison Balsom, the world-class classical trumpeter, has said that her career would not be possible for a state-school pupil now. Julie Walters and Michael Sheen have spoken out about the challenges facing children from working-class backgrounds hoping to become actors.

Sir Keir Starmer was hailed as the most musically accomplished prime minister since Ted Heath, playing four instruments as a child and becoming a junior exhibitioner at the Guildhall School of Music. “To everyone who makes music happen – this government is on your side,” the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, has promised. Scrapping the Ebacc last year was a welcome start. Other plans include the National Centre for Arts and Music Education, finally launching this autumn. Andy Burnham, an English graduate and music fan, has already put vocational education on the agenda. Now he must take up the baton for the arts. Mood music is not enough.

Every child should have the right to discover their gifts and fulfil their potential. Music and drama help develop discipline, confidence and social skills, and enhance wellbeing. The creative industries – a source of great economic value and soft power on the world stage – must be accessible to all. Reversing elitism in our recording studios, concert halls and theatres starts at school.

As Femi Koleoso of the jazz quintet Ezra Collective put it in their acceptance speech at last year’s Brit awards, giving a young person a trumpet or a saxophone might be the solution to many of society’s problems: “Because when you do that, you give them a dream, an aspiration and a goal.”

How much does Donald Trump care about winning the midterms? Apparently, not much at all

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 16:01:18 GMT

Such is the US president’s narcissism that he would see a Democratic victory as proof that he’s indispensable – meanwhile, his every decision spells calamity for voters

What is Donald Trump playing at? If it’s true that the best way of understanding the behaviour of an organisation is to assume it’s controlled by a secret cabal of its enemies, perhaps that same logic extends to the current conduct of the president of the United States. Maybe he secretly wants Republicans to lose the looming midterm elections that will decide the balance of power in the US for the next two years and for which the first postal ballots were sent out today.

That’s not as mad a theory as it sounds. Indeed, there are at least two reasons why Trump might either be unbothered by Republican defeat in November or even covertly desire it. We’ll come to those, but let’s start with a pattern of behaviour that is hard to explain as anything other than calculated self-sabotage.

At the centre of it is the single act that is already defining Trump’s second term: his reckless, failed war of choice against Iran. No matter how many times he declares mission accomplished or claims to have destroyed the Iranian military or to have reopened the strait of Hormuz, the facts keep telling a different story. In the past week, the two sides shifted from an economic standoff back to a shooting war, with the US firing on Iranian targets that included a wedding party, killing four, and Tehran striking out all over the neighbourhood, hitting Iraq, Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain.

The impact on US voters is severe, felt most directly through rising petrol prices and grocery bills. But look at the graph measuring the cost the US government must pay to borrow money: it’s been a steep upward climb since 28 February, the day the war began, hitting a fresh high on Tuesday. For consumers, that rise translates into an expected jump in interest rates. It means that many of those casting ballots are likely to be doing so just as they start paying more on their credit card bills and mortgages. Given that Trump was elected in November 2024 on a promise to bring down inflation, it’s hard to think of a worse environment for a governing party about to face the voters’ verdict. And that’s before you consider the disenchantment of the Maga faithful, who thought the whole point of Trump was an end to forever wars in the Middle East.

And yet, Iran may not even be the most electorally damaging of Trump’s foreign adventures. He is, and it would once have been absurd to write this sentence, leading his country into a state of war with … Canada. It’s easy to laugh at the petty gestures, such as Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move shamefully followed, and therefore endorsed, by Apple and Google in their map apps. But the economic confrontation is serious – and seriously damaging to Republicans’ electoral prospects.

For which US states are hit hardest by Canada’s “dollar-for-dollar” response to Trump’s tariffs? Why, it’s Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Texas, all of which just happen to have key senate contests this year. Republican candidates in those states now have to explain why a crucial and previously friendly export market – Canada takes nearly a third of Iowa’s exports, for example – has suddenly turned icy.

What’s odd is that Trump’s trade wars are also wars of choice, and they are hurting especially badly what should be a reliable Republican constituency: farmers. Take Iowa: Democrats have not won a senate seat in that farming state for nearly 20 years, yet now, thanks to Trump’s tariffs, they have a genuine shot.

Still, perhaps the most egregious illustration of Trump’s apparent determination to ruin Republican chances in the midterms is his support for datacentres. Few issues have seen their salience rise so quickly and in such a clear direction: almost overnight, they have become objects of fear and loathing across the country and across the political spectrum, with seven in 10 Americans saying they would not want one anywhere near where they live. Even among Republicans, there is deep concern over their environmental impact, energy consumption and water use. For others, datacentres have become a lightning rod for a broader anxiety over AI and what it may do to our jobs and our lives. Either way, they are kryptonite to voters.

So where does Trump stand? “The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want data centres is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” the president posted on Monday. In that remark, he not only put himself at odds with most US voters, he insulted them too.

It’s almost a talent, this ability of Trump’s to land on the wrong side of so-called 80/20 issues, siding with one-fifth of the electorate against the rest. Likewise, strong majorities oppose his vanity projects, whether demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom or putting his signature on the dollar bill, yet he persists not only in doing them but in talking about them constantly.

And all the while, he has hobbled his party by endorsing radioactively unpopular candidates. Few politicians in the US are more tainted than Ken Paxton, who as attorney general of Texas was impeached by his fellow Republicans on a long list of charges that included bribery and abuse of public trust. Yet who did Trump back as the Republicans’ senate choice in Texas? As a result, now even that red-state stronghold is shaky.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Put it all together, and these look like the actions of a man who has no fear of the blue wave that seems to be coming and who could not care less if it sweeps away the Republicans’ current majorities in Congress. That’s curious, given how useful it has been for Trump to have Capitol Hill serve as a rubber stamp that, combined with a largely pliant supreme court, has allowed him to rule with the scarcely fettered power of a would-be autocrat. What could explain the insouciance?

One answer is that Congress’s most potent weapon – the power of subpoena and investigation – holds no terror for Trump because he knows that the House and Senate have no means to enforce their will. They have no police or troops at their command. They can issue their writs and summonses, and he will simply ignore them – comforted by the near-blanket immunity he has already been granted by the supreme court. If Congress goes after his aides and advisers, he will instruct them to follow his lead, on the promise of a comprehensive presidential pardon protecting them from any and all legal consequences. The only real weapon Congress has – impeachment and removal from office – he knows they will never use. If senate Republicans could acquit him after the 6 January insurrection, as they did, he knows they will never vote to convict him of anything, no matter how great the crime.

But that only goes so far. It explains why Trump does not fear Republican defeat in November, but not why he would actively seek it. For that, one has to look into the abyss that passes for the president’s soul. The bestselling new book Regime Change, by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, spells it out: “If Republicans were wiped out in the 2026 midterm elections, or in 2028, he could simply boast that they couldn’t win without him” on the ballot paper. Such is Trump’s narcissism, he will take an epic Republican defeat in two months’ time not as a repudiation, but as a compliment. And, it seems, he is doing all he can to earn it.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

Premier League, Italian GP, WSL and US Open tennis – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 04 Sep 2026 14:43:02 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

After the off-field fun of the transfer window the Premier League returns – and it is also the opening weekend of the Women’s Super League. David Tindall and Tom Bassam bring you all the buildup and breaking news. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

It’s day four of a rain-affected round of County Championship fixtures as the season enters its final month. Tanya Aldred will bring you all the action from around the grounds.

Matthias Jaissle’s Newcastle have taken four points from what should have been a tricky opening pair of fixtures, against Newcastle and Tottenham, so will be confident of a victory that would take them temporarily top of the table. Bournemouth are yet to win and are cursing their inability to see out games, having conceded a 92nd-minute winner against Manchester City and a 91st-minute equaliser against Everton. David Tindall is on liveblog duty, Louise Taylor reports from St James’ Park.

There are five 3pm Premier League kick-offs for Rob Smyth to keep his eye on in the blog. Brentford face Sunderland, Brighton welcome Leeds to the south coast, Fulham and Crystal Palace meet in a London derby, Manchester City take on Coventry in a battle of the Sky Blues and winless Tottenham travel to the City Ground to face Nottingham Forest. And we’ll have live updates from the Championship, Bundesliga and beyond.

Philip Cornwall is at the wheel as F1 screeches on to the track at Monza, where Max Verstappen has won three of the last four editions of the Italian GP. His Red Bull doesn’t look quick enough to challenge this time around however, and Lando Norris in the McLaren has taken the last two poles of the 2026 season, breaking the Mercedes stranglehold at the front of the grid. Giles Richards reports from the track.

The third round continues at Flushing Meadows, where plenty of big names are in action in the women’s singles – Elena Rybakina, Naomi Osaka, Coco Gauff and Iga Swiatek all continue their campaigns on a bumper Saturday. Katy Murrells brings you all the action on the blog, while Tumaini Carayol reports from New York.

The Greatest Rivalry series has done a decent job of living up to its name thus far with the Springboks taking the opener and the All Blacks levelling things up at Ellis Park last weekend. Now for the third Test. Daniel Gallan helms the blog and Gerard Meagher reports.

One of these teams have won two out of two in the league, without having conceded a goal. The other have lost two out of two and are yet to score. And it’s not the way round you would have expected at the start of August. Billy Munday is on the blog to see if Villa can break their duck, while Ross Heppenstall reports from an MKM Stadium that is sure to be rocking for the undefeated hosts.

John Brewin is on hand to review Saturday’s action and preview Sunday’s games in the Premier League, WSL and beyond. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your notions and queries.

England have dominated the series thus far, cruising to back-to-back six-wicket victories to clinch the series with a game to spare. Can they make it a clean sweep on Sunday? Tanya Aldred and James Wallace are on over-by-over duty, while Raf Nicholson reports from Worcester.

Kimi Antonelli arrives at his home grand prix at the top of the drivers’ championship and hoping to end a long drought for the home fans at Monza – no Italian has won the Italian Grand Prix since Ludovico Scarfiotti in 1966. Michael Butler provides lap-by-lap coverage on the blog, while Giles Richards is at the track.

It’s a new season in the WSL and last season’s runners-up, Arsenal, will be hoping to get off to a winning start after improving their squad with some star signings. They travel to Broadfield Stadium to take on Brighton, who are still reeling after the departure of head coach Dario Vidosic this week. He has been hastily replaced by Arturo Ruiz, who led Real Sociedad into the qualifying stage of the Women’s Champions League. Rob Bleaney will bring you live updates.

Deadline day was a tough one for Everton, who failed to land the striker they so badly need. David Moyes’s side are unbeaten in their first two Premier League games, however, and might fancy their chances against a United side still finding their feet. Tim de Lisle helms our liveblog, while Andy Hunter and Will Unwin will be at Hill Dickinson Stadium.

The final major of the year reaches the fourth-round stage (or the last 16 if you prefer). Seven Americans made the last 32 in the men’s singles – can any of them push into the latter stages at a tournament that has not had a US winner in the men’s singles since Andy Roddick in 2003? Daniel Harris is in the liveblog hotseat and Tumaini Carayol reports from Flushing Meadows.

Perhaps the game of the weekend in the Premier League, with Xabi Alonso’s new-look Chelsea taking on Mikel Arteta’s not-much-changed Arsenal. Both sides have won two out of two in the league so far, so something will have to give. Rob Smyth is on liveblog duty, while David Hytner, Jacob Steinberg and Barney Ronay are all at the Emirates for reports, reaction and analysis.

Trump Officials Draft Plan to Pay At-Home Parents, Using Funds for Working Ones

The New York Times September 05, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The proposed benefit, a top policy priority for Vice President JD Vance, would apply only to married couples and tap a fund intended to provide federal child care subsidies to working parents.

By Coral Davenport

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration is moving to allow married couples with a stay-at-home spouse to collect child care subsidies, a policy championed by Vice President JD Vance, using funds from a federal program intended to assist working parents, according to people familiar with the discussions.

The change would create the only federal subsidy to pay parents to stay home and raise their children, one of the most significant efforts to date by the Trump administration to harness federal funds to promote a traditional view of families.

To do so, officials are seeking to use a Health and Human Services Department fund that was created in the 1990s to help low-income and working-class parents afford child care so they could work or go to school.

Under the draft new rule, parents who stay home with their children could benefit from the program, which typically provides about $9,000 per child each year, potentially reshaping which families get federal child care money.

The move could end up redirecting money away from working parents and their child care providers, causing some to raise their rates or even close, critics said, potentially worsening what many experts say is a child care crisis in the country.

About 80 percent of the 870,000 families who currently get the child care subsidies have single working parents, most of them mothers, according to Health Department data.

The policy change would effectively create a government incentive for parents to stay home with their children, an idea embraced as part of a broader conservative effort to advance policies that promote more mothers staying at home.

The new rule being drafted would allow married couples with one stay-at-home parent in certain income brackets to collect a subsidy, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the plan before it is finalized. The change could be made without approval from Congress.

More than 80 percent of stay-at-home parents are mothers, according to the Pew Research Center.

The plan is being pushed by the White House and is seen as a top priority of Mr. Vance, according to several people familiar with the discussions. The draft rule also incorporates policies in legislation written by Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he was a senator from Florida.

Representatives for the White House, Mr. Vance and the Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Vance, whose wife Usha, a former corporate lawyer, gave birth to their fourth child in July, has long advocated for more mothers to stay at home with young children and called for efforts to open up child care subsidy programs to those providing “kinship care.”

In 2021, Mr. Vance co-wrote an opinion essay in The Wall Street Journal contending that day care can harm children and declaring, “Young children are clearly happier and healthier when they spend the day at home with a parent.”

He also wrote then on Twitter that “normal Americans” want a “family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap day care so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force.”

Some family policy experts said the changes to the program would hurt parents who have to work and have difficulty affording child care.

“I am a big proponent of more support for stay-at-home parents. But this is not how I would choose to do it,” said Joshua McCabe, director of social policy at the Niskanen Center, a centrist think tank.

“Expanding the eligibility without increasing funding would mean more parents competing for the same dollars, and leaving more parents — particularly single working parents — worse off,” he said.

The $12 billion Child Care and Development Fund, which is run by the Health Department’s Administration for Children and Families, was created during the Clinton administration to support the employment of low to moderate-income parents. It subsidizes the care of children up to age 13 and currently offsets the costs for caring for about 1.3 million children.

Under the current rules, most of the money is distributed to states, which in turn distribute it to parents, usually in the form of vouchers or direct deposits to child care providers.

To qualify, parents must prove that their income is lower than 85 percent of their state’s median income and that they are working, in school or receiving job training. Some states set a lower threshold of 60 percent of the state’s median income.

Under the proposed rule changes, the same pot of money would also be used to pay married parents who meet the income requirements when one parent works and the other cares for the child. The money would be intended to help offset the lost income of the stay-at-home parent.

The proposal “creates the option for a new category of care, parent-based child care, that will allow one married parent to receive C. C. D. F. assistance to care for their own child, while a spouse works at least 35 hours per week,” according to a draft document viewed by The Times.

Unmarried couples in which one parent stays at home would not qualify under the draft. Single parents who do not work are currently not eligible for the subsidy, nor would they be under the new proposal for married couples.

The rule, which could still be changed before publication, would need to be approved by the White House and then would be posted online for public comment. If it is finalized, it could go into effect as soon as next year.

Some department lawyers working on the plan have questioned the legality of requiring recipients to be married, according to the people familiar with the matter. Some have also raised concerns about whether the change could increase the risk of fraud, since the money would be going to individuals rather than businesses. The administration has sought to crack down on fraud in social services programs, particularly child care.

The idea of paying parents to stay home was outlined in Project 2025, the conservative blueprint published by the Heritage Foundation ahead of Mr. Trump’s return to office, much of which overlaps with the administration’s policy agenda.

“Instead of providing universal day care, funding should go to parents either to offset the cost of staying home with a child or to pay for familial, in-home child care,” it says, although it does not specify how or which fund to use.

“You don’t need statutes to do it, and with existing programs we can end discrimination against stay-at-home parents,” said Roger Severino, a vice president at the Heritage Foundation who wrote the Project 2025 section on child care policy.

“It would be a welcome change to see equal treatment between commercial day care and the contribution stay-at-home parents provide in caring for and raising the next generation,” he said in an interview. “It doesn’t get more pro-family than that.”

Mr. Severino said he believed that the provision privileging married parents would most likely withstand a legal challenge. He said that under the Supreme Court decision Obergefell v. Hodges, married same-sex parents would most likely also qualify for the subsidies.

In a letter to governors on Mother’s Day, Alex Adams, the head of the Administration for Children and Families, previewed that policy changes were coming and urged states to “use every available” flexibility to distribute federal money in ways that “support married two-parent families,” and particularly “families who choose to have a parent remain at home with young children.”

Child care policy experts said they anticipate that in some states, the rule change could lead to much of the money going to stay-at-home parents. States have some flexibility in determining how their subsidies from the Child Care and Development Fund are allocated, and lawmakers in some red states, including Idaho, Wyoming and Utah, have pushed for new policies for the states to support stay-at-home parents.

That outcome could in turn shutter some of the roughly 225,000 child care providers that rely on the subsidies for tuition payments.

Krystal Gastineau, the owner of Cribs 2 Crayons, a child-care center in Aurora, Colo., said that about half the children she cares for receive the subsidies, which are paid directly to Ms. Gastineau’s business via direct deposit. “If they could, I think parents would choose to take the money and stay home,” she said. “That would take away a major source of income.”

“I think that’s a misuse of the system,” she said.

Lezlie Cranston, in Auburn, Wash., uses the subsidy program to pay for care for her 4-year-old son, Ricky, and her 2-year-old daughter, Samantha, while she pursues a certification at Skagit Valley College. The subsidies have “helped tremendously with allowing me to do my coursework,” said Ms. Cranston, a single parent.

“But changing it to let the money go to stay-at-home parents is going to create conflict between parents,” she said. “That’s a bad situation. We’re already trying to figure out how more working parents can get the subsidies. This could lead to single parents not being able to afford child care again.”

Coral Davenport covers energy and environment policy, with a focus on climate change, for The Times.
