Ugly AI Food Photos Are Only the Beginning

Wired September 03, 2026

I can’t stop staring at the AI-slop images of Mexican food I see during my morning walk to work. On the menu posted outside, the taco truck displays lunch options that appear uncanny and unappetizing, as if an alien who’s never eaten human food before drew a taco from memory. This food truck is not alone in putting AI-generated images on its menu. It’s everywhere.

AI menu slop is now going viral for being disgusting, and these posters seem to be an evolution of the “ChatGPT flyer pandemic.” Whether it’s a maggot-infested burrito or a plasticky pasta, consumers are expressing online how gross these fabricated images look. The aesthetic is distinctively off-putting, sometimes with random holes throughout a dish or otherworldly cuts of meat served as an entree.

The images are immediately noticeable but only scratch the surface of how generative AI tools have already overhauled restaurant menus. Sellers aren’t just generating AI images of burgers, they’re also relying on AI to decide what goes in between those two buns.

The birth of the online menu set us on the path toward these monstrosities. More consumers started deciding what to eat based on online menus and by ordering delivery from their phones to their doorstep. Faced with growing pressure, restaurant owners digitized their menus and created additional visuals.

Stores wanted to capitalize on delivery sales and leaned into generative AI images, vying for a visibility boost on third-party apps like DoorDash without paying for a photoshoot. While the most powerful models currently on the market can output photorealistic images of food, many of these images appear to be generated by tools with worse capabilities, like the default setting of a free chatbot.

“I went to order pizza one night on Uber Eats,” says Brendan Sweeney, CEO and cofounder of Popmenu, a digital marketing software company for restaurants. “There were five different pizza places that were using the same AI-generated image.” He says if the food image appears “completely inauthentic” and “obviously AI,” then the restaurant is making a worse decision than foregoing photography altogether.

What was originally generated to satisfy digital demand is now creeping its way into the physical world. AI menu slop expanded from its online origins into posters in coffee shops and signs displayed as deli menus. Restaurant owners sometimes seem oblivious to how off-putting low-quality image generations look.

Noticeably AI-generated images stand out on modern menus for all the wrong reasons. But AI tools are influencing what appears on your local coffee shop’s menu, beyond just images.

Tastewise, one of the largest data insights companies in the food and beverage industry, partners with companies like Nestlé, PepsiCo, and Kraft Heinz. It’s currently all-in on “agentic” automations for every step of the food creation process.

Tastewise’s library of automations is meant to help companies decide what foods to sell and how to sell them. There’s an agent to help you track how product launches are going, an agent to test new concepts (banana creatine smoothies, anyone?), and an agent to find opportunity gaps in current menus.

“I think the bigger question for them is how do they guide and train the AI on what should be in that burger and what should be on the menu,” says Michael Bortinger, Tastewise’s director of marketing and partnerships. “We have billions of data points understanding what consumers are doing with food, what’s actually happening on menus and in the retail landscape.”

The result is TasteGPT, a chatbot-style tool powered by food-specific insights. Companies can pay for access to the bot, though the website offers you a few free queries, so I tried it out.

Two of the suggested prompts were about what competitors are doing with protein-enhanced foods and the current trending flavors in plant-based snacks. When I picked the latter, TasteGPT flagged dates as a “standout rising star” and “cake-flavored plant-based snacks” as another relevant—though not as hot—trend. Looking at what’s already available, I’m not sure I’d ever buy some cake-drizzled mini-rice cakes.

Bortinger rattles off cold foam, hot honey, and strawberry matcha as flavors and menu additions that are high on the consumer interest list. “Ube is a trending flavor, but that also may be starting to be past its peak,” he says. When I asked about pickles, as a lover of the limited-time dill-flavored Grinch-themed fries from McDonald’s, he assured me that companies are still finding “new formats” for delivering the innovative, pickle-y goodness. The dill-pickle pizza slices I keep seeing on Instagram do look quite delicious.

The tension between food marketing and reality existed before the generative AI boom. Food stylists for commercials have long used creative methods to present objects of consumption, like swapping ice cream for similarly textured mashed potatoes or painting the perfect grill marks onto a burger patty. While those changes often make the food seem more tantalizing than reality, most of the cheap menu slop I see day-to-day still looks puke-inducing.

Despite their many mistakes in deciding how to present food images, restaurant owners will keep turning to AI tools to automate aspects of their businesses and optimize their online offerings. Around 85 percent of restaurateurs currently "feel comfortable" using AI tools and plan to use them even more extensively in the future, according to a recent poll from Toast.

Rather than using fully AI-generated images, Sweeney wants restaurants to use software—like Popmenu—to enhance images of real food captured by the smartphones in their pocket. “AI can now very easily patch those up, plate them all the same, and make the lighting consistent,” he says. “I think that’s where the value is.” He sees these enhancements as a professional way to present the dish, based on what they are actually selling.

Not all food sellers want to put AI on their menu, though, and for good reason. These synthetic images of food are becoming a cultural touchstone in the broader, highly effective AI backlash. Popular local restaurants are going viral for their refusal to participate, posting handwritten notes about not using generative AI posters for promotion.

We are living under the uncanny reign of the AI slop menu. In a few years, even the cheapest AI image of food may look more tempting than these current iterations. That said, I don’t mind a slightly ugly, albeit real, photo of dishes on the menu when I dine out or order delivery. If anything, I prefer their more authentic rough edges.

When I walk home from work today, I think I’ll finally give that food truck a chance, keeping my fingers crossed that the tacos on my plate look better than the AI ones on the poster.

The Blood of Dawnwalker Is a Bloody Balm for My Completionism

Wired September 03, 2026

I drink the blood of my fourth rat tonight. It’s only got so much life to give, so as soon as I drain it, I know I'll need to feed again. My hunger is not fulfilled. My health bar is only half full. I need more blood. Now.

I toss the rat away as my glowing eyes flicker to another, just across the street. I bare my sharp, bloody teeth, turn into a cloud of shadow and bats, and teleport to my unsuspecting prey. I bite down hard. It’s too late to realize my target has changed. As I swarmed, a human city guard happened to walk right in front of me. My teeth sink into his throat instead. I could let go, but I do not. I drink, drink, drink. Then he falls to the ground. Dead. I wipe my mouth as the last rat scurries away into the dark.

“Well, I guess I’m going to Hell anyway,” my character quips.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is a vampire simulator and role-playing video game that launches today. It’s a dark adventure where you play as the titular Dawnwalker—human by day, monstrous vampire at night.

You can’t talk about The Blood of Dawnwalker without talking about The Witcher 3. They’re both third-person monster-slasher video games starring handsome protagonists with cool scars on their faces, both made by some of the same people.

Konrad Tomaszkiewicz, a former director at the Polish game studio and Witcher developer CD Projekt Red, was one of three directors of the very popular The Witcher 3. His new studio, Rebel Wolves, even feels like a cheeky nod to Geralt, the main character of The Witcher series who is often called the White Wolf. The gameplay and graphics feel very similar. Combat involves swinging your sword and blasting magic abilities, while cutscenes and dialog have familiar dialog trees and quick-time events. You have a special sense that makes important items glow so you can find footprints and track down monsters.

The music also sounds almost identical to The Witcher 3 soundtrack—think somber swelling violin strings plucking away while you wander a gloomy open world. I was almost ready to allege copyright infringement before realizing that Dawnwalker features the work of fellow Witcher composer Mikolai Stroinski.

Ah, so, “We have The Witcher at home,” is that it? Well, not exactly. The sameness might feel derivative at first, but give it a minute. Once you get through the prologue, the world opens up in a way that invites exploration of its very pretty, blood-soaked world. There’s no way to beat The Witcher 3 in depth, breadth, or sheer volume, but The Blood of Dawnwalker doesn’t try to replicate or surpass that scale. Instead, it gives you a simple goal and a limited time to pull it off. That sounds restrictive at first, but it plays out in a way that's more freeing than you’d expect.

Dawnwalker takes place in a fictional plague-era medieval world. You play as Coen (I call him Young Geralt), a poor peasant who lives with his family in a town controlled by evil vampires. After some inciting events, the Draculean boss vampire kidnaps Coen’s family and turns him into the Dawnwalker—a vampire hybrid that manifests as a human in the daytime and a bloodthirsty vampire at night. You’ve got 30 in-game days to save Coen’s family. You’re already running out of time.

Gameplay is split into day and night cycles, each with eight time segments. Completing a quest or doing anything of consequence will pass one or a few time segments. Otherwise, time does not pass idly. If you’re running around and exploring, you have all the time to fart around in the world that you need. The game warns you when something you're about to do will pass the time, so you can choose to keep going or leave and find something else to do.

I worried this system would feel constricting, like being forced on a set path in an open-world game. Turns out, it was exactly what I needed to stay motivated and keep exploring.

My problem with The Witcher 3 and open-world games like it is that there is so much of it. You’re tasked with some time-sensitive mission—rescue your daughter before the world ends, etc.—but then you while away hours and hours on side quests. Games like this can punish you if you rush the main storyline, cutting off quests, choices, and even characters that those smaller efforts would have unlocked. When I play, I feel obligated to do all the small stuff first, then build to the main quests. When a narrative and world gets that dense, it can start to feel like a chore.

Dawnwalker gives you many activities across the world. Some are clearly story quests; many are treasure hunts or things that feel much smaller-scale. Knowing I can’t do everything lets me prioritize what needs doing. A ticking clock always counting down on the screen usually would make me anxious in games, since failing to do the right things at the right time means you lose. Weirdly, Dawnwalker’s countdown feels less punishing and more like motivation to do the very best you can with the limited resources you have. If you know you can’t see everything in a single playthrough, it’s easier to let go of the things you miss.

It’s by no means a perfect game. The Blood of Dawnwalker is a clunky name. It really should be Blood of the Dawnwalker or just Blood of Dawnwalker. (Dawnwalker is your character’s title after all, not his name.) There is also undeniable jank throughout, like when you sheathe your sword, it floats directly behind the center of Coen’s butt. When you run with your heightened vampiric sense, the sword bounces around and spanks Coen’s behind as he runs. It is very funny, and I hope the devs don’t change it.

It is particularly unfortunate for Dawnwalker that the game is launching in the shadow of news that The Witcher 3 is getting a free remastered update later this month and a whole new expansion pack in 2027, 11 years after its original release.

Despite all the blood, gore, and sorrow, Dawnwalker has charm and a lightness to it. Combat is bloody, wet, and satisfying. At night, Coen’s vampiric abilities are a hoot, letting you teleport around across the rooftops, drink the blood of any crawly creature you like, and sprint across the map as a wolf. Most of the vampires, aside from smokeshow Coen, are the truly monstrous kinds, all claws and teeth and gory bloodsucking. But the world slowly reveals some real beauty. The other characters develop and become much more interesting than they first appeared. The voice acting that carries some pretty wrenching story beats and character moments is stellar.

Above all, it does something remarkable: It takes an established game formula and really infuses it with its own personality and quirks. It takes a bite out of the Witcher formula and makes it its own. And has a bloody good time doing it.

The Best Air Quality Monitors for a Healthier Home

Wired September 03, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Having An air quality monitor for your home is more important than you may think. As climate change speeds up and wildfires increasingly engulf large swaths of land, leaving behind smoke that makes air potentially hazardous to breathe, it's more important than ever to ensure you're breathing clean air. An at-home air quality monitor is a simple way to ensure that, whether it be car exhaust, wildfire smoke, pollutants from seasonal changes, or simply fumes from your gas stove, the air around you is safe to breathe.

These air quality monitors test the air quality both indoors and outdoors, and on top of measuring PM2.5 (particulate matter) in the air and AQI (air quality index), they can also give insights into the air you're breathing, including measuring temperature, humidity, CO2, VOCs, and more.

Our top pick, IQAir's Air Visual Pro ($330), measures for several factors and has an easy-to-read display, while our more basic budget pick, Temptop S1 PM2.5 Air Quality Monitor & Indoor Thermometer ($28), has been solid throughout prolonged testing.

For more ways to keep your air quality in check for a healthier environment, take a look at our guides to the Best Outdoor Air Quality Monitors, Best Air Purifiers, and Best Multiuse Air Purifiers. Plus, check out how we test them and how to pick the right air purifier for your home.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

IQAir

Amazon

IQAir

Best Buy

The AirVisual air quality monitor has an easy-read 5-inch LCD display screen and a graphic of a boy’s face along with the AQI color scale that lets me know my indoor air quality from across the room. As the air quality gets poorer, the little boy will stop smiling with a green background and become solemn with a yellow background; finally, if the air is truly dangerous, he’ll put on a gas mask and the color turns dark purple. I like that I don’t have to log on to the internet or open an app to know if I have clean air. Plus, the AirVisual has the added feature of giving both indoor and outdoor air quality data. This saves me the extra step of checking the outdoor air quality on my phone. And it cycles through various displays—it has the time, then it will show both indoor and outdoor readings, along with congratulating me for achieving excellent indoor air quality or it will recommend that I open a window. The AirVisual air quality monitor measures PM2.5 and CO2 and displays the temperature and humidity. It has an easy-to-read dashboard on the app and keeps data for a year, but its biggest strength is its display, especially when I burn a pizza and the boy gets sad and dons a gas mask. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

PurpleAir

Purpleair

The Zen air quality monitor uses the EPA AQI color scale: green for good air, yellow for moderate, orange for unhealthy for sensitive groups, red for unhealthy, purple for very unhealthy, and deep violet/maroon for hazardous. The colored glow’s intensity can be controlled by the number of taps of your finger and can be mounted onto a pole or wall or can be placed on its circular stand. Each Zen air quality monitor can be linked to the crowdsourced PurpleAir’s Real-Time Air Quality Map. Linking the Zen is optional, but to see the actual Air Quality Index number that the Zen is reading, I had to link my specific monitor with its unique ID code to the PurpleAir website. There’s an option to have the monitor be public or private; by clicking public, you get to contribute as a citizen scientist to the Real-Time Air Quality Map. I was surprised to see just how many PurpleAir monitors there are in New York City, not to mention Brooklyn. It gave an accurate close-up of my block and my neighborhood. In this current climate of extreme weather, the PurpleAir Real Time Map is especially useful. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

Temtop

Amazon

I've been testing air purifiers, measuring each unit’s efficacy by using a sealed tent and smoke pellets to see how quickly each air purifier clears the pellet smoke and returns the air to healthy quality when on auto mode. I time both visually when the air turns clear again and also measure with this little guy above for each test—comparing my results to the built-in AQI monitor numbers on the machines or their connected app to ensure that the measured levels (especially for PM2.5 and air quality) are correct. I'll be honest, this cheap monitor doesn't do everything that the more expensive models do, but it has worked for the simple tests I run.

This compact device measures and displays PM2.5, AQI, temperature, and humidity levels. It only measures PM2.5 particles and uses US EPA Standards to calculate the AQI. It doesn't measure for any other pollutants, so if you want a more comprehensive assessment with pollutants like CO2 or VOCs, you'd need another model. It has eco mode, which takes samples of the air every 30 minutes and lasts up to 60 days on a single charge; A mode, which samples air every three minutes and lasts about 20 days; and real-time mode, which samples air every 1.5 seconds for the most up-to-date and accurate current air quality readings—though it needs to be plugged (with a USB charger) in to work in this mode. This cheap device isn't perfect—it would get stuck in certain readings and not update, and I'd be forced to restart or plug in for accurate measurement. However, it's suitable for measuring indoor and outdoor environments and can operate within a range of -14 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit. If you just want a simple air quality monitor to gauge both indoor and outdoor pollutants, this model will do.

Airthings

Amazon

Airthings

Airthings' solid, unassuming minimalist design has an easy-to-read display screen, and it’s the first indoor air quality monitor I’ve tested that has a dedicated radon sensor. It also measures PM2.5, CO2, VOCs, temperature, humidity, and air pressure. And while the Airthings View Plus has an easy-to-use app, the monitor will not work without internet/Wi-Fi. It also needs time to calibrate. I saw radon, PM2.5, and humidity almost immediately, but the app told me I needed to wait days before the monitor calibrated the CO2 and VOC sensors. You'll also need to wave your hand in front of the device for an air quality check. The movement from my hand triggers the sensor to show any value above the recommended levels, along with the indicator light, which shows green for good, yellow for fair, and red for poor. The more I test air quality monitors, the more I appreciate those with color-coded indicator lights that I can see from across the room. I recommend Airthings because of its ability to measure everything from radon to PM2.5, and it also has backup batteries in case of a power outage. —Lisa Wood Shapiro

How I Tested

In the past, I've relied on my phone's weather app to measure the air quality around me, and the government’s free AirNow website, where you can plug in your zip code and see its easy-to-read air quality meter. Now, as I test air purifiers, I always make sure to corroborate the purifiers' built-in PM2.5 or AQI measurements with an independent outside source—a separate air quality monitor—to test both the accuracy of the machine and the purifier's efficacy in filtering pollutants and getting the air quality back to a healthy level.

These air quality monitors were tested in various locations around my house, when cooking on my unventilated gas stove, under my living room window that draws in a lot of building and exhaust fumes, and outside my cat's litter box. Plus, I did additional testing outdoors, where I measured the monitors’ readings against local weather apps. And when field testing air purifiers with a sealed tent and smoke pellets as mentioned above, I always use an air quality monitor to check pollutant levels and the purifiers' efficacy when timed to get back to healthy levels.

Why Do I Need an Air Quality Monitor?

Like I mentioned above, I think it's especially important to have an air quality monitor to test whether your air both inside and outside the home is healthy if you don't have an air purifier. But it's also important to have one to measure the efficacy of the air purifier(s) in your home to ensure they are doing their job as efficiently as claimed. Especially since after prolonged use (and time), the built-in sensors can clog and give inaccurate readings.

When placing or installing an air quality monitor, try to measure at the breathing zone height, around 3 to 6 feet off the floor. An air quality monitor is especially helpful against some of the more harmful effects of things like wildfire smog, which can't always be smelled or seen. But an air quality monitor can sense that there is too much bad air, and then you can adjust the air purifier fan(s) accordingly.

It can also help to instill healthy habits, as WIRED Reviews contributor Lisa Wood Shapiro notes, using air quality monitors taught her to turn on the kitchen exhaust fan and crank up an air purifier before she turns on her gas stove. In the past, she didn’t think much of a little smoke from cooking. Now she takes proactive steps to avoid inhaling harmful pollutants.

Once you start noticing bad air and take steps to correct it, you'll notice fewer allergy symptoms and, often, fewer upper respiratory sicknesses and improved sleep. Even innocuous household things like lit candles, cooking on a stovetop without an exhaust fan (guilty), or aerosol air fresheners can negatively impact indoor air in real time. Get yourself an air quality monitor and see for yourself.

What to Consider Before Buying

Even though many current air purifier models have built-in air quality sensors, having a designated air quality monitor is a great way to independently corroborate or monitor air quality and pollutants. Plus, these handheld monitors are also portable and able to more accurately test air quality outdoors.

Before you purchase your own indoor air quality monitor, here are some things to know: Sensors on the WIRED-tested AirVisual Pro and PurpleAir all performed well in an independent study. Low-cost consumer air quality monitors are much cheaper (in the $200 or less range) than what's used by the professionals, but are also less accurate and not as easily calibrated. When testing multiple air quality monitors, they will not usually give the exact same AQI, but they are usually very close.

Consumer air quality monitors use sensors to detect tiny invisible particles in the air and other contaminants, with some sensors using light scattering to detect fine particulate matter known as PM10, like the dust visible in light, and invisible health hazards like PM2.5, which can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

DOGE Affiliate Asked for College Credits for Participating in Takeover

Wired September 03, 2026

Christopher Sweet, an affiliate of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency, requested college credit for his time in government, according to new documents obtained by a Freedom of Information Act request filed by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit legal organization.

Sweet was stationed at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, and in emails between Sweet and Scott Langmack, another DOGE affiliate at HUD, it appears that Sweet was looking to frame his work at HUD as an independent study worth three college credits. Sweet joined HUD in the spring of 2025 as an undergraduate college student at the University of Chicago to work on building an AI tool that would crawl through the agency’s rules and regulations and flag them for rescission—the cancellation of contracts. The tool, called SweetRex, was intended to be rolled out across the federal government.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

In an August 26, 2025 email titled “Which of these should go to U Chicago,” Langmack wrote to Sweet saying, “I need to send them something that has specific framework of the different courses/credits we want them to give you.”

Documents attached to the email show that Sweet’s work was divided into four potential courses, Advanced AI Prompt Engineering for Legal Reasoning, Applied Data Science for Federal Regulatory Analysis, Computer Programming for Scalable Al-Legal Systems, and Legislative & Regulatory Authority in AI-Driven Reform. It appears these were meant to lead to a final proposed thesis focused on “the design, implementation, and impact of integrated AI, data science, software engineering, and legal authority analysis to rationalize outdated federal regulations.” The documents make clear that Sweet’s work was not an internship but “graduate-level, multi-disciplinary research producing real-world outputs that are already influencing federal regulatory reform."

It appears that the final outline that was created to send to the University of Chicago for approval was created by AI. In an August 27, 2025 email, Langmack tells Sweet, “I did the outline on ChatGPT.”

HUD and the University of Chicago did not reply to requests for comment. WIRED confirmed that Sweet did, in fact, graduate from the University of Chicago this June with a degree in economics, though it is unclear if credits from his time with DOGE contributed to the school’s requirements.

Langmack came to HUD from the property technology company Kukun—whose website describes it as being on “a long-term mission to aggregate the hardest-to-find data”—with zero experience in the federal government. He is now executive director of deregulation AI at the Office of Management and Budget, according to his LinkedIn. Langmack did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“These documents raise serious concerns about how one of DOGE’s unqualified employees has been entrusted to handle legal work, rewriting rules and regulations that affect millions of Americans, while attempting to count this work toward an undergraduate degree,” says Daniel McGrath, special counsel for oversight at Democracy Forward, describing the case as part of the “Trump-Vance administration’s relentless pursuit to cripple the important work of the federal government.”

Is It Even Possible to Understand Quantum Mechanics?

Wired September 03, 2026

A big problem with physics is that it’s invented by humans. We see stuff around us and use our observations to build a mental model of the world. Children do this, and of course physicists keep right on doing it. In many cases, this is awesome. It's how we got Newton's laws of motion. But it goes sideways when we try to picture the behavior of tiny, invisible things like subatomic particles.

This is the “quantum realm,” as they call it in Ant-Man. It's not really a place you can visit in a special suit; you're already in it, and it's in you. But quantum phenomena are so alien that this deep layer of reality may as well be an alternate universe. The physicist Richard Feynman once famously said, “Nobody really understands quantum mechanics.”

Feynman didn't mean we can't explain quantum behavior. Today we have models that predict quantum outcomes with incredible accuracy. What he meant is that it's impossible to ever wrap our macro-scale arms around it. The stuff I'm about to tell you is true, and it makes no sense whatsoever. You just have to accept the absurdity and proceed from there.

To see this in action, let's revisit one of the most famous experiments in science: the double-slit experiment. Thomas Young first used this setup in 1801 to show that light travels in waves. Then, in 1961, Claus Jönsson built a minuscule version to show that subatomic particles with mass also behave like waves.

Think about that. In our world of big things, if you toss a marble into a pond, it causes ripples, yeah? Well, in the quantum realm, it's like physical matter is both a marble and a ripple. And I'm afraid it only gets more preposterous from there.

Let's start in the world of big things. Imagine a wall with two narrow, vertical windows, and we have a machine that shoots tennis balls. Some hit the wall, some pass through on the left, some pass through on the right. In back there's a second wall covered with Velcro, so when a ball hits this back wall, it sticks. What does that look like?

As you’d expect, the balls end up in two clumps, corresponding to the two inlets. But what if we run the same experiment with teeny-tiny slits and a machine that shoots electrons? Well, we tend to picture electrons as little balls orbiting an atomic nucleus, so by analogy you might expect a similar result on the screen. Nope. Instead of two clumps of electron hits, we get multiple bands:

This is very similar to what you see when light passes through two slits, as Thomas Young discovered. Since light is a wave, it does two things: First, there is diffraction. As the light passes through each opening, it spreads out like an ocean wave passing through a gap in a sea wall. Second, the waves from the two slits overlap and create an interference pattern.

Where the waves are in phase, you get a bright spot. Where they're out of phase, you get a dark spot. Here's what that looks like in real life with a red laser as the light source:

So, if electrons produce an effect similar to that of light, can we model these tiny particles of matter as waves? Yes, and this is the idea behind Schrödinger's equation, which is the foundation of quantum mechanics. It tells us how a quantum system changes across time and space.

That's useful, but it's not entirely satisfying. We still want to know what's happening here. Are electrons truly like waves that pass through both slits and interfere, or does any given electron pass through one slit like a tennis ball? The answer is … yes.

We can turn our electron gun down so that it shoots just one electron at a time. And guess what? Even when the electrons go through one at a time, so that they can’t interfere with one another, the same interference pattern of multiple bands emerges over time. They are somehow interfering with themselves.

So physicists don't say the electron goes through one or the other slit. Instead, we say the particle is in a superposition state—it’s a combination of going through the left slit and going through the right slit. And that is not the same as going through both slits.

Wait! Couldn't we actually determine which slit an electron went through? Absolutely. We can place a tiny light source near each slit, and if it reflects off the electron, we'll know which one it went through.

But guess what? If you use a detector like this, you no longer get the interference pattern. You get a result that looks like it's an electron going through one slit (the tennis ball pattern). The double-slit pattern occurs only if you don't measure it! We say that measurement “collapses the wave function” of a system, so that the electron is no longer in superposition.

That's just silly, right? It's crazy that the act of measurement changes the outcome. Does this mean that physics experiments can change reality? Maybe.

I mentioned Erwin Schrödinger above. He was one of the pioneers of quantum theory, but he couldn't bring himself to accept this idea of superposition. Using his macro-world common sense, he insisted there must be a flaw in the model, and that a complete theory of quantum mechanics would eventually be deterministic like classical physics.

When scientists don't like something, they make up absurd scenarios to invite mockery of its proponents. So Schrödinger created a famous thought experiment you may have heard of. It's called Schrödinger's Cat, and it goes like this:

There is a cat in a box. This box also contains a radioactive atom, a detector, and a vial of poison. If the atom decays and produces radiation, the detector will open the vial and the cat will die. But if the box is closed, the atom is in a superposition state, being both decayed and not decayed—meaning the cat is both dead and alive. Only when you open the box and observe the cat will its wave function collapse into either dead or alive.

Nice try, but Schrödinger's scenario was easily dismissed. First, no one was saying superposition translated to big objects like cats. Second, there was already a measurement before the box was opened: The device that releases the poison was monitoring the state of the atom.

In fact, Schrödinger was wrong—as was Einstein, who agreed with him. Since then, numerous experiments have proved that superposition is real and that uncertainty is fundamental to the universe. And a good thing it is, too, even if it makes no sense. Superposition is what gives quantum computers their immense parallel processing power.

It's important to understand that superposition of states isn't the same as saying we don't know. If you flip a coin and cover it up when it lands, the coin is already either heads or tails—you just don't yet know which. In the double-slit experiment, we know: It goes through only one slit and it goes through both slits.

Quantum systems have other properties that will scramble your brain if you try to grok them, like entanglement, where measuring the state of one particle determines the state of another, no matter how far away it is. This happens instantly, with no time for a signal to travel between them.

But by now these are well-established phenomena, so is it fair to call them bizarre? Are we only exposing the limitations of our human minds? Clearly, the level of reality we inhabit is only part of the story, so we should be skeptical of our intuition. If nothing else, quantum mechanics teaches humility. We keep doing science—and the farther we go, it seems, the greater the mystery.

This Is Flock’s AI Search Tool for Cops

Wired September 03, 2026

Flock Safety’s latest search tools give police several ways to find people on camera, not just the license plates on their cars. The capabilities sit inside a suite of software now at the center of dozens of police stalking cases. WIRED collected and analyzed that software and created a mock-up of what officers see when interacting with the system.

Among the tools is an AI-powered watch list. An officer can cordon off an area of a city and make the cameras inside it run a continuous, automated search for anyone fitting a written description.

Over the past year, Flock has faced backlash against its technology. Police departments across the country have canceled contracts, and city councils that once approved Flock have quietly voted the cameras back out. Two members of Congress wrote to Flock CEO Garrett Langley after a Texas deputy searched more than 83,000 cameras for a woman who had an abortion. And Illinois found the company had let federal immigration agents access state camera data in violation of state law.

Flock answered in August with a package of changes that shortens the default period over which data are retained, requires case codes for every search, and adds automated auditing to catch officers misusing the tool—all of which Flock says will be mandatory by the end of the year. WIRED examined the code those promises run on, but much of what governs a search happens on Flock’s servers. Crucially, the analysis found that Flock’s guardrails may discourage some abusive uses of its tools, and will record them, but will not stop them.

Experts who study automated screening and police technology say Flock has given its AI a job no technology does reliably. Flock’s system decides, out of sight of the department using it, which descriptions of a person an officer may search for—and no screen operating at that scale is accurate, the experts say. Further, nobody outside the company can measure how often it is wrong, or in which direction. This puts users in a bind: The company itself warns officers that results may be inaccurate or incomplete and should not be relied on alone but puts the “risk of any inaccuracies” on the officer running the search.

Some of those decisions experts find harder to defend than others. Flock’s system scores an officer’s written description against several categories of sensitive content, including race and religion, and “political, social, and cultural expression” is the only one that will not stop a search.

Tom Bowman, policy counsel with the Center for Democracy and Technology's security surveillance project, says the one sensitive category Flock treats with a speed bump instead of a stop is the one courts have guarded most closely. Political and cultural expression is “one of the most protective areas” under the First Amendment, he says, and it “seems like that actually has the least concern from a policing perspective.”

WIRED sent Flock a detailed description of each of its findings along with 16 questions. The company responded with a written statement saying its search tools are built to help police find relevant information “while maintaining clear safeguards around how the technology can be used.” Queries are evaluated against its content policies, it says. The statement does not describe how its AI model was built, what instructions it works from, or what separates one verdict from another.

Data flows in both directions. When the software flags a search, it sends Flock the language the officer used, the category and confidence score the model assigned it, and whatever the officer did next, whether continuing, dismissing, or disputing the warning. Flock’s statement does not address how long those records are kept, who inside the company can see them, and whether they are used to evaluate or improve the moderation system.

Flock’s interface holds several tools, and each one works differently. A search that uses text to find images, for example, produces a statistical ranking of which footage best fits the words. Every image a camera captures is stored as a set of numbers describing what it shows, and any description typed into the search box is converted into numbers the same way. A model then compares the two, ranking the nearest footage at the top. Anything that might otherwise influence the rankings—additional filters, thresholds, or instructions fed to Flock’s model—remains out of view on the company’s servers.

A feature called Smart Sort lets the officer approve or reject each image that comes back. A few votes rearrange the ranking, moving footage that resembles the approved images to the top. “Too many results?” a tooltip asks. “Vote on a few results to quickly refine.”

An officer looking for a vehicle picks from menus of colors, body types, makes, models, and features like roof racks and bumper stickers; a person search, by contrast, includes no filtering and accepts only a written description. An example offered by the system: “person wearing scrubs.” Flock calls this plain-language search FreeForm and says it has sold it for years. 404 Media reported in July that officers were using FreeForm to search for people using descriptions of clothing and tattoos.

Standard vehicle search and FreeForm are separate capabilities, Flock says, with standard search running on defined vehicle attributes and FreeForm on natural-language descriptions. On video cameras, the company says, FreeForm searches “clothing, colors, objects, or other case-relevant details.” On license plate cameras, it is limited to vehicles, and person attributes cannot be searched there at all.

The code, which WIRED collected using custom software that gathers files Flock sends to a user’s browser before they log in, sets out which searches officers can run, which controls and warnings they see, and how one result becomes the basis for the next. Out of reach on company servers are any actual search results, camera feeds, or department settings, along with the AI model that answers police prompts.

The code WIRED collected holds Flock’s user interface and shows both the network calls it makes and the answers it expects in return. It shows that departments can, for now, configure the tool for some searches without a reason or a case number linked to a real investigation and can leave off the automated system that flags suspicious use; Flock says the controls will be mandatory by year’s end.

Search activity is recorded in audit logs, Flock says, and required search restrictions apply across its search tools. The company did not say whether anything on its servers would stop a search submitted without a reason or a case number.

Police officers have already used Flock’s software to track people for reasons unrelated to police work. At least 50 officers in the US have recently been charged with or accused of misusing license plate readers, according to The Washington Post. Forty-six of those cases involve Flock. In more than half, the alleged target was a wife, a girlfriend, an ex-partner, an ex-partner’s new boyfriend, or a woman the officer wanted to meet.

Details of how police databases can be abused appear repeatedly in the reports of officer misconduct: A Milwaukee officer searched for a woman he was dating 124 times and her former partner 55 times, and logged each search as an “investigation.” A Georgia police chief ran his ex-girlfriend and her daughter 600 times, was charged, and took his own life five months later. A Kansas chief, who was never charged, ran his ex 164 times and her boyfriend 64 times, and lost his badge. A North Carolina officer ran her boyfriend's ex-wife 31 times and filed 29 of them as traffic infractions.

Police abusing investigative tools is not new. A 2016 Associated Press investigation found officers running database searches on exes and people they found attractive, with police employees at state agencies and dozens of the nation’s largest departments fired, suspended, or forced to resign, more than 325 times from 2013 through 2015. WIRED reported in 2023 that Immigration and Customs Enforcement employees and contractors had been investigated at least 414 times since 2016 for misusing sensitive government databases and found hundreds more allegations against Customs and Border Protection employees this year, among them officers who queried databases to track down women they wanted to date, monitor family members, and follow colleagues’ phones.

Two notification systems in Flock’s software are aimed at human beings. The watch list based on police search queries is one. It runs on an officer’s own written description: They draw a shape on a city map, the alert runs against every camera inside it, and anyone the model decides is a match triggers a notification. The frequency of alerts can be adjusted.

The other, dubbed a People Detection Alert, takes no description at all. Here an officer draws a box inside a single camera's field of view—a doorway, a stretch of pavement—and is notified when a person is inside it. One person is enough to trigger it. The software will not accept an alert set below 75 percent certainty that what the camera is looking at is a person.

Flock described its moderation system in April, saying it was designed to ensure First Amendment protections are “baked in.” The code WIRED reconstructed shows an AI model on Flock's servers scoring an officer’s description of a person against eight categories of sensitive content before it runs against stored footage, then returning one of three verdicts: allow, block, or warn. The model relies on a confidence score to reach that verdict. Because the model runs on Flock’s servers, the department never sees that score. All it gets is a canned warning or block.

Blocked categories of search include race or ethnicity, religion, nationality, “subjective or biased terms,” and “offensive content,” which the code describes as sexual content, innuendo, offensive words and phrases, and slurs. In vehicle mode, the tool blocks any search using person-related terms, including gender, clothing, and behavior.

Religion and nationality are the only two categories written both ways, with wording for a block and wording for a warning that lets the officer proceed. Political, social, and cultural expression is written only as a warning.

Flock tells WIRED that officers cannot run searches using prohibited attributes, including religion and nationality, and that an attempt to search prohibited terms “will be blocked.” Asked what circumstances produce a warning in those two categories instead, the company did not say.

When a T-shirt or a bumper sticker draws a warning because the text includes speech with “constitutional protections,” officers are told the search will be logged and that administrators will be notified. Officers then have to tick an acknowledgment box and leave a comment before they’re free to click Continue With Search Anyway.

Flock says the warning leaves room for legitimate work, offering as an example a victim who describes a suspect in a biker-gang jacket bearing “a certain gang logo or emblem containing a flag or other insignia.” An officer who proceeds is reported to an administrator at their own department for review.

Kate Ruane, who directs the Center for Democracy and Technology's free expression project, has spent years studying how automated moderation systems work. Political, social, and cultural expression is “an incredibly amorphous category,” she says, and one reason an officer’s search might contain language including it is to see who attended a protest. That's already happened. The category worries Flock enough that the system returns a warning, she points out, “but you can still get the results if you just click through.”

“No content moderation done at scale is necessarily accurate,” she says. Analysis of moving video, she says, is harder still, and it goes wrong more often.

The categories that do get blocked can be worked around, Ruane says. The system blocks searches based on religion but not clothing, meaning that in practice an officer could get around the block by searching for the distinctive dress worn by some members of a particular faith. “Lots of people are having their images returned in response to these types of queries that would probably be upset if they knew about it.”

In a search last year, an officer in California typed “American flag.” The search drew a block when aimed at a person, then ran across 11,000 cameras when aimed at vehicles instead.

A warning stops only those officers not already determined to run the search, says Deepak Kumar, an assistant professor of computer science and engineering at UC San Diego. Kumar, who studies trust and safety systems, points to interfaces built to address online harassment, where motivated users sometimes did more harm after being warned, and to browser alerts meant to steer people away from malicious websites, where the effect depends on how warnings are presented.

“This kind of logging can be useful administratively, to see which officers or end users bypass warnings often, but that value depends entirely on whether anyone administrates it,” Kumar says. “It functions less as a deterrent and more as a record.”

Reviewing search terms before a query runs will inevitably catch many attempts at misuse, but in isolation, such safeguards are known to fail without equal scrutiny of what the model sends back. “Best practice examines both inputs and outputs,” Kumar says, “which is why so many AI safety efforts now check both to prevent models from generating harmful outputs.”

Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the ACLU's Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project, agrees that the moderation system addresses a narrow slice of the problem. The filtering, he says, is “a speck on the back of a giant surveillance machine” whose database can be probed by AI for “your-imagination-is-the-limit fishing expeditions.” Nobody outside Flock can say how its statistical models reach those calls.

Like Flock’s other recent reforms, he says, the moderation appears to be aimed at “bad-apple cops” and leaves the structural dangers of mass surveillance untouched.

The searches described so far are run against every person or vehicle Flock’s cameras have seen, back as far as an agency stores footage. Besides a written description, the tool takes a plate or a cropped photograph, returns information about cars present at locations that an officer marks on a map, and infers associations from driving patterns, handing police who enter a plate number the vehicles seen beside it. How far a search reaches depends on the search mode, the agency's permissions, and the agreements it holds with other organizations. A search can run on the agency’s own cameras, on cameras other organizations share, or, for some plate searches, across statewide and nationwide networks.

Flock says much of the responsibility for governing its technology sits with local agencies, which set their own rules for access and use. Don De Lucca, a former Miami Beach, Florida, police chief and past president of the International Association of Chiefs of Police, says that is largely right. Vendors can recommend safeguards, he says, but departments have to set the rules before the technology goes into use. “It has to be tied to some kind of legal reason.”

A police commander who oversees special investigations at a Southern California police department, and who requested anonymity because he’s not authorized to speak, says the possibility of abuse is not unique to Flock or surveillance technology. New technologies routinely create opportunities for both legitimate use and for misuse, he says. The real question is “whether the technology gets implemented with strong guardrails, active oversight, auditability, and consequences for any misuse.”

As scrutiny of Flock intensified this spring, the company announced Audit Assistance, which surfaces patterns that may warrant review. Flock says more than a third of its customers enabled it in August. The code WIRED reviewed shows it currently off by default. It can reportedly flag repeated searches by one officer for the same plate, searches limited to other agencies’ cameras, and for one plate searched under multiple case numbers.

Flock says account lockouts for abnormal activity will arrive alongside it. A South Carolina sheriff's office turned Audit Assistance on earlier this month, and an internal-affairs officer identified more than 2,700 allegedly unauthorized searches the next day.

Smart Toilets Are Already Using AI to Analyze Your Poop

Wired September 03, 2026

It was only a matter of time before wellness trackers—already out there trying to optimize our heart rate, sleep, stress, steps, blood sugar, and menstruation—came for perhaps the most private biosignal of all: our poop.

The global gut health market is expected to reach nearly $106 billion by 2029, and a handful of companies are betting they can use stool data to provide in-depth health insights, nudge people to change their diets or lifestyles, and advise them to see a doctor if their bathroom habits seem amiss. But gastroenterologists are skeptical that products that rely on AI to analyze images of what’s going on in your toilet bowl are worth the price just yet, and data-privacy advocates warn that people can get locked into long-term subscriptions just to access their own health data.

Among the companies touting smart toilets are Kohler Health—an offshoot of the eponymous plumbing giant that sells its device for $449 plus $130 for an annual family membership—and Throne, a startup that raised $10 million in July. Its product is $399 plus $70 for an annual membership.

Both companies’ stool trackers are sleek white devices that clip to the toilet and have cameras facing down into the bowl. (They are adamant that the cameras cannot turn skyward.) When you sit down, the device uses a light sensor to record a video of your deposits, then feeds them into an algorithm that analyzes your urine and stool consistency and color, as well as other metrics. A few minutes later, you get your bathroom-break report card care of an AI-powered app that tracks gut health and hydration scores.

The companies say they are taking a completely different approach from at-home gut microbiome test kits. Those kits, which claim they can use stool samples to identify food sensitivities, provide dietary guidance, and more, come with thin to nonexistent evidence of their efficacy. The new stool trackers aim to identify what's normal for an individual rather than issuing a binary healthy-or-not verdict.

“This is all deeply personal and very individual—digestive patterns are very different,” says Nora Tophof, Kohler Health’s managing director.

Even so, for healthy people with regular bowel movements, stool trackers may not offer much in the way of new insights, says Daniel Freedberg, a gastroenterologist in New York and a spokesperson for the American Gastroenterological Association.

“It kind of seems like overkill,” he says. “If you want to look at your stool, you can just look at it yourself. I don't know that the AI is bringing a lot of new science to this.”

Tophof says that for healthy people, the real value comes from long-term tracking to identify patterns they can act on—for example, if they realize they’re always dehydrated over the weekend or that a particular food or medication tends to upset their stomach.

Scott Hickle, Throne’s cofounder and chief executive officer, says people with inflammatory bowel disease or other digestive conditions can benefit from regular, automated stool monitoring. “Their physicians ask them to track, or keep stool logs … and compliance for that is basically zero,” he says. “No one wants to journal about their poop.”

Throne plans to offer more than helping users track their gut health. Rates of colorectal cancer have risen among younger adults over the past decade, and it is now the leading cause of cancer death among those under 50. Doctors don’t quite know why, but exposure to ultra-processed foods, microplastics, and antibiotics are prime suspects. Screening for colon cancer typically involves a colonoscopy—or a stool-based test that looks for hidden blood in feces.

Hickle says the next generation of Throne’s device will be capable of detecting blood in fecal matter using multispectral imaging that is much more sensitive than the naked eye. Early tests with a prototype are promising, he says, and the updated device could launch within two years. The company has yet to determine a price, but Hickle says Throne's goal is “to make it as accessible as possible so that this can benefit as many people as possible.” He hopes that blood-based data will eventually help detect colorectal cancer, though it’s not clear whether this approach would be as good as testing in medical labs.

“We don't want to be in the business of making diagnoses,” Hickle says. “Looking for those patterns of bleeding over the course of weeks and months should be enough to get someone to at least escalate the conversation they have with their physician.”

Kohler Health says its tracker already alerts users when it detects blood in the toilet. While often harmless—common examples include menstrual blood and hemorrhoids—it can also be a sign of serious health conditions.

“We really want to help people and ultimately save lives,” Tophof says.

Even if the trackers’ blood-detection technology bears out as a clinically meaningful signal, they are still too expensive to be widely used as screening tools for cancer or other health risks, says Gianluca Ianiro, an assistant professor of gastroenterology at the Catholic University of Rome.

“A screening test should be non-invasive but also cheap—and this is not cheap,” Ianiro says.

Would-be buyers should also consider how much personal data they’re willing to give up for what they get out of using the device—especially because “you’re having to pay time and time again in order to access and analyze your own information,” says Lauren Hendry Parsons, a digital rights advocate at the Mozilla Foundation. If customers keep re-upping their subscriptions, “it may feel harder to detach yourself if you've got years and years of data and information about yourself inside that particular service,” she adds.

In addition to the contents of your toilet bowl—and any details you tell the app about your health, such as diet or medication—Throne and Kohler Health both collect the usual litany of personal data, including name and demographics. Kohler Health also tracks your precise location, while Throne does not.

Both companies say they don’t share user health information for targeted advertising purposes, but they can still share this data with law enforcement, another company in a merger or sale, and third-party service providers for things like IT, customer service, and engagement, according to their privacy policies.

Tophof says Kohler Health doesn’t plan to sell users’ health data. Throne also says it will never do so without express permission. Eventually, Hickle wants to share user health data with universities doing gut health research—but people will have to opt in, and refusing will not affect their ability to use the app or device, he says.

Hendry Parsons has advice for privacy-minded buyers: “Be informed. Know what the trade-offs are, know what you're sharing, know what your data is being used for, and weigh that up against the benefit that you are deriving from the product.”

That calculus might be different for someone “suffering from Crohn’s disease, and this is something which will materially improve your day-to-day life,” she says, compared with a “health optimizer who's casually thinking it might be fun to understand the impact of your homemade kombucha.”
